body:
Woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband speaks out as abusers found guilty
- Published
A woman who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband has said she will "never feel completely safe" after four men were found guilty of sexually abusing her, in the first trial of its kind in England.
Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said: "The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."
Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire. He invited men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to the couple's home without her knowledge.
On Thursday, Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.
Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it."
On the steps outside the court, she said: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to."
Joanne Young said the crimes committed against her had resulted in "a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children".
She said: "I live with a pain that is hard to put into words and this is something that will affect our lives forever. It is terrifying that this could happen to anyone.
"What I have been through means I now never feel completely safe and while it can now be hard for me to leave the house, this horrific abuse showed me that home offered no protection either, even though at the time I believed I was safe."
She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".
She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her case had raised "serious questions".
Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.
She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.
The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.
Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.
- 'Silence is not an option' - full statement of wife abused for 13 years 
  - Published6 hours ago
- How Joanne Young was drugged by husband and raped by strangers over 13 years 
  - Published6 hours ago
The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".
One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.
As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.
Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men to have sex with her without her consent.
He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.
James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."
The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.
Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.
- If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.
Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.
Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.
The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.
Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.
They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".
Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.
A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.
"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.
"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

summary: Joanne Young said the actions of her husband over 13 years had "cost me my life as I knew it."
title: Woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband speaks out as abusers found guilty

body:
Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
- Published
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day, with shares closing at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.
The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.
  - Published8 hours ago
summary: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut

Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
- Published
This judgement that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people is historic. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The Rohingyas are getting justice that is long overdue. At least 10,000 were killed when their communities were attacked by Myanmar's security forces and local militias in 2017.
In the huge camps in Bangladesh where more than one million Rohingya refugees have been living since they fled the terrible events of 2017, crowds gathered around screens to watch the President of the ICJ, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, deliver the court's verdict.
He recalled some of the evidence heard by the court since the Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It described acts of mass murder, rape, torture and the destruction of villages, sometimes with Rohingya residents burnt to death inside their homes.
- Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules 
  - Published3 hours ago
The decision by a majority of nine votes to six at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will also have a significant impact on the other genocide cases currently being heard by the court by reasserting and clarifying the standard of evidence needed to prove genocidal intent.
They include South Africa's case that Israel committed genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza in its response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Israel has repeatedly and vehemently denied the allegation.
The court's landmark decision also reinforces those who believe in the rules that were made to regulate the way that power is wielded after World War Two. The 1948 Genocide Convention was a vital part of the structure that was built around the United Nations to stop a repeat of the unfettered brutality, war and genocide in the years before the defeat of the Nazis.
The rules and conventions established after 1945 have been under unprecedented pressure in the era of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. On the day of their summit in China, the ICJ issued a reminder that international law still exists and perhaps can show that the use of force against civilians has consequences.
Lawyers will study the way in which the Gambia proved the crucial point that the state of Myanmar intended to commit genocide.
Proving intent is the biggest challenge in a genocide case at the ICJ. Showing that atrocities occurred is not in itself enough.
The key phrase from the Genocide Convention, adopted by the United Nations after the Nazi Holocaust of European Jewry, defines the crime as "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national ethnical, racial or religious group".
The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.
That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.
In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.
Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.
According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent.
"The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."
In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.
The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.
The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".
The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide.
"If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over.
"But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."
The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.
The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.
That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.
The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".
It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.
Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.
Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.
But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".
Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.
He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.
She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
But whatever the threats coming from the Trump Administration, it is clear that delivering justice to the Rohingya people will refocus attention on Israel's conduct in Gaza, South Africa's case at the ICJ and on the continuing plight of Palestinians in the ruins of Gaza, where more than 1,400 have been killed by Israel since the ceasefire just over a year ago.
It would be wrong, lawyers say, to view the Myanmar case as a dress rehearsal for the case against Israel.
"It risks distracting from the Rohingya, who should appropriately be our focus," according to Janina Dill, from Oxford University.
"Litigation on their plight is not a test case for a conflict that the world has chosen to pay more attention to."
summary: Lawyers will study the way in which Gambia proved the crucial point that Myanmar intended to commit genocide, writes the BBC's international editor.
title: Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications

body:
Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation
- Published
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.
Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.
France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.
It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.
In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.
Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.
The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.
Thousands of fridges taken off-line
The security threat was discovered by ethical hackers at a firm called Omega Systems - it was then verified and expanded upon by experts at Pentest Partners who helped raise the alarm.
The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) and Food Standards Agency (FSA) were then involved in the campaign to plug the security holes.
They held industry conference calls and tasked teams to contact firms at risk.
Thousands of devices controlling tens of thousands of refrigeration devices were taken off the open internet either remotely, or in some cases, physically - with staff ordered to remove internet cables and monitor temperatures manually.
BBC news has learnt most major supermarkets have been forced to divert IT teams to address the risks, with a worker at one large chain saying they took hundreds of devices offline every day over the course of a week.
"It did feel like a race against time as we were expecting another wave of these fridge hacks to come," said the person, who did want to be publicly named.
"From a business perspective it could have been potentially devastating with business interruption and supply chain problems. Our warehouses have millions of pounds worth of food that could have been spoiled if any hackers found out about this method of attack," they added.
There have been three waves of hacks on refrigeration temperature controllers so far this year:
- In August, fridges at a small number of US military bases were impacted
- On 11th and 12th October hundreds of supermarkets and food processing sites in France were hit when Danfoss temperature control systems were targeted
- On the 1st and 2nd of November dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries were hit, with Belgium, Luxembourg the were worst affected. A small number of blood bank sites in France were also impacted
The waves of attacks prompted an expert at Omega Solutions to examine the security of the most popular refrigeration controllers in the UK, made by British firm Resource Data Management (RDM).
RDM disputes the critical nature of the vulnerabilities exposed but has been praised for its professional response to address the concerns, the BBC understands.
As well as supermarkets, multiple other areas of UK food and beverage industry were also warned to take action about the risks.
These include convenience stores, petrol stations, restaurants and fast food chains, sports arenas, hotels, food processing plants and cold storage sites.
"These popular controllers had a similar weak password problem to the Danfoss and other controllers that were attacked so successfully in previous hacks so we had to get the message out as soon as possible and keep it secret," said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners.
"There is so much extra attention on these ubiquitous bits of kit now that it was likely a matter of days until criminals or nation state hackers figured it out," he added.
RDM, though, says comparisons with the units attacked in mainland Europe are not fair because hacking their fridges and freezers would have involved getting hold of a piece of hardware.
The ethical hackers say this would have been achievable as the hardware in question can be purchased cheaply online on sites like eBay.
"This was a vulnerability identified in a test environment," said Ged Evans, CEO of RDM.
He said the test "went beyond" what such exercises usually involved, as it "included, dismantling our hardware".
"In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps," he added.
RDM confirmed that there is no sign of any malicious activity on the controllers and that it continues to work with the NCSC and other authorities to monitor the situation.
Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. Outside the UK? Sign up here.
summary: Supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants and stadiums have been scrambling to make their devices safe.
title: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation

body:
BBC correspondents discuss what Trump, Xi and Putin got out of historic talks
Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have concluded their historic 90 minutes of trilateral talks by issuing a "joint declaration of peace", but what did each leader actually get out of the meeting?
The highly anticipated meeting of three of the world's global superpowers held in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, marked the first time that the three had met together.
The BBC's Russia editor, China correspondent and North America correspondent got together to discuss the outcome of the meeting.
summary: Trump, Putin and Xi have issued a "joint declaration of peace" after historical trilateral talks, but what did they get out of meeting?
title: Watch: What did Trump, Xi and Putin get out of their historic meeting?

body:
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
- Published
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
- Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance 
  - Published6 hours ago
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.
Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.
  - Published6 hours ago
summary: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say

body:
William and Catherine's India tour was 'particularly special', aide says
- Published
The most senior advisor to the Prince of Wales has said this week's visit with the Princess of Wales to India was "particularly special" and described the royal couple "as very much a team".
Prince William and Catherine are now back in the UK after spending three days in Mumbai and Delhi - the first time they have travelled together on overseas royal duties since the princess's cancer treatment.
The visit focused on the prince's Earthshot Prize which were hosted in Mumbai. His wife last attended the Earthshot awards when they were held in Boston in 2022.
"The prince has really enjoyed having the princess alongside him for Earthshot, and for her to see first-hand how much it has grown in scale since she last attended in Boston," Ian Patrick, the prince's private secretary told reporters.
"She's enormously proud of what he's achieved, and it has been particularly special for them to experience this moment together. They are very much a team."
The prince and princess also met the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at his residence in Delhi where they discussed UK-India partnerships.
In a social media post after the meeting, the prime minister said it had been "a pleasure to meet their Royal Highnesses" and praised the Earthshot Prize for "showcasing Indian ingenuity in addressing global environmental challenges".
The meeting was a late addition to the prince and princess's plans. Prime Minister Modi altered his schedule to return to India from a summit in the Philippines to ensure he could meet the royal couple.
"The prince and princess have had a thoroughly enjoyable time in India. They've been incredibly touched by the warmth of the welcome they've received," said Patrick.
The couple were last in India for an official tour in 2016.
"It's been wonderful for them to return together after ten years," the private secretary said. "They were incredibly inspired by the people they met. They leave with very happy memories and a real enthusiasm for building on the connections they've made with the next generation."
There was a focus on young people and their potential during the three day visit. This year, for the first time, there was a Children's Earthshot Awards where 15,000 schools across India took part creating solutions for environmental problems in their own communities.
"We cannot look into the eyes of the next generation and tell them that we knew what was happening, we knew what was at stake, and yet we did not do everything in our power to change it," Prince William said in his speech at the Earthshot Prize Awards Ceremony. "They will not judge us by the promises we made, but by the world we leave behind."
"The prince and princess don't want young people to feel unheard or that the challenges facing the planet and society are beyond their control," said Patrick. "They want them to feel optimistic, empowered and part of the solutions."
The Earthshot Prize was designed as a ten-year project - it is now in its sixth year and Prince William remains ambitious for it.
"Companies including Amazon, IKEA, Nvidia, Standard Chartered and Uber are now stepping forward to help their impact spread even further," said Jason Knauf, the chief executive officer of the Earthshot Prize.
"This is enormously encouraging but the prince wants to see more of the world's biggest businesses and investors get involved... every business and investor who joins us helps these solutions grow faster, building a healthier, happier and more prosperous future for us all."
Now that the prince and princess are travelling together on international duty, the visit was an insight into way their royal trips will operate in future.
The days of royal tours lasting two weeks will not be the approach of the royal couple who think they make a big impact over shorter trips with the additional help of social media to amplify their engagements. They also want to limit the amount of time they spend away from their three children.
"The prince and princess want their overseas travel to have purpose, meaning and impact. It's about building stronger relationships, creating opportunities for collaboration and supporting projects that deliver real results," explained Patrick.
Despite plans to keep future royal tours short, it's believed a visit to Australia could be in the plans for the couple in 2027.
At the Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony on Tuesday, Prince William was heard by reporters saying "Big year next year, Australia!"
Kensington Palace has not yet confirmed any further travel plans for the Waleses.
They last visited Australia in 2014 with nine-month-old Prince George. It is possible that their three children could join them on a future Australia trip.
Additional reporting by Charlotte Scarr in Delhi

summary: Prince William's most senior advisor described the royal couple as "very much a team".
title: William and Catherine's India tour was 'particularly special', aide says

body:
EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10
- Published
Negotiations between the EU and UK are "going down to the wire" ahead of Friday's summit in Brussels, Downing Street has said.
The summit is aimed at reaching new agreements between the two sides on food trade rules, visas for young people and carbon emissions pricing.
Sources have told the BBC the UK is set to agree to a quota of 100,000 young people per year coming to the UK as part of a new youth mobility scheme.
Downing Street has not commented on the details, which would also allow young Britons to live in Europe.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions and debates" of the Brexit referendum.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, she said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but added "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from the deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.
"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal is secured, the government will introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.
Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.
The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in the talks, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
An agreement on trade could also remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
On immigration, Burnham has said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister has said the summit would allow the UK to raise concerns about the Made in Europe scheme, which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subject has divided his cabinet with one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, speaking to The Sun, external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.
He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."

body:
UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide
- Published
After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.
There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews., external
Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.
GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.
Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating, external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".
One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.
The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.
Bugzy Malone’s Grandest Game
It's the game that shocked and thrilled the world: Grand Theft Auto. As a new installment is released in 2026, go deep into the history of the game with rapper Bugzy Malone.
The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".
It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.
"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.
Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.
Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".
About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".
Meanwhile in Germany, Timur told the BBC he was impressed by how lifelike the game was.
"It really feels like a life simulation with the amount of in-game encounters," he said.
The Guardian's Keza MacDonald, external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.
"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.
"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".
Newsbeat's GTA Special
From the memes to the music - from the controversies to the culture - you have your say on GTA 6 with Newsbeat's Jordan Kenny and De-Graft Mensah.
After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.
Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".
The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.
On Monday, 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
A group of Rockstar workers who were sacked by the company have also been protesting outside its offices, ahead of a tribunal which heard they were penalised for discussing working conditions in a private online forum while working on the game.
They claimed they were punished for being part of a workers' union, but Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar, said employees made disparaging comments about the company on a semi-public Discord server and shared confidential information.
Players were able to download the 212GB game ahead of time, in order to be able to play it as soon as it was made available.
Some had even gone to the lengths of buying a whole new console dedicated to the game.
Broadband providers Virgin Media O2, as well as BT and EE, said internet traffic records had been broken in the days leading up to the UK release.
The BBC has heard from people planning to take time off work - as well as a company which has given its employees the day off - in order to dedicate time to the game.
Kieran Youens-Byrne, 34, from Manchester said he was "going on a pilgrimage to Wales" where he would be "completely off grid" for a week.
He added his partner Clare "has been incredibly understanding, although I suspect she's questioning why our romantic getaway revolves around a PlayStation".

body:
Dutch watchdog tells people not to buy AI smart glasses
- Published
The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.
It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.
While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.
The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.
The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.
Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.
It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.
The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.
Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.
Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.
The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.
But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.
Testing results
AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.
During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.
It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.
One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.
The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.
And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.
It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.
Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.
It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.
Controversial tech
In February, reports revealed outsourced workers were able to view sensitive content recorded on Meta smart glasses
Meta said at the time such workers might sometimes review content, including video and images, in order to help improve its AI.
It said it took the protection of people's data very seriously, and was constantly refining its efforts and tools in that area, and would filter it first to blur faces in images.
The AP investigation was not primarily focused on data protection - instead it was concerned with algorithms and AI.
In the UK Paul Arnold, chief executive of privacy watchdog the Information Commission, who has a severe visual impairment has previously stressed the complexity of the argument, external around smart glasses.
"They can help me and others better understand our surroundings, access information and navigate the world with greater confidence," he wrote in September.
But he said he had been "shocked and appalled by some of the irresponsible and harmful ways people are using these technologies".

summary: Tests of glasses showed some misread medicine instructions or pretended to have called an ambulance
title: Dutch watchdog tells people not to buy AI smart glasses

body:
Judge finds Thomas Markle mentally fit to stand trial on child abuse charges
- Published
A judge in Florida has declared Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, to be mentally competent to stand trial for possessing indecent images of children.
The hearing came after an evaluation by a court-appointed psychiatrist conducted on Prince Harry's 82-year-old father-in-law.
Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was ordered to stay in jail pending trial earlier this month after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home that specialises in dementia. His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.
Markle appeared in court in Tampa in a wheelchair, and his lawyers did not dispute the court-appointed psychiatrist's finding that he is mentally competent to understand the nature and consequences of the charge against him.
His next court hearing is scheduled for early December, but any trial is expected to take place in California, where the federal charge was filed.
Inside the storage units in Los Angeles the FBI says agents found about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades.
Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".
He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.
On Monday, police in the Philippines asked prosecutors to charge Markle with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
Last month, police there obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018, and he did not attend her wedding in London that same year.
The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

summary: Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse was deemed competent after an evaluation by a court-appointed psychiatrist.

body:
Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
- Published
Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.
The actress wrote on Instagram, external how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".
"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"
She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."
In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."
Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".
"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.
"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."
The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".
"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."
She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".
"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."
Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, external, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.
"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.
"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."
Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.
In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".
"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."
She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.
"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.
"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."
Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.
'Please be gentle'
Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.
"I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.
The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance.
"I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said.
"But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance.
"I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us.
"It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

  - Published26 April 2025
  - Published28 April 2017
summary: The actress said how stressful" it was with people "talking about you... in ways you can't comprehend".
title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation

body:
Why fibbing about stolen snacks is an important part of childhood
- Published
When drawings appear on the wall or biscuits disappear from the tin, your child might blame the dog or claim there was a ghost - even if they are clutching crayons or covered in crumbs.
Children telling fibs is something most parents experience, but such dishonesty and deception is an important part of mental development.
"It's actually a skill that they're developing and that they will play with in order to get better," clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern tells the CBeebies Parenting Download podcast.
Here, experts explain why learning to lie is a sign of healthy behaviour - and how to help encourage honesty.
Young children aren't quite sophisticated enough to lie, says Redfern, but they are capable of deception before the age of one.
One of the studies mentioned on the podcast comes from the University of Bristol, external, which found that around a quarter of children appear to understand some form of deception by the time they are 10 months old.
Prof Elena Hoicka, who led the study, says it was fascinating to see how "surprisingly young" kids could be so adept and cunning, including her own.
"As a mother of three, I can certainly vouch for how artful and wily they can be.
"Hiding under the table or in the bathroom to eat sweets or chocolate is their common ploy."
Hoicka says that the kind of deception a child uses from the age of two is quite basic - like pretending not to hear their parent or denying they've done something.
CBeebies Parenting Download
Clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern explains why young children may lie and Traitors winner Rachel Duffy discusses how she encourages hers to tell the truth
"It could also extend to doing forbidden activities in secret," she says. "For example, looking in a bag they were told not to look in when no one is apparently watching, or making excuses, such as claiming to need the toilet when asked to tidy up."
By the age of three, they have become much more proficient and creative in their deceptions, showing a deeper understanding of language and how other people's minds work.
She says they also start to withhold information. For instance, truthfully telling their parents that their sibling has hit them but omitting the fact that they hit their sibling first.
These deceptions are a sign of them developing something Redfern calls "theory of mind".
"As children grow up, we want them to learn and develop the skill that they are their own human being with a separate mind and intentions," she explains.
"This is how [they] develop the skills in empathy, or being able to think about another person's thoughts and feelings that might differ from their own."
Another reason a child might lie is self-preservation as they don't want to upset or disappoint their parent.
"All human beings are driven by attachment," says Redfern. "[Children are] driven by being able to preserve that relationship with their caregivers as they depend upon it."
Early on, they learn what brings them closer to their caregiver and what pulls them apart, she says. With this in mind, Redfern thinks you can encourage honesty by creating a safe environment for a child to tell the truth.
"[We] have to think about ways we can help children feel safe enough to tell us the truth [when] they've made a mistake... and they don't want to disappoint us."
This is something Rachel Duffy, who won the latest series of The Traitors, tells the CBeebies Parenting podcast that she has been trying to do.
The mum-of-three recalls one occasion when her eldest son borrowed his brother's bike and broke it after crashing it into a car. Initially, he tried to lie about what happened.
"I said to him, 'You'll not get into big trouble when you tell me the truth.' I just left and gave him a little space.
"And he went, 'Yeah, that was me.' And then he knew that space was safe. We had a conversation - no raised voices, no roaring or shouting."
Redfern says this is a good example of how to deal with such a situation and that there are occasions when a lie, or nuance, might be appropriate - such as when they receive a gift they don't want or describe other people physically.
"My kids delightfully told me recently that I was very wrinkly," she says. "Again, I try to take it with open curiosity."
She does this by talking about why they think she is wrinkly.
"I think just being able to explore as children get older, just having open, curious conversations - it really develops empathy for somebody else's feelings when they've been shown and modelled empathy over and over again."
More stories like this
  - Published12 November
  - Published14 October
summary: Research shows lies and deception can start "surprisingly young" and are not always a bad thing.
title: Why fibbing about stolen snacks is an important part of childhood

body:
Joanne Young was drugged and raped by strangers after her husband offered her online
- Published
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse
When Joanne Young awoke tied to her bed, she had no idea about the horror that had been unfolding while she was unconscious.
After hearing her then-husband Philip Young calling for someone else to "get down", she quickly realised another person was in the bedroom with them.
Unbeknown to Joanne, Young had advertised online for other men to abuse her. He then drugged her and invited a series of strangers into their bedroom to sexually assault her.
This had been going on for 13 years.
On Thursday, four men were convicted of a number of offences including raping and assaulting her. Her ex-husband had already pleaded guilty to a number of rape charges.
Young, a former Conservative councillor, and another man, Dean Hamilton, pleaded guilty to rape and sexual assault at a previous hearing.
The group came from a variety of backgrounds. One of the men worked on Ministry of Defence nuclear defence projects while another drove Red Cross trucks to Romania in the 1980s.
Speaking outside court after the verdicts earlier, Joanne said "silence is not an option if we are serious about preventing abuse" - you can read her statement in full here.
Her case has striking comparisons with the repeated rape of Gisèle Pelicot in France, with experts saying the crime was "deeply abusive".
Online, Young portrayed the abuse as a shared sexual kink known as "cuckolding". The photographs used in the adverts posted on sites like Craigslist and Grindr showed Joanne inanimate and tied to the bed.
James Foster, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Young "would drug her so that he could then sexually abuse her and record that sexual abuse and also arrange for other men to attend the address to sexually abuse her".
One of the men who answered the advert was Dean Hamilton, 46, who admitted to raping Joanne and abusing her in 2015.
The other men who were convicted of sexually assaulting Joanne were Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48 and Mohammed Hassan, 38 - the man Young told to "get down" when Joanne woke.
They told the court they believed they had the consent of both Joanne and Young and were told Joanne was pretending to be asleep - when in fact she was heavily sedated.
"But not once during any of this abuse did they ask Joanne Young what she wanted or show any interest in what her wishes were," Foster said.
The law states the sexual consent can only be given if the person involved "agrees by choice ... and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".
Investigators are told to establish "what steps, if any, the suspect took to obtain the complainant's consent".
Professor Marianne Hester, emeritus professor at the University of Bristol, said Joanne "clearly" had no capacity to say no, adding a "women cannot consent if they are asleep".
"So it's the same if they are completely drugged. They cannot make the decision to agree to sex," she added.
Hester, who has researched gender-based violence for years, said those cases raise broader questions about attitudes towards women and sex.
"We have to question the men, the way men think it's okay to do sex and how they keep normalising, we keep normalising all these very abusive acts within sex and that's really problematic," she said.
Hester added: "We know that investigations have now started on certain websites and that individuals have been identified in a number of different countries who have been up to exactly the same kind of thing.
"So I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline."
The case has also reignited questions about the role of websites used to facilitate abuse.
Lisa Sugiura, Professor of Cyber Crime and Gender at the University of Portsmouth, argued online platforms have a responsibility to address content that normalises violence against women.
"Often these sites are accompanied by image-based abuse and deeply violent language and rhetoric about women anyway," she said.
"You think, how are these forums allowed to act with impunity without oversight and accountability?
"Before we even get to the question of whether we should simply accept the word of a man claiming to speak on behalf of himself and his wife."
Data shows hundreds of similar potential crimes are currently being investigated across the UK.
The National Crime Agency said there was an "urgent need" to deal with the problem as an international issue.
NCA investigators have identified more than 270 individuals linked to one online forum and successor groups.
The CPS describes this type of offending as an emerging challenge for investigators.
"This particular type of offending, where a husband is drugging and abusing his wife and arranging for other men to abuse her, does seem to be a new type of offending," said Foster.
A spokesman for Wiltshire Police explained the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.
He said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.
"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."
Sugiura disagrees the offending itself is new.
She believes technology has made it easier to facilitate and conceal abuse that may have existed for years.
"The use of technology enables anonymity, it enables that division of identity, the protection of the respectable face offline, and these heinous deeds online," she said, adding offenders often operate within wider online communities where misogynistic attitudes are encouraged and abusive material is shared.
"These are not always isolated incidents," she said.
"They can be part of larger networks where people are swapping tips, encouraging one another and sharing material that is deeply abusive towards women."
"I think that there are potentially quite a lot more cases in the pipeline," she added.

body:
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
- Published
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and it appears that he left with little in return.
In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as an historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.
- Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting 
  - Published6 hours ago
- This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls 
  - Published19 hours ago
In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" – as evidence that the trip already was a success.
That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.
So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.
While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.
On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.
For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique, released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".
That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric.
"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.
A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire.
If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.
While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.
But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism.
"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday.
"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."
Democrats, for their part, did not mince words.
"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.
Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.
In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.
Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.
Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.
