  - Published15 hours ago
summary: The visuals of the historic trilateral meeting may be the only lasting impression left by the summit.
title: Anthony Zurcher: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance

body:
The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
- Published
"Stop Me If You Think You've Heard This One Before" sang Morrissey, as part of The Smiths in 1987, shortly before the band's acrimonious divorce.
It's a lyric Brexit veterans might be humming to themselves this week. Maybe even the prime minister, who is an avid fan of the Manchester band.
Some of the names - and arguments - that defined the Brexit period inside and outside Parliament are starting to emerge again, as the debate about the UK's relationship with the EU returns.
"It's like déjà vu with knobs on," said one veteran of the Leave campaign to us.
A new group called Stay Out has been set up, backed by figures who were part of the official Leave campaign in 2016. Boris Johnson has been back in the headlines, saying he still thinks Britons would choose to be outside the bloc.
Pro-EU groups such as the European Movement are raising their voices, pointing to the range of politicians, diplomats and academics they have supporting their argument. And a steady stream of Labour figures are now emerging to say they want to rejoin.
The former Deputy Prime Minister David Lammy made the argument on the BBC on Wednesday, saying Labour should go into the next election backing renegotiating membership of the EU and then putting that to people in another referendum.
He joins a list of cabinet ministers under Sir Keir Starmer who want to revisit EU membership; a list that includes former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, former Business Secretary Peter Kyle and former Welsh Secretary Jo Stevens. Others who served around Sir Keir's cabinet table think the same privately.
That is significant. Yes, they all backed Remain in 2016. But these are figures who were part of a government elected on a manifesto saying it was important to make Brexit work.
They set red lines in that manifesto because they thought the public had moved on. But they have now decided to say - most of them very publicly - that they think the picture has changed and the UK needs to think again.
The prime minister has opened the door to all options, from single market membership to rejoining the customs union to a referendum on full membership.
But in recent days, his language has softened a little from the clear commitment in his party conference speech that around the time of this Friday's summit he would "lay out to the country" the different options for Britain's long-term relationship with Brussels.
After some confusion about when this would take place, the government now says this will happen around the time that Burnham presents his 10-year plan, right before Parliament's Christmas break.
Burnham's allies say this will allow him to tie his EU policy more closely to his domestic agenda, arguing that a different arrangement with Europe would help with his other priorities such as the cost of living and re-industrialisation.
Others worry that the all-consuming nature of the EU debate means that it will drown out the other parts of the 10-year plan.
What remains unclear is the timeframe for the process that will follow Burnham setting out what he sees as the different Brexit options.
The prime minister has always been clear that Labour's commitments in its 2024 manifesto not to rejoin the single market or the customs union - let alone the EU altogether - still stand until the next general election.
And it was to those manifesto red lines that Burnham returned when asked about rejoining the EU at PMQs on Wednesday.
Yet those would not preclude Burnham initiating negotiations now on an arrangement breaking those red lines, which would take effect after the next general election.
Nevertheless, some on the prime minister's own side ponder that - having turned the volume up on the whole issue this autumn - he might be wise to turn it down a little in the new year, so it doesn't risk drowning out other things ministers want to talk about.
Andy Burnham is a prime minister who likes to explore things out loud. It's part of what he sees as a new way of doing politics, where he answers questions honestly and is prepared to discuss ideas while they are being formed, not just after they are a settled position.
It is a style that seeks to present a sense of a desired direction, even if some of the specifics end up being walked back from.
But even though it might be some time before the government has an official position on the future relationship, plenty of people are discussing what might happen next.
"It is all go again! My inbox is full of the same old stuff I thought I'd seen the back of years ago," one senior figure told us.
There are some nerves in the Labour Party about what might happen next. MPs who we have spoken to hold a range of views, which shows why this won't be plain-sailing.
Some are worried about re-opening the debate, calling it "toxic".
Others worry that the prime minister could disappoint pro-EU voters if he doesn't go far enough.
Others still wonder if the argument has changed enough that voters would decide differently in a new referendum.
"Both sides need fresh arguments, not the ones we all got tired of last time," said one.
"If this just looks like politicians wanting to rejoin because they never got over leaving then it's dead on arrival.
"If we can show that actually this is being led by businesses, by farmers, by different parts of society who need to rejoin because of the ways Brexit has harmed them, then it's a different matter," said another.
And what would the new EU the UK could rejoin look like?
Some Labour MPs ponder that the EU is changing – with the possibility of more right-wing leaders at the top table. They question whether they would want to be part of that.
- EU-UK talks going down to the wire, says No 10 
  - Published1 hour ago
- Burnham to set out options next month for long-term EU relationship 
  - Published2 days ago
- The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left 
  - Published1 day ago
- UK lost more than it gained from Brexit, Burnham says ahead of EU summit 
  - Published3 days ago
A long standing diplomat from an EU member state said that the possibility of political change within the EU, alongside the recent offer of associate membership to Canada and at least the possibility of a potential future arrangement with Ukraine after any peace deal, could mean Brussels becomes more open to looser forms of membership that it has not been willing to consider before.
But then there is Scotland. If the government backs another EU vote, some Scottish MPs worry it adds to the argument for another vote on Scottish independence.
Despite the warnings, plenty of MPs are delighted that the Europe debate is back on the agenda.
One summed it up like this: "It doesn't really matter to me at this point where the PM is heading on this – it's all good for appealing to progressive voters. Just being seen to talk about this even without it necessarily being clear what we're going to do is a big change from before."
That seems to be a prevailing mood at the moment. Lots of Labour MPs are happy the EU debate is back. But not all of them.
Andy Burnham will on Friday sign a new deal with the EU which ministers believe will drive economic growth and cut red tape for British businesses. It will be heralded as a new moment for the relationship.
But how much further could the reset go?
The government hasn't decided yet - but plenty of others have their own views.
- New campaign against EU membership launches ahead of UK-EU summit 
  - Published6 days ago
- Brexit referendum 'possible' in Labour election manifesto, says Burnham 
  - Published30 September
Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.
summary: Many of the names and arguments that defined the Brexit period are emerging again, as the debate over the UK being part of the EU is back on the agenda.
title: The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next

The comedian and author Bob Mortimer returns to his hometown to discuss his new novel 'Michael', in front of a full house at Middlesbrough Town Hall.

England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain
- Published
England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.
European football's governing body have fined the Football Association £12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.
BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.
A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.
There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.
Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.
That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.
"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."
England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

summary: England are punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.
title: England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain

body:
Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs
- Published
US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.
The Alabama-born singer was named entertainer of the year at Wednesday's ceremony, weeks after the song became the longest-running number one in Billboard chart history.
"At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."
Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving."
Langley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.
She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.
Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.
Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means.
"Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry.
"This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."
Taylor Swift also performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.
Her performance began with Swift walking backstage and featured cameo appearances from country stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, and Brooks & Dunn.
Swift then sang her recent hit I Knew It, I Knew You, from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, using a blue guitar with bedazzled clouds on it, in a nod to the animated franchise.
The singer also mixed in some of her 2006 country hit Our Song, while Keith Urban joined her on the banjo.
Swift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year.
Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.
Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.
The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.
Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.

  - Published10 October
  - Published29 September
summary: Langley won six awards, weeks after her hit Choosin' Texas broke a Billboard chart record in the US.
title: Ella Langley sweeps Country Music Awards as Taylor Swift performs

body:
Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme
- Published
More than 90% of homes fitted with faulty insulation under energy-saving government schemes have not yet had repairs completed to fix the botched work, a minister has said.
The government found almost all homes that had external wall insulation installed as part of two of the government's ECO schemes had defects that needed repairing.
Speaking to a committee of MPs on Wednesday, Energy Minister Martin McClusky said repair works had been completed at 2,227 out of the 24,600 homes impacted.
He said he was shocked by the extent of the failures and has assured affected households they would not be asked to pay to sort out these problems.
McClusky told MPs the insulation schemes "didn't have correct oversight".
Ofgem oversees the ECO schemes and alongside TrustMark, a government-backed consumer protection service, is responsible for auditing homes to identify faulty installations.
The government and its partners have known about significant levels of defective and unsafe insulation for years, with audits finding poor work in October 2024.
Ken Palfrey, a 66-year-old retired builder from Birmingham, is among the home owners waiting for repairs.
He had external wall insulation installed through the ECO programme in 2024.
He claims the installation was "botched", causing damage to his window sills and leading to damp and mould on his walls.
He said he complained and after some months an inspection concluded the insulation had been fitted incorrectly and he was told it had to be removed immediately.
Palfrey said for two years he had been on a "merry-go-round", spending "hundreds and hundreds of hours writing emails and complaining to people".
Earlier this month, TrustMark referred his case to the National Energy Foundation (NEF), a charity that has funding from energy suppliers to put right damaged homes where the installer has gone out of business.
"It's been an absolute nightmare," Palfrey said.
"Every day of my life, every time you look at the insulation, you're worried about it."
A TrustMark spokesperson said it was working to contact affected households and to fix "the unacceptable problems left by this faulty external wall insulation scheme".
"We're sorry for what Mr Palfrey has been through and have referred him to the National Energy Foundation which should be able to get his insulation put right," the spokesperson said.
'Failures in the system'
Labour MP Bill Esterson, the chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, told the BBC he was seeking assurances that the victims "will be supported in a timely fashion".
But he said he was concerned that Ofgem, Great Britain's energy regulator, had "failed to identify whether work had been carried out or completed to a decent standard".
When asked if he had confidence in Ofgem at the committee, McClusky did not answer the question directly.
He said: "There's clearly been failures in the system. We're designing a system now."
He added Ofgem was a "very different organisation than it was a number of years ago".
A spokesperson for Ofgem said: "It is unacceptable that households have been left with substandard ECO4 work. Ofgem was not responsible for assuring the quality of installations."
The spokesperson said the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) "is responsible for the design and overall outcomes of ECO, and that Ofgem's role did not include assessing installation quality".
"Our role, set by government, is to administer the scheme and hold suppliers to account for meeting their obligations," the Ofgem spokesperson added.
"When serious quality problems emerged, we went beyond our core role to support affected households and help establish the scale of the problem."
The BBC has asked TrustMark for comment.
The two ECO schemes that have caused widespread issues are known as ECO4 and Great British Insulation Scheme (GBIS).
ECO4 was launched in 2022 and since then, more than 300,000 homes have had heat pumps, solar panels and insulation fitted under the £4bn scheme. It is closing in December.
GBIS - which opened in 2023 and has now closed - was more narrowly designed to help households lower their energy bills by installing cheap insulation.
The BBC has been reporting on the impact of faulty insulation installed under these schemes in recent years.
Fuel Poverty Action, a campaign group, argues that problems with faulty upgrades under a range of government energy efficiency schemes could be affecting as many as 100,000 homes.
"Ignoring the other defective measures is shockingly negligent, and is causing huge harm," said Jonathan Bean, policy lead at Fuel Poverty Action.
"Defective internal wall insulation causes major hidden damage, making it a ticking time bomb in homes.
"The government estimates that 29% of it is defective but chose not to include it in the Find and Fix process."
A spokesperson for DESNZ said: "We inherited the failing ECO4 scheme, which we ended after it clearly let families down.
"No household should have to pay to put the issues right and TrustMark is working to support those affected to ensure this is the case.
"Our Warm Homes Plan will overhaul the system to protect consumers and ensure failings are not repeated."
  - Published14 October 2025
  - Published23 January
summary: People who signed up to a government insulation scheme have been struggling to get their damaged homes repaired.
title: Faults not fixed in 90% of homes in government insulation scheme

body:
Cleverly to run as Tory London mayor candidate
- Published
Former home secretary and foreign secretary Sir James Cleverly has been selected as the Conservative candidate for mayor of London.
The MP for Braintree in Essex was chosen in a poll of party members in London, winning 86% of the vote.
Sir James saw off a challenge from Westminster City councillor Festus Akinbusoye and Richmond Park parliamentary candidate Sara Gezdari.
He said London's "best days are ahead if we make a change at the forthcoming election". The next mayoral election will be in May 2028.
'It's shameful'
Labour incumbent Lord Khan, first elected in 2016, is yet to confirm whether he will seek a fourth term.
Sir James, a former head of the London Fire Authority, was widely expected to win the nomination after he stood down from the shadow cabinet in August.
He said he would not seek re-selection as the candidate in his Essex seat at the next general election.
At the announcement of the result, he said Lord Khan was "letting London down".
Sir James added: "People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place - businesses, job creators, families leaving London - and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related.
"The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. When I ask Londoners, 'Do you feel safe walking home at night?', the answer is no."
"It's shameful, it's a failure, and it's not just crime.
"We have had the worst period of housebuilding since the Second World War and only the highest-earning Londoners can afford the cheapest houses in London."
'Crime went up'
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the Labour Party, said: "James Cleverly has a record of failure and now wants to inflict his disastrous CV on London.
"He backed a no-deal Brexit and Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget, voted for cuts to policing and youth services and opposed action to clean up London's air.
"Londoners should never forgive and never forget the damage the Conservatives did to our capital."
Sir James, an Army reservist, represented the Tories on the London Assembly before his election as MP for Braintree in 2015.
After rising through the backbenches, he unsuccessfully ran for Conservative Party leader in 2024, losing out to Kemi Badenoch.
The only other confirmed party choice for the mayoral race is Laila Cunningham from Reform UK, whose candidacy was announced in January.
She told BBC London: "It's the Conservatives that cut police, they cut the magistrates' numbers, crime went up, they politicised stop and search, and as a result knife crime has gone up massively."
'Take London backwards'
Sarah Olney and Rob Blackie are both candidates for the Liberal Democrats' nomination.
Olney, the MP for Richmond Park, told BBC London the city "really needs a champion but the Tories are not going to be able to effectively hold Labour to account given their record in the capital".
She added: "James Cleverley simply is not a credible contender for mayor of London.
"In the past decade he has enthusiastically championed Brexit and he was a huge supporter of Liz Truss's mini budget and both of those things have done so much damage to London."
Should Lord Khan decide not to run again, there are a number of London Labour figures with ambitions to be the next mayor, including MPs Dawn Butler and Rosena Allin-Khan.
The Green Party, which won outright control of three London boroughs at the local elections in May, leads minority administrations in Haringey and Lambeth, and runs Southwark in coalition with the Lib Dems, has yet to begin the process of picking a candidate for the 2028 mayoral race.
Mayor of Hackney Zoë Garbett, who was the Green candidate in the 2024 mayoral election, said Sir James would "take London backwards".
She added: "Cleverly's platform is all about dividing our communities and making people's lives harder and more expensive."

title: Cleverly to run as Tory London mayor candidate

body:
Fiona Harvey to appear at Crown Court on harassment charge
- Published
A woman who allegedly inspired the stalker character Martha in the hit Netflix drama Baby Reindeer is to appear at Harrow Crown Court on charges of racially aggravated harassment without violence.
Fiona Harvey, 61, is accused of sending several emails and three voicemails including antisemitic material to lawyer Mark Lewis, between 4 September and 9 October 2025.
During a hearing at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday, the court heard that Lewis initially believed Harvey was a potential client.
Harvey of Camden, north London, did not indicate a plea, but elected for a Crown Court trial.
The charge is an either-way offence, which means it can be heard in either a magistrates' court or Crown Court.
She will next appear at Harrow Crown Court for a pre-trial preparation hearing on 17 December.
Harvey has previously identified herself as the woman on whom Martha is based, after the release of Richard Gadd's Emmy Award-winning series in 2024.
She is suing the streamer £128m for defamation, negligence and privacy violations, arguing that that Netflix told "brutal lies" about her to over 50 million viewers around the world.
Netflix denies the claim, which will be heard in front of a jury on May 18, 2027, at the US District Court for the Central District of California.

body:
Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
- Published
Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
Here's what you need to know.
UK blind to how quickly Covid was spreading
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
Once established, it was effective.
But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.
It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.
But it didn't need to be like that
Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.
The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
Many self-isolating 'felt forgotten'
When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.
Flights and borders - the mistakes
Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.
The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".
Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."
By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.
By contrast, the UK government only requested travellers arriving from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days. The UK government implemented no further border control measures until June 2020.
The report says that border controls were a "critical gap in the UK's ability to limit the spread of the virus" and recommends that in the future "international border control measures should be in place at the earliest stages of a pandemic".
Smart phones and the 'pingdemic'
The inquiry report is more positive about the use of smartphone apps, saying digital tools can have a "significant impact on reducing the spread of infection".
It quotes a mathematical modelling study from the US which estimates that, when 75% of people used a contact tracing app in the pandemic, infections were reduced by at least 50%.
Three different apps were developed during Covid - one for England and Wales, another for Scotland and a third for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.
The inquiry says that took up "valuable time", and it recommends developing a UK-wide digital tool to use in any future outbreak.
It says it is "fundamentally important" that apps and digital tools are as accurate as possible – and people have confidence in them.
In the summer of 2021, as Covid restrictions were relaxed, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, something dubbed by the press as the "pingdemic".
It quotes Treasury estimates suggesting that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.
Get in touch
Are you affected by the issues raised in this story?
summary: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail", the public inquiry has found. Here's what you need to know.
title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'

body:
Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd
- Published
"We have to find a way to create the best habits and culture that makes us close to winning every single game."
Mauricio Pochettino has used his first interview as Manchester United head coach to outline his vision for the club.
The former Tottenham, Paris St-Germain and Chelsea boss wasted no time getting across the Atlantic Ocean after completing his stint in charge of the United States on Tuesday.
He met key staff on Wednesday, took training for the first time on Thursday and conducts his first wider media conference at United's Carrington training ground on Friday.
The 54-year-old is facing a packed schedule, starting with a trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday.
Pochettino accepted a big challenge. United are 18th in the table. By 17:00 GMT on Saturday, they could be bottom.
So, what are the Argentine's priorities as he begins the task of trying to transform United's season?
There is a clear non-negotiable.
"To create the culture is the most important [thing]," he told United's in-house media in a 15-minute introductory chat.
- Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator 
  - Published5 hours ago
- Manchester won't always be blue - Pochettino 
  - Published1 day ago
'Making the players feel like winners again'
It would be easy to point to areas of the pitch where United have been deficient this season. However, it cannot be totally dismissed that virtually the same group of players were transformed over the second half of last season by the recently sacked Michael Carrick, who guided them to third in the Premier League and Champions League qualification.
Remarkably, Pochettino has won twice as many matches in charge of the USA this season than the three victories United have managed, with a 100% record from six games.
United, by contrast, have not won in the Premier League since August, while two of their three victories have required the Red Devils to come from behind. Their single clean sheet came against Azerbaijan outfit Sabah FK in the Champions League in September.
One of the most immediate tasks for Pochettino will be to alter the mindset of players who seem to have become restricted by the pressure they have found themselves subjected to.
"It is a mistake to see the situation," he said. "We need to see the potential of this club.
"We need to understand it is a game, and to connect with the game we need to feel free. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is our priority now; to work with them and take the pressure.
"Pressure needs to bring energy. Responsibility needs to bring energy because if not, it is too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back."
Fixing a leaky defence
That said, there are some glaring issues that Carrick was unable to fix and Pochettino must find an answer to. The most obvious is defence.
Who should the cornerstones of United's defence be?
The Carrick regime felt Leny Yoro was the player with the attributes - pace, strength and control - most suited to their needs. Yet, at 21, Yoro is prone to mistakes and he has also been needed at right-back because regular right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui have, at times, been required on the left.
Lisandro Martinez and Matthijs de Ligt have not been reliable fitness wise. Pochettino knows the baggage attached to Martinez, given his post-match criticisms of the club hierarchy after the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid, and the knowledge his fellow countryman's contract expires in the summer.
Harry Maguire has started all 10 league games this season but suffered a back spasm in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, immediately before the international break, and had to be replaced at half-time. Maguire has many attributes, but his presence does restrict the ability to press high up the field.
Ayden Heaven has made eight appearances in all competitions but has previously been regarded as being behind Yoro in terms of his overall development.
Then there is Dalot.
The 27-year-old was consoled by Joshua Zirkzee when he was replaced against Villa, such was the negative fan reaction to his performance, which included conceding a penalty at the start of the second-half.
It can justifiably be argued if Dalot has the talent to match the 260 club appearances he has now made.
However, for his faults, coaches love his attitude.
Dalot has been described to BBC Sport as having one of the most committed and professional approaches to the game, that he is someone willing to take responsibility, happy to play in unfamiliar positions if it benefits the team, the first to offer support to team-mates, and a positive influence in the dressing room.
Solving the Fernandes issue
Bruno Fernandes' alarming drop off in form has been one of the most noticeable features of the current campaign.
The Portugal playmaker has been a shadow of the star who scooped all the player of the year awards last season and broke the Premier League assist record.
He was axed for the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth after criticising Carrick's tactics in the 4-1 Champions League humiliation by Como and seems to be affected by concerns around his future - his contract also expires in the summer, although United are almost certain to trigger their one-year option on the 32-year-old - and the summer arrival of Youri Tielemans.
For the short term at least, Pochettino must decide whether to pick Fernandes in his favoured number 10 role and work around that, or drop him deeper, as Ruben Amorim did, or play him wide, which has not brought the best out of him.
What else? Can any youngsters step up?
Fernandes' status affects other areas. Carrick never seemed convinced by Andrey Santos, a £50m summer arrival from Chelsea. But with £70m Carlos Baleba out for an extended period, a partner needs to be found in midfield for Kobbie Mainoo.
Tielemans did not seem to have the running ability for the role, and Amorim wouldn't pick Mainoo with Fernandes.
Further forward, with Benjamin Sesko out, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo have tended to be used in the number nine role. But Cunha likes to drop deep, while, after a bright start to the season, Mbeumo has scored twice in his past 12 appearances.
Neither Shea Lacey nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Both caught the eye on England Under-20 duty during the international break. Pochettino has history for giving young players a chance and the pair could benefit from that.
A united club?
There is one issue Pochettino mentioned in his interview he will soon discover requires delicate handling.
United's match-going fans have stood by every manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired. There is no reason to think that will change now.
However, their relationship with the club's ownership is fractured, possibly beyond repair. Fresh accounts to 30 September show the club's overall debt remains more than £1.1bn and a further £14.5m was spent on finance costs in the previous quarter.
This fuels discontent in the stands, already heightened because of various ticketing measures, none of which are viewed by most supporters as being positive.
"We need to be united," said Pochettino.
"Chemistry is really important, chemistry between us and the staff and the fans and the players, the directors, the owners and everything."

summary: Culture, defence and Bruno Fernandes - the key issues facing Mauricio Pochettino as he takes over as Manchester United boss.
title: Culture, defence, Fernandes - Pochettino's priorities at Man Utd

body:
Pochettino's first Man Utd training session filmed by drone operator
- Published
Manchester United fans have been given a unique and unexpected insight into Mauricio Pochettino's first training session after footage was captured by a drone flown next to the club's Carrington training ground.
Twelve minutes of the session was filmed by a drone operator and uploaded onto YouTube.
Pochettino and his players, who were split into three groups, are clearly visible, with the session filmed from a variety of angles and distances.
"For the people asking about legality. It is unrestricted airspace, meaning anyone can fly over it," said the drone operator.
"The drone remained in line of sight at all times, it didn't fly over anyone or even near anyone so was a perfectly legal flight going by the CAA rules that regulates drone usage.
"The drone is correctly labelled, and I hold all the relevant licences, public liability and insurance required. As for leaking team news/tactics, it was half an hour into the managers first training session, there are many media there so certainly won't be the only footage of training released."
The session was also filmed by United's own media channel, who regularly film club training sessions.
Civil Aviation Authority guidelines include the following warning: "If you use these devices where people can expect privacy, such as inside their home or garden, you're likely to be breaking data protection laws."
Manchester United have declined to comment.
Did we learn anything?
There were 10 outfield players working with Pochettino, although it seems unlikely it will be the starting line-up for Sunday's trip to Liverpool.
While Harry Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo are regular starters, Ayden Heaven and Andrey Santos have had less involvement, and neither Joshua Zirkzee nor Harry Amass have started a Premier League game this season. Jaume Camacho 17, who is yet to feature at senior level, was also with the group.
On an adjoining pitch, skipper Bruno Fernandes is shown in one group playing the 'rondos' game, where two players are in the middle trying to intercept the passes of the five players in a circle on the outside. Youngster Shea Lacey and last season's FA Youth Cup-winning skipper Dan Armer are also involved, along with England youth international Bendito Mantato.
Next to that is another group which includes more experienced players in Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount, Leny Yoro, Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot.
The identical twins Jack and Tyler Fletcher are split between the two groups, with Pochettino's assistant Jesus Perez across both.
Not all the players were identifiable and United confirmed defender Patrick Dorgu was involved.

body:
Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level
- Published
It is only 18 months since Arsenal tasted European glory, but they are not a team on many people's list of favourites for this season's Women's Champions League.
That is because not only have the Gunners disappointed across their opening 15 matches of the season, but also the elite teams in Europe seem to have gone up another level.
In the space of seven days, Arsenal have witnessed first hand what it takes to reach those heights - and the gap they must bridge.
Last week, they were resilient at Barcelona to earn a very respectable 1-1 draw, but were fortunate the Spanish side were not clinical with their chances at Camp Nou.
On Thursday night, they were outplayed at home in losing 2-0 to an excellent Lyon side, who look on course to match or better their runner-up finish from last season.
One point from such games could be pleasing - but that only shows the work Arsenal need to do to be considered one of the top teams in Europe.
Lyon superior in every department
Arsenal came into Thursday's defeat by Lyon off the back of a fifth successive Women's Super League draw at Emirates Stadium against London City Lionesses.
In contrast, Lyon have been flying domestically, winning all nine of their matches, scoring 49 goals, and then not conceding any in their unbeaten Champions League run.
Such form sets the pace and it was clear at Meadow Park that they were superior to Arsenal in every department.
Vibrant Germany international Jule Brand gave them the lead midway through the first half and Melchie Dumornay sealed the win with a powerful strike in the 57th minute.
Arsenal defender Leah Williamson said the "better team won the game" and manager Renee Slegers highlighted the difference in physicality between the teams.
"Compared to last year when we played Lyon [in the semi-finals], they are even better now. They have standout individual quality," Slegers said.
"They dominated in the first half. We had solutions for the second half and had more presence. We wore them down better but it still didn't lead to open chances."
Lyon had a 3.33 expected goals ratio on Thursday, serving up 23 shots to Arsenal's seven. They created six big chances and 14 of their shots were inside the box.
Dumornay oozed quality, midfielder Lily Yohannes showed composure and Brand was very impressive both defensively and going forward for Lyon, deployed in a new position.
Those individuals have benefitted from the expertise of former Barcelona manager Jonatan Giraldez, who joined in June 2025 - the month after Arsenal won the Champions League - and has now had the time he needed to impose his style.
As a result, Lyon have gone up another level and the gap between these two teams has widened by Arsenal's drop-off this season.
Slegers also said Arsenal had "prepared all we could" for the intensity that Lyon brought in London - but it still did not have an impact.
Asked how far off Lyon they currently are, Slegers said: "It's 2-0 today and they are better than us but it doesn't mean if we were to play them again soon, this season, that it would be the same game again.
"We saw moments where we did well and we know from the last couple of years we can hurt Lyon.
"But for today, their pace and physicality helped them get too much dominance in the game and that is one of their strengths. Then it became hard for us."
Williamson 'aware of where the gaps are'
Williamson said Arsenal "know what they need to do to be better" and that they are aware of "where the gaps are" to Europe's elite.
They are already 12 points off the pace in the Women's Super League title race and are unlikely to qualify automatically for the Champions League quarter-finals.
"The level rises year on year. Everybody cops goals - we have to try not to and we have to create," said Williamson following the defeat by Lyon.
"We're all focused and we're all together. That's the most comforting thing for me - but this has been a tough period."
It has not all been bad despite disappointing results - and context is important.
Over a gruelling seven days, they have faced European holders Barcelona, WSL high-flyers London City Lionesses and record Champions League winners Lyon.
They showed grit and resilience out in Barcelona last week - traits that have not been on show enough for Arsenal this season, but are clearly there.
Players like Williamson, striker Alessia Russo and summer signings Georgia Stanway and Ona Batlle know what it takes to compete at the highest level.
Arsenal invested in the summer transfer window and brought in proven, experienced players, but that has not translated into results - yet.
Giraldez said time with his players has helped improve Lyon and perhaps that is what Arsenal need - patience.
"I think they are changing now. They made a good game against Barcelona and it's very difficult to go there and get a point," said Giraldez.
"The game against London City was much better. It's not just about them, but also about us. Now we have improved and play better football than last year.
"I think it is a matter of time [for Arsenal]. They have a good coach and good players. In general, they have all the ingredients to have a good season."
summary: In a difficult defeat by French giants Lyon, Arsenal were shown the gap they need to bridge to challenge for the Champions League.
title: Arsenal 'have ingredients' but Europe's elite on another level

body:
Unseeded Sykes stuns Humphries in Grand Slam thriller
- Published
Luke Humphries followed Luke Littler in exiting the Grand Slam of Darts after losing 10-9 to unseeded Tom Sykes in a second-round thriller.
Having trailed 4-0 and 9-7, the second seed battled back to force a deciding leg and had the advantage of throwing first.
But his fellow Englishman Sykes was unfazed, quickly took control of the leg and when Humphries missed double 10 for a 128 checkout to snatch victory, the world number 81 nervelessly hit double 18 to secure a place in his first major quarter-final.
"It's unbelievable," Sykes, 34, told Sky Sports. "Luke let me off a few times in the first bit but I set off really well.
"When he got it back to 5-5, I thought 'here we go' and he started turning it on in the last 10 legs, but I'm just buzzing to get over the line.
"I was a bit nervous [going for double 18 for the match]. I thought the game was over when I saw Luke hit the the first treble 18, then the second.
"But I was so cold on that last one, I thought 'just hit it first dart, no messing about' and I did. I'm riding a wave at the minute and I'll keep trying to ride it."
Sykes' victory was all the more impressive given Humphries did not play badly at all, averaging 102.02 and hitting 37% on the doubles.
But the Castleford thrower made a flying start, averaging just shy of 108 in the first mini-session, to earn a sizeable lead and maintained his composure as the former world champion fought back.
He will face three-time Grand Slam champion Michael van Gerwen in the last eight after the Dutchman beat seventh seed James Wade 10-8.
In a high-class contest that saw six 100-plus finishes, Wade earned a 7-5 lead but Van Gerwen, who finished with an average of 103.83, took out 121 to level at 7-7.
He broke again to go 9-7 up and although Wade hit a 130 checkout to break back, 10th seed Van Gerwen made it three breaks in a row to avoid a one-leg shootout.
With Humphries and Littler gone, third seed Gian van Veen is the top-ranked player remaining in the draw in Wolverhampton.
The Dutchman beat Germany's Martin Schindler 10-7 and was completely dominant before a slight wobble as he tried to close out the win.
Van Veen raced into a 9-3 lead but then proceeded to lose four legs on the spin, missing three match darts, before eventually finishing the job.
England's Nathan Aspinall awaits last year's World Championship finalist in the quarters after a 10-7 win over German Gabriel Clemens.
'The Asp' averaged 100.72 and posted an impressive 53% checkout rate as he came out on top in a back-and-forth match.

body:
Cummins' Australia captaincy at a crossroads - Agnew
- Published
Australia captain Pat Cummins, much like his fellow bowlers, is in the eye of the sandpapergate storm at the moment.
The reason is simple to me. The very notion that Cameron Bancroft - the most inexperienced batsman in the Australia team at the time – would use sandpaper on the ball against South Africa without the bowlers knowing has never made sense.
It has never seemed remotely plausible to me, as a former bowler, that the bowlers didn't know what was happening in Cape Town in 2018. It just doesn't seem possible.
Therefore, this day of reckoning was always going to come.
Let's be clear - as long as there has been cricket, there has been ball-tampering. There is no point hiding from the fact.
Back in the day it was about shining the ball, maybe using something like a sweet to get a sheen on one side.
Reverse swing was a ball-tampering game-changer. There was a requirement for a wearing process, roughing up and drying the ball.
But, to get one thing straight, whether a ball is being tampered with or not, it belongs to the bowlers. It is the bowling attack's weapon. As much as a bowler would not fiddle with a batsman's bat – sanding an edge or changing the grip - a batsman would not work on the ball without the knowledge of a bowler.
Some might wonder why revelations relating to the sandpaper controversy have not come to light before.
In response to that, I would say it would have been very difficult for a player in the Australia team to go public at the time. They would have been worried about their own futures, their careers.
Only when a player has retired, or believe their time as an international cricketer has come to an end, do they feel more comfortable to speak up.
I have also seen suggestions that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner have had their guilt diminished by what has emerged in recent days, that they took bullets for their team-mates.
Smith was captain and should have been in control of his team. Warner cooked up the sandpaper idea. Bancroft executed it. If they did take bullets, they were bullets they deserved.
Now, the spotlight has fallen on Pat Cummins, whose agent has repeated his client's version of events in the last 24 hours.
The junior bowler at the time, Cummins has ascended to the captaincy, often joked to be the second-most important job in Australia, behind only the prime minister.
Cummins is not a typical Australian captain. He is not abrasive, or in your face. When he says he has worked hard to correct the image of his team, he is credible. Then again, he missed a trick to really prove Australia are no longer a win-at-all-costs outfit with the Jonny Bairstow stumping in the 2023 Ashes Test at Lord's.
After everything he said in public, and the way he has been backed by Cricket Australia (CA), there seems to be no obvious suggestion Cummins has considered resigning, or that he will be sacked.
He is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on 9 December.
Looking ahead to that match, it is difficult to see how the build-up will be anything other than a circus, dominated by questions about sandpaper, who knew what and who said what to whom.
The litmus test for Cummins will be the public reaction. Remember, that Test is being played in Bancroft's home city, in the state of the newspaper where his 4,000-word testimony was first published.
If Cummins is still in his position by then, the response of the Perth crowd to the captain will be very interesting.
Even if Cummins does get through that, the Australian media will not let up. This is a huge story, one of the biggest in the history of Australia sport. The press will bang away until they feel they have got the truth.
And what about next summer's Ashes? If Cummins is tossing the coin at Trent Bridge on 18 June, then he is extraordinarily resilient.
Right now, I can't imagine that happening. He has said he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, which is ludicrous when you think what he will face on that tour: scrutiny from the media, constant baiting from the crowds.
Cummins will have to decide if he has the stomach for all of that, and whether he can see it through.
His way out could be to resign, without admitting guilt. To say the speculation has become a distraction for the team and the pressure is taking a toll on his family life – we have seen more pictures from Australia overnight of Cummins being confronted outside his home.
Cummins could perhaps continue in the ranks, just as Warner and Smith did. A resignation without an admission of guilt may also take the heat off the other bowlers – Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon.
Whether Cummins continues or not, questions will remain for others who were in Cape Town, Cricket Australia and the whole culture of the sport in that country.
Looking now at what happened in 2018, it appears there was an attitude in the Australia camp that they were fireproof, that they could get away with anything.
Credit goes to their media manager Kate Hutchison, who, according to Bancroft, made a stand about what was going on and knew what would happen if and when the Aussies got caught.
What about the others involved, coaches who were supposed to guide and protect young men? Darren Lehmann and his position at Northamptonshire, or David Saker, who has recently been working with England.
Cricket Australia has seemed so reluctant to get involved. If the big idea was to give individuals the opportunity to "tell their truth" behind closed doors, it is surely dead in the water.
What about telling THE truth? Nothing else is good enough.
  - Published1 day ago
  - Published1 day ago
  - Published7 October
summary: Jonathan Agnew says he struggles to see how Pat Cummins can lead Australia into next summer's Ashes series in England following latest developments in the sandpapergate scandal.
title: Cummins' Australia captaincy at a crossroads - Agnew

body:
Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'
- Published
Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for an employee of the country's football federation to "falsely" take the blame for the winger's positive drugs test.
Tottenham winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.
The 25-year-old said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.
In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk firmly placed the blame for his 20-month absence from the sport on his national association, which has led to Shevchenko's response.
In a statement, former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko, who is now president of the UAF, said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally" and called on the player to retract his words.
He added: "His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample.
"The UAF refused, as such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work."
He added that "numerous investigations and audits" undertaken as part of the case were unable to shed light on when or where the substance entered Mudryk's system.
In his interview Mudryk also claimed Shevchenko had offered him little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and said its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.
However, Shevchenko went on to say that national team staff had complied with a request from Chelsea not to provide Mudryk with any medication while on international duty.
And he also challenged the former Shakhtar Donetsk forward to provide evidence "to back up his words".
"Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps," Shevchenko added.
"These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.
"The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.
"I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism.
"If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question."
BBC Sport has contacted Mudryk's representatives for comment.
Related topics
  - Published1 day ago
summary: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko accuses Mykhailo Mudryk of a "baseless slander" after the on-loan Tottenham winger blamed his failed drugs test on the nation's football association.
title: Shevchenko accuses Mudryk camp of 'baseless slander'
