summary: Scott Colom is now this Southern state's first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years. Scholars and Mississippi natives Eddie Glaude and Kiese Laymon discuss the historic significance of his victory.
title: 'Bigger than Barack Obama's election': Scholars reflect on Mississippi Senate race

body:
The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years
With vote counts concluding and the closest House races being decided, we now have a clearer picture of Democrats' dominant midterms.
Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That's a 14-point spread on the House ballot.
It's the biggest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.
Loading...
Democrats' wins in 2018 and 2006 — the earlier of which then-President George W. Bush described as a "thumping" — and the 2010 "shellacking" that Democrats took, as former President Barack Obama called it, were all less-than-10-point House margins. Obama's 2008 election comes the closest at almost 11 points.
Nearly 50 House seats flipped
So far, Democrats have flipped 46 House seats currently held by Republicans.
That number could rise to 49, as Democrats lead in three other races that have not yet been called.
It's the second-most number of flipped seats this century. The first was in 2010 when Republicans flipped 66 seats, netting 64, a backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, which has since become more popular.
Loading...
The biggest House majority in a generation
This year's drubbing was so resounding that when all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s.
If Democrats win all the races where they are leading, they will have 260 seats, the most since the 102nd Congress, which spanned 1991 to 1993.
Loading...
Democrats controlled the House for 40 years until the 1994 Republican Revolution that ushered in GOP control of Congress.
This century has seen some of the slimmest House majorities in American history and the most changes of party control of the chamber in 130 years. Starting in January, control of the House will have changed hands five times in the last 20 years. In a 20-year stretch in the post-Reconstruction era after the Civil War, there were six changeovers of the House, beginning in 1875.
Now, three decades after former House Speaker Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America" — and a decade into Trump's grip on the Republican Party — House Republicans are back to where they were before the Republican Revolution.
summary: Some 56% of people cast votes for Democrats in House races, compared to 42% who voted Republican. That 14-point spread is the widest win for either party in 50 years, since after Watergate.
title: The midterms were the largest win for either party in 50 years

body:
The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
International Court of Justice issues ruling on Myanmar genocide case
The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.
Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority. Myanmar's military-backed government has not yet responded to the ruling at the time of writing.
Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.
But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.
"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."
Genocidal campaign
For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.
The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.
Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.
"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."
She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."
Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."
"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."
Rejected defense
Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.
She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.
"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.
The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.
A group long denied recognition
In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.
Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.
The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.
But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.
In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.
Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."
The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.
However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.
The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.
Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.
Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.
Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.
"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.
She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.
Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.
summary: The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar security forces "acted with genocidal intent" against the Rohingya during military operations in the northern Rakhine state in 2017.
title: The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

body:
World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)
The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
Let's eschew the euphemisms
World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott, the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.
This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.
There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp, the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?
The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.
What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab, who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
A toast to toilets
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."
If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.
summary: Yahoo for the loo! November 19 marks the 25th anniversary of World Toilet Day. The theme this year: "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures."
title: World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets

body:
Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker
Trump Trilateral Summit In China, House Democratic Leadership, Anthropic IPO
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.
- 🎧 Jeffries, who has served as the top Democrat in the minority since 2023, ran unopposed for the speaker position. But that is not the case in the Senate, NPR's Elena Moore tells Up First. Current minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen has positioned himself as an anti-status quo, progressive leader. Both Van Hollen and Schumer have served in Congress for decades. The vote for that Senate position is set for early December.
- ➡️ Rep. Robert Garcia, poised to chair the House Oversight Committee, sent document-preservation letters to more than a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members in preparation for investigations starting in January. These letters focus on four main areas: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct and the White House Epstein cover-up."
Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met today in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Xi and Putin met separately the night before the trilateral meeting. Trump also had one-on-one meetings with Putin and Xi. It's the first time the three leaders have held a summit together.
- 🎧 The three leaders had different agendas as they went into their meeting, NPR's Jennifer Pak says. Trump aimed to prioritize nuclear arms control. He said that they had a unique opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons, a stance Beijing has typically resisted due to its smaller stockpile compared to the U.S. and Russia. Putin sought discussions to end the war in Ukraine, but on Moscow's terms. The complexity of these issues makes substantial outcomes unlikely, Pak says. Xi aimed to position China as a stabilizing global force by bringing together Russia, its old ally, and the U.S., its direct competitor.
Anthropic is set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange today. The company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued the company at around $1.5 trillion. The company sold 956 million shares at $83 each, surpassing its initial target range of $70 to $78. The seven founders sold over 23 million shares as part of the IPO, and the company's prospectus outlines plans to introduce an extra $26 billion in shares through private placements with Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
- 🎧 In its IPO filing, Anthropic was optimistic that AI would have a bigger impact on the economy than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet, NPR's John Ruwitch says. The company's paperwork suggested that the addressable market for Anthropic's products could be as big as $40 trillion annually, exceeding the GDP of the United States. But CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the danger of losing control over AI. The prospectus flagged some political risks, including the company's current dispute with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. Ruwitch says that now that Anthropic and SpaceX are on the market, OpenAI could potentially join next year.
Watch this
Go face-to-face with the person of the moment. NPR's Newsmakers video podcast brings the biggest names in politics, business, sports, arts, and culture out of the headlines and into the interview chair to discuss the mark they're making on the world. Follow the Newsmakers podcast or subscribe to NPR's YouTube channel to get new episodes as soon as they're available.
Ben Shapiro says he remains committed to his values during Trump's turbulent presidency. The conservative podcast host voted against Trump in 2016, but actively campaigned for him in 2024. Shapiro expressed disappointment in the president's tariffs, alleged corruption and the handling of the war in Iran. He says that Trump's strict immigration policies and the "whiff of corruption" surrounding the White House contributed to the GOP's midterm losses. The co-founder of the media company The Daily Wire warns that Republicans face an "uphill road in 2028," and he doesn't see Vice President JD Vance as the right GOP presidential candidate. Shapiro argues that Vance could alienate key voter groups like Hispanics, the working class, women and the college-educated. In conversation with Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep, Shapiro discussed who he thinks could be a potential 2028 GOP candidate, his new movie, Confession, and the recent decline in his show's YouTube subscriptions.
Watch or listen to the interview or read the article about their discussion.
Today's listen
The West-Eastern Divan Orchestra is an ensemble founded by Edward Said and Daniel Barenboim nearly 30 years ago in Germany to unite Middle Eastern musicians. Despite the deep personal grief and heightened tensions following the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the Gaza war, members of the orchestra strive to confront, rather than sidestep, political realities. Longtime musicians say Barenboim has helped them bridge painful cultural divides and foster enduring cross-border friendships. The space has also given some participants a safe space to discuss Gaza, allowing music to resolve the dissonance.
3 things to know before you go
- Abdelrahman ElGendy has won the National Book Awards' non-fiction prize for his memoir, Huna, which recounts his six years as a political prisoner in Egypt.
- "Choosin' Texas" singer Ella Langley won six of the seven categories she was nominated for, including song of the year, at the Country Music Awards.
- In this week's edition of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Esme Nicholson sends greetings from a Berlin square, where children play around a Käthe Kollwitz bronze cast. In the wake of World War I, the German artist's work often portrayed undernourished children in their mothers' arms.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
summary: Despite growing concern over a possible AI bubble, Anthropic had a record-breaking initial public offering. And, Hakeem Jeffries could become the first Black Speaker of the House.
title: Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker

body:
Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., on the Democratic Party's agenda for the new Congress
House Democrats needed a bigger room Wednesday to accommodate their newly expanded caucus, according to Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts.
Nominated to become the first woman to serve as House majority leader next year, Clark reflected on the moment in an interview with Morning Edition on Thursday.
"It was really looking at the diversity of that caucus, people who have been sent to Congress from all walks of life, that gives me the optimism and the energy that we can really deliver for the American people," she said.
Clark, who is currently the House minority whip, was nominated for House majority leader by a unanimous voice vote. Democrats also nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker and Pete Aguilar for majority whip.
The incoming leadership faces the challenge of lowering living costs while investigating alleged corruption in the Trump administration.
"Of course we can," she said when asked whether Democrats could accomplish both. "That's our responsibility."
She also called President Trump's description of himself as "Mr. Veto" a "stunning statement," expressing hope for bipartisan cooperation on healthcare.
But Democrats face divisions within their own ranks.
Jeffries won his nomination 251-11. Opposition came from incoming progressives including Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Adam Hamawy of New Jersey. They have pressed for Medicare for All, immigration enforcement reforms and an end to the war in Gaza.
The two leaders have differed over U.S. aid to Israel. In July, Clark voted for a Republican amendment that would have cut military aid to Israel, while Jeffries opposed it.
Despite that disagreement and concerns among other Democrats about Jeffries' leadership, she emphasized party unity when asked whether the 11 votes against him could complicate Democrats' agenda.
"We are having conversations with every part of our new caucus, and they are united behind making life better for working people," she said.
Listen to the full interview by clicking on the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by Ally Schweitzer. The web copy was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
summary: As Democrats prepare to take control of the House, incoming majority leader Katherine Clark discusses the party's ambitious agenda and divisions within its ranks.
title: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity

body:
Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit
Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., on Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping
Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.
"I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.
His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.
Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.
Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.
"When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.
Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by J Mai and Olivia Hampton. The web version was adapted by Majd Al-Waheidi and edited by Treye Green.
summary: Rep. Gregory Meeks raises concerns about U.S. alliances after Trump's summit with Xi and Putin. He also discusses Chinese espionage amid the Nvidia scandal.
title: Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit

body:
Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, report says
Muslims will soon become the largest religious group on the planet, according to a new report by the Pew Research Center released today.
Christians will be the second-largest cohort by 2035. The Muslim and Christian populations are both expected to grow, but researchers anticipate Muslims will grow faster.
If recent demographic trends continue, Pew expects the world's Muslim population will reach 3.6 billion by 2070 while the Christian population will be just under 3 billion.
The Pew Research Center arrived at its projections using data from national censuses worldwide, combined with data on fertility rates and religious switching patterns. The projections also use findings from United Nations reports and global migration estimates, along with Pew Research Center's earlier studies on religious migration.
Hindus and Jews are projected to grow in absolute numbers but decline as an overall percentage of the world population. Buddhists, meanwhile, are expected to shrink in both number and portion of the global population in the coming decades.
Some of these trends, according to Pew, can be explained by population growth trends. For instance, most of the population growth in the 21st century is expected to occur in Africa.
By 2070, more than a quarter of the global population will live in sub-Saharan Africa. The vast majority of those who live there are either Christian or Muslim. The region's high fertility rate and lengthening lifespans mean the numbers of both faiths there are expected to grow, with the Muslim population growing faster than the Christian one.
In fact, Pew projects that by 2070, the Democratic Republic of the Congo in sub-Saharan Africa will surpass the United States as the country with the largest total number of Christians. The Pew Center's religion research director Alan Cooperman calls this a "global change in what one might think of as the center of gravity of Christianity."
Birth rates drive religious shifts
Pew points out that differences in fertility rates have major effects on religious populations. Around the world, Muslims tend to have more children than people of other faiths. In recent years, the fertility rate for Muslims has been 3.1 children per woman. The average rate for non-Muslim women has been about 2 per woman.
Among the other religious trends anticipated by 2070 in the Pew Research Center's report: The overall populations of China, Japan, and South Korea will shrink, and their Buddhist populations will shrink by half. And, an increasing portion of the world's Jews will live in Israel. In 2020, 46% of global Jewry lived there, but Pew projects that by 2070, 62% of Jews will live in Israel.
One of the more surprising projections is that while the percentage of people who identify as having no religious affiliation will increase in many countries, the global population of "nones" is expected to drop. The reason for this is that a very large portion of the religiously unaffiliated live in China, and that country is expected to have dramatic population losses in the coming decades due to dropping birth rates there.
U.S. religious trends reflect overall global patterns
The report also details how religious change will affect the United States. Pew says the U.S. will no longer have a Christian majority by 2070, yet Christians will remain the largest single religious group in the country. Christians are expected to decline to just under 48% of the population. (They currently make up 62% of the U.S.) During this same period, the percentage of the population of those who are religiously unaffiliated is expected to rise to 41%.
The anticipated population change in the U.S. among Christians and the religiously unaffiliated will be driven mostly by people changing their religion rather than by birth rates, according to the report. Christians tend to shed more adherents than they gain through what demographers call "religious switching," most of whom switch to being religious "nones" rather than taking on another tradition.
The U.S. is expected to become increasingly religiously diverse, with Pew projecting that both Muslims and Hindus in the country will outnumber Jews by 2070 if current demographic trends continue. 
Correction Nov. 18, 2026
A previous version of this headline incorrectly said Muslims would outnumber Christians by 2070. They will outnumber Christians by 2035.
summary: By 2070, the Democratic Republic of the Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the largest total number of Christians.
title: Muslims will outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, report says

body:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.
The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.
The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.
The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.
Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”
Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.
“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.
The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.
Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.
“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”
Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.
The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”
Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.
The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.
A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.
summary: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia. The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions. Continue reading...
title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

body:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”
summary: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report. In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund ( UNFPA ) published on Thursday. Continue reading...
title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.
On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.
summary: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya. The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. Continue reading...
title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.
Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.
In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.
If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).
According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.
In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.
“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.
The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.
The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.
In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.
On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.
Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.
Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.
For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.
Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”
In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.
Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.
summary: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi. The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen , the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza. Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, said on Monday the move had no “future or humanity”. “I don’t see any future or humanity in that. It’s not the solution,” Sanchez, an outspoken defender of immigration in a Europe that has tilted to the right in recent years, told Telecinco television.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.
summary: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country. Continue reading...
title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.
Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.
summary: Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse. Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States. Continue reading...
title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president

Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.
“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.
In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.
“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.
Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.
“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.
During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”
Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.
Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.
“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.
Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”
Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.
But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”
summary: Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”. Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999. Continue reading...
title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military

body:
The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.
The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.
In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.
In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.
He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.
“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.
The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy was “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.
“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.
Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting
summary: St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned. On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis. Continue reading...
title: Caribbean nations fear economic impact of shuttering citizenship program after EU threats

About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.
“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.
Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.
Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil, with others in Indonesia and India.
The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.
summary: Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory. According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”. Continue reading...
title: Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life
