An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.
Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”
The Haitian Bridge Alliance, an immigration advocacy group, confirmed that the third-grader had been released from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody.
“An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love – not in immigration detention. We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry,” Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, said in a statement.
The third-grader at Fay elementary school was put in restraints and taken into custody by federal immigration officers at a check-in earlier in the month, according to video obtained by NBC News and an oversight letter Democratic lawmakers sent to the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services.
A spokesperson for the homeland security department said ICE took the child into custody “out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child’s safety”.
The uncle, the spokesperson said in a statement to the Guardian, was unable to prove legal guardianship – and that officials were obliged by federal anti-trafficking laws to take the boy into care as an “unaccompanied alien child”.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy was in the care of his uncle and cousins after his father was deported last year.
“I’m so grateful that he’s home, but this should have never happened in the first place,” Vargas said in a second social media post, adding that he would be asking the Trump administration for answers. While he was detained, the child was “held in a facility in Texas, far away from his home in San Diego”, Vargas said.
Celebrating the boy’s return, Jozef of the Haitian Bridge Alliance told NBC News: “The aunt was literally crying, and she said: ‘I have not eaten since the Wednesday they took my baby.’ They haven’t been able to sleep because of that.” She added: “The cousins were there when they took him, and wondering: will they ever see him again? But today [Monday] they are able to see him again. They are able to hug him.”
summary: Child reunited with family after he was detained by immigration agents in San Diego and transferred to Texas An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California . Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.” Continue reading...
title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.
summary: Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’ China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants. The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity. Continue reading...
title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway.
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep. Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News.
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health, often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.
summary: US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China. The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him. Continue reading...
title: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China

body:
It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.
But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.
It’s true that the meeting could yet be an icebreaker and the start of a permanent new dialogue. It’s also true that each leader can return home with something from the 90 minutes they spent together.
Despite falling asleep during the main Apec summit, Donald Trump had a chance to show his proximity to two authoritarian leaders he admires. With Ukraine having destroyed Russia’s bridge into Crimea, the US president greeted Putin as not just a friend but almost a wartime ally.
The Russian president, although occasionally pushed to one side by protocol during the early photo opportunities, will be able to show back home that it is Moscow, and not his adversary Europe, let alone Ukraine, that commands the respect and attention of Trump and Xi Jinping. As such, the summit was a free gift to Putin, and underlined that Trump was no longer the leader of the free world, as the former British foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt commented.
From Putin’s perspective, a meeting in Berlin of the coalition of the willing was a sideshow. Europe’s attempts to isolate Russia had failed and the Asia-Pacific region had become the centre of the global economy, Putin boasted. His relationship with Trump, he said, despite the difficulties, was founded on “similar civilisational values”.
For Xi, it was a prestigious chance to play host and implicitly demonstrate that the era of American hegemony is over. No longer the sole arbiter in world affairs, the US, the consumer economy, must share the stage with China, the manufacturing giant, and Russia, the energy bank.
The trio’s brief joint statement covered four pretty disparate topics: boosting energy supply, reforming the United Nations, limiting the powers of the international criminal court (ICC) and a tentative commitment to discuss nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation.
For grandeur at a time of various global crises, these ambitions hardly matched Yalta in 1945 or even the declaration after the Tehran summit in 1943, when the leaders of the UK, US and Russia sat on the veranda of the British embassy and pledged that their countries would work together after the war to build a “world family of democratic nations” free of tyranny and oppression. Winston Churchill declaimed in Tehran: “In our hands we have the future of mankind.” Joseph Stalin went further. “History has spoiled us,” he said. “She has given us very great power and very great opportunities.”
Shenzhen, by contrast, felt like a meeting in search of an agenda. The vacuum was filled with platitudinous commitments to “maintain strategic stability and international security”, a task that – looking around the world – none of those in attendance are currently pursuing with great effect.
Perhaps technology, multipolarity and their own divisions mean even they do not have “very great power”. Certainly there were no accompanying plans for how to reform the UN, let alone boost energy production or show respect for international law – a subject Trump’s current favoured successor, Marco Rubio, had just disparaged in a speech as a plaything of the global elite.
It was the summit’s chief instigator, Putin, who was the most eager of the three to set the meeting in a historic context, describing China, Russia and the US as the victors of the second world war, in a deliberate slight to Britain. A pledge to “preserve and strengthen the system of international law” seemingly referred to ensuring certain world leaders were freed from the prospect of the ICC serving them with arrest warrants.
By coincidence, the other world court, the international court of justice (ICJ), found a state – Myanmar – guilty of genocide for the first time on the same day. The Shenzen statement did not name the ICJ as a target, beyond an oblique reference to the ICC and “other similar institutions”. Doubtless that is only because ICJ rulings can be dismissed with near impunity.
Xi, nervous that China’s status as protector of the global south might be damaged by being involved in a global superpower carve-up, stuck to a familiar script: “History tells us that when major powers are at peace, the world is secure. When they clash, there is chaos.”
It may be that behind the scenes, or at other events, serious progress is being made on how China might act as a guarantor of a peace deal with Iran, or on who should lead the UN through its coming phase of reform, or even on how Putin might bring himself to seek peace in Ukraine in a way that protects Ukrainian sovereignty.
For the moment, though, it looks as if what little history was made in Shenzhen was made for exclusively the wrong reasons.
summary: Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”. But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century. Continue reading...
title: New page in history? Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.
Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.
Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.
Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.
By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.
In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.
The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.
This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.
The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.
Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.
The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.
summary: Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog. The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth. Continue reading...
title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns

body:
Apec summit as it happened: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
Wed 18 Nov 2026 17.48 GMT
First published on Wed 18 Nov 2026 03.46 GMT
Wed 18 Nov 2026 17.48 GMT
First published on Wed 18 Nov 2026 03.46 GMT
Closing summary
- The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official. The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
- Meanwhile, a meeting between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media on Wednesday. “No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
- Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua. Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.
- Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen, reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.
- Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace. Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
- Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin. In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.
- Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age. “Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.
- Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen. World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
- It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.
- Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just concluded a “very big trade deal” with the Philippines, but he did not provide any details, and Manila did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it is a fair deal for both countries,” Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.
Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America’s status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the US public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the US worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump said Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
The meeting between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media.
“No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a separate meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official.
The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
If confirmed, it would be their first bilateral since they met in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to reach a deal on the war in Ukraine.
Trump had already suggested he might meet with Putin, as well as with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but neither option had been added to his official schedule.
Trump treated to fried chicken by Philippines president
Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace.
Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
The gift may have gone down particularly well with Trump, who has something of a reputation for his love of fast food. The US president has long been associated with McDonald’s and KFC, with his former campaign aides revealing in 2017 that his usual McDonald’s order included two Big Macs, two Filet-O-Fish sandwiches and a chocolate milkshake. The Guardian reported on their revelations at the time in this article:
Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen.
World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
Sheinbaum, however, flew in economy class from Mexico City to Shenzhen on a China Southern Airlines flight, media reports said. She arrived in China on Monday.
Posts on Chinese social media platform Weibo showed the Mexican leader in the plane chatting with passengers, though the photos could not be independently verified by AFP. A hashtag on Weibo about her arrival in China garnered 10.2m views as of Wednesday.
Meanwhile, Sheinbaum said on Wednesday she had a “very good meeting” with her US counterpart Trump as the two countries pursue negotiations aimed at easing trade tensions.
“We continue to make progress on our shared agenda,” Sheinbaum added in a post on X.
Carney and Trump discuss trade deal in meeting on sidelines of Apec summit, PM's office says
The Canadian prime minister’s office has issued a statement following Mark Carney’s meeting with US president Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen.
It said:
 This evening, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, met with the President of the United States, Donald J. Trump, on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, in Shenzhen, China.
The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty. They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact.
Here is more of Xi’s speech (as per Xinhua):
 At tomorrow’s Leaders’ Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual openness, explore pathways for innovation-driven growth, broaden opportunities for pragmatic cooperation in various fields, and promote the implementation of more outcomes. I look forward to discussing the grand plan for Asia-Pacific cooperation and jointly advancing the cause of Asia-Pacific development with you all.
Now, I propose that we raise a glass together.
For the common prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region,
For the success of this informal leaders’ meeting,
For the health of all guests and their families,
Cheers!
Xi hails Shenzhen's transformation in Apec banquet speech
China’s state news agency Xinhua has published the text of Xi Jinping’s welcome speech at tonight’s Apec banquet in Shenzhen.
In his remarks, Xi praised the city’s transformation into an international economic and innovation hub, describing it as a symbol of China’s development.
Here are a few passages from his address:
 This evening, the shores of the South China Sea are aglow with lights, and autumn is in full swing here in Shenzhen, the City of the Phoenix. As the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting is about to commence, I would like, on behalf of the Chinese Government and the Chinese people, to extend a warm welcome to all our distinguished guests.
I have often said that to see a thousand years of China, one should visit Xi’an; to see five hundred years of China, one should visit Beijing; and to see a hundred years of China, one should visit Shanghai. Today, I would like to say to you all: to see fifty years of China, come to Shenzhen.
Shenzhen is a place with a rich history. In 1978, when I first came to Shenzhen, it was still a small fishing village. More than 40 years have passed in the blink of an eye, and now it is filled with high-rise buildings and bustling traffic. The changes are truly remarkable.”
Trump and Putin shake hands ahead of Apec welcome banquet
US president Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian president Vladimir Putin, as China’s Xi Jinping looks on, ahead of the welcome banquet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China:
summary: This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse. Continue reading...
title: Apec summit as it happened: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’

Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.
Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.
The research, published in the journal Science Advances, involved a sensitive detection device known as a gravimeter, which was set up on the floor of a men’s bathroom adjacent to the lift.
The gravimeter was able to detect the position of the elevator’s 1.8-tonne counterweight as it moved between two levels – representing 0 and 1 in binary code – which enabled the scientists to send a message.
The experiment is reminiscent of a plot point in the Christopher Nolan film Interstellar, in which a gravitational anomaly creates messages in binary code.
The researchers chose to transmit the word “gravity”, or 1000111 1110010 1100001 1110110 1101001 1110100 1111001 in binary code. At a transmission rate of one bit (digit) per minute, the single word took nearly an hour to send.
The scientists say that while gravitational communication is currently far from usable given its extremely slow speed, an advantage is that it is a “practically unblockable wireless communication scheme”.
“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” said co-author Dr Charles Woffinden, of UQ’s school of mathematics and physics. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with wifi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”
Study co-author Prof Matthew Davis told Guardian Australia: “At the moment, it’s very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful.” But he added that the experiment was “theoretically interesting enough that it was worth doing”.
To put into perspective how slow the message transmission was, Davis said that Nasa’s Voyager 1 spacecraft, which after 49 years of travel had just reached a distance of one light-day away, could “communicate with Earth at a faster data rate than our communication concept”.
According to Davis, the new method of communicating could theoretically occur at ranges of up to 500 metres and at a rate 15 times faster, if more sensitive quantum gravity sensors were used.
The idea for the elevator study arose from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge – which would use quantum sensors to detect changes in the strength of gravity due to a passing truck, allowing scientists to determine the mass of a large vehicle.
Classical gravimeters can be thought of as a mass on a spring. “If you stretch the spring, the mass bounces up and down at a certain rate, which is determined by the spring and the gravitational field,” Davis said. “If the gravitational field changes ever so slightly, the rate at which it bounces back and forth changes.
“Quantum sensors are still under development
“Sometimes doing physics leads in unexpected ways and it’s a bit of fun … you get to do quirky things on the side. It’s one of the great joys of science to have stuff like this happen.”
Other near-unblockable methods of communication – involving neutrinos or gravitational waves – have been proposed “but these approaches are somewhat hindered by the difficulty in generating a measurable signal”, the scientists note.
The physicists conducted the research in UQ’s Parnell physics building, which is also home to the world’s longest-running science experiment – the pitch drop experiment, which began in 1927.

body:
Former Liberal MP Sharman Stone has died via voluntary assisted dying after spending much of her political career advocating that people should have autonomy over their bodies.
Stone died aged 75 on Wednesday surrounded by family after a long fight against glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer. She had a long political career, serving as the minister for workforce participation from 2006-07 and the ambassador for women and girls from 2016-20.
During her time in office, Stone championed contentious medical research and supported access to abortion, and readily – and publicly – disagreed with former leader Tony Abbott on both topics.
“Sharman and I disagreed on ‘life’ issues … but she was always upfront about what she thought and always handled disagreement well,” Abbott told the Sydney Morning Herald after her death.
“That actually made her a good colleague because being straight with people is just about the most important quality anyone can have.”
Stone was one of the first female superintendents in the Victorian Office of Corrections, the first female director of the Victorian Farmers Federation, and the recipient of an economics PhD.
She was elected to federal parliament in 1996, serving through the Howard years in what was then the seat of Murray in northern Victoria.
Nationals MP Sam Birrell, who now holds the same seat Stone once held, paid tribute to his predecessor in a post on Facebook.
“Sharman was an articulate and intelligent fighter for our region, and made significant contributions to parliament and Australian public life in areas such as women’s rights, regional manufacturing and indigenous affairs,” he wrote.
“Sharman was particularly strident in her advocacy for regional communities in relation to the Murray-Darling Basin plan, and she always warned of the dangers of water buybacks to the economies of the regions affected.
“She was never afraid to confront anyone on issues she believed in, even those in her own party.”
Stone was remembered as a strong voice for her local community, right up to her later days.
“She was born and bred in the heart of the electorate she served – a sixth-generation northern Victorian from a farming family,” the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said after her death.
“She understood the rugged and regenerative nature of the land and what makes regional Australia tick.”
Stone spent two decades in parliament and was characterised by her independence.
“Over all the years, on every day, I have striven to make a difference, to create more opportunities and more choices for the people I love, the people of Murray,” she said in her retirement speech from federal parliament in 2016.
“My Murray electorate is magnificent. Its people are heroic, innovative and resourceful.”
She held several roles during the Howard government, including as parliamentary secretary to the environment and finance ministers.
She also held the shadow environment portfolio after the Liberals’ defeat to Kevin Rudd.
Stone retired from politics in 2016, and served as the Australian ambassador for women and girls until 2020.
Her celebration of life is expected to be held after the 28 November Victorian election.

body:
Former New South Wales opposition leader Mark Speakman will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.
In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.
He is the eighth out of 24 current Liberal MPs to announce they will not re-contest their seat in March, following Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor.
The announcement comes almost a year to the day after Speakman resigned from the leadership of the opposition in a spill in favour of Sloane, who was elected unopposed.
In that time the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in NSW to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.
Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is currently at 26%.
Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.
In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.
Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.
“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.
“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”
Speakman, a barrister, served as environment minister between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.
He was chosen as the Liberal and opposition leader after Dominic Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.
On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and, while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.
He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.
Speakman’s resignation, ending speculation that bubbled up again when he spoke during question time on Thursday, is the latest blow for Sloane, who he said in his leaving speech had the “attributes to be a great premier”.
In a statement on Friday morning, Sloane thanked Speakman for his “extraordinary contribution to the people of Cronulla and to NSW”.
“Since his election in 2011, Mark has been a dedicated local member, a thoughtful colleague and a principled leader of the NSW Liberal Party,” she said.
“Mark has been a generous and supportive colleague. I’m grateful for the confidence he placed in me when I became leader, and for the contribution he continues to make to our team.”
Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.
Investigative reporter Sarah Martin won the award for print/text news report for her exclusive story that revealed the One Nation leader and her chief of staff, James Ashby, travelled with Rinehart on the mining magnate’s Gulfstream 700 on 27 October last year.
The pair stayed at Rinehart’s Palm Beach mansion, close to US president Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.
After Guardian Australia published details of Hanson’s flight, her office lodged an amendment to the registrar of senators’ interests declaring the sponsored travel.
Queensland correspondent Ben Smee and the Guardian team won the award for coverage of Indigenous affairs for the story of the betrayal of Kardell Lomas, who repeatedly sought help – from domestic violence support services and the police – to escape the violent and dangerous man who killed her.
Lomas had 24 interactions with various agencies – and she repeatedly disclosed fears for her safety, death threats, serious violence and other abuse.
Nick McKenzie won the 2026 Gold Walkley, regarded as the highest honour in Australian journalism, for his investigation into Victorian underworld figure Mick Gatto, and how the state Labor government handled the $100bn infrastructure program, Big Build.
Walkley judges called it “truth-to-power journalism, in the face of attempts to shut him down with actual violence. It’s not just a Victorian story, it speaks to our nation and the way our democracy works. Tenacious reporting presented in accessible ways, instrumental in bringing down a government.”
Smee and Martin were also finalists in the long feature writing category, Martin for “Inside One Nation” and Smee for “‘Starting to frighten me’: the final weeks of Hannah Clarke’s life”.
Guardian Australia’s business editor, Jonathan Barrett, was a finalist in the short feature writing category for his story “‘A child goes to bed and doesn’t wake up’: the families left in shock after the sudden death of their healthy children”.
The 2026 Walkley print/text award for feature writing under 4,000 words was awarded to the Australian Financial Review’s Sam Buckingham-Jones for the story “Maccas in a Rolls: inside Kyle Sandilands’ pivot to $100 tradie plans”.
For feature writing over 4,000 words, the Age and the Sydney Morning Herald’s Melissa Fyfe and Carla Hildebrandt took home the award for their story “Virginia: the Final Chapter”.
The scoop of the year was awarded to the ABC team behind “Bondi: what ASIO knew”, which included Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop, Olivia Caisley and Michael Workman.
Tony Wright, an associate editor and special writer for the Age and the Sydney Morning Herald, took home the award for outstanding contribution to journalism.
summary: Stories revealing Pauline Hanson’s US trip with Gina Rinehart and the systemic betrayal of Kardell Lomas before her death recognised Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart. Investigative reporter Sarah Martin won the award for print/text news report for her exclusive story that revealed the One Nation leader and her chief of staff, James Ashby, travelled with Rinehart on the mining magnate’s Gulfstream 700 on 27 October last year. body:
The music industry has declared it will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.
The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.
The Albanese government would not comment on the reported proposal but senior ministers have raised concerns about current copyright law in recent days, hinting reforms were needed.
Annabelle Herd, the chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria), and Claire Pullen, the CEO of the Australian Writers’ Guild, said the creative community – which this week launched a major AI campaign – would remain united in rejecting such changes.
“I can’t see any creative workers leaving their colleagues behind,” Pullen said.
The Australian Financial Review reported on Thursday the government was considering a copyright change under which AI companies would buy permits to train on Australian content but that music may be exempted. Such a proposal would be more in line with AI companies after Anthropic suggested a model of “conditional approval” to scrape content unless a rightsholder objected, and OpenAI told a parliamentary committee it would “potentially” support paying into a fund for creators.
Guardian Australia was not able to independently verify details of the proposal. One senior member of the creative community, involved in copyright discussions with government, said they had heard some details of such an idea – but others said they had not and doubted the Albanese government would seriously entertain it. One source in the AI industry, who declined to be named, said they would welcome such a plan.
Herd said she was unaware of the proposal before Thursday but the music industry would not desert other creatives.
“Had we been consulted, we would have advised this scheme is unnecessary, unworkable and designed to suit the commercial interests of AI companies, not protect creators,” she told Guardian Australia.
“Our position is unchanged: we stand with the rest of the creative and media industries.”
Herd and Pullen said such a scheme would be difficult to implement technically, questioning how content such as movies or TV shows – which combine copyrighted elements such as music, video and screenwriting – would be treated if just one element was exempted from AI scraping.
“This just seems like such a convoluted path, when AI companies have had an open invitation to sit down and negotiate for years,” Pullen said. “We have been working with government to come up with a model since 2024. We’ve come up with solutions and tech has steadfastly refused to even talk.”
While the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, and that artists “need to be compensated”, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law.
The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance said it would be “alarmed” at the reported proposal and demanded protections promised by Albanese “must apply to all creative sectors”.
While government MPs declined to comment on the report, senior Labor figures have recently begun more forcefully pointing to what they claim are shortfalls in copyright law in the AI age – despite major rightsholder groups rejecting the need for change. The industry minister, Tim Ayres, on Tuesday said “the status quo is no good” for creative workers, a line repeated by the acting prime minister, Richard Marles, on Thursday. Marles added on News24: “People are being ripped off”.
The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, also used newly strengthened language when contacted, promising “certainty and strong protections for Australian artists”.
“Right now, the work of Australian creatives is being used without their consent or payment,” a spokesperson for Rowland said.
“The government has long advocated for tech companies to strike commercial deals with Australian artists, and we will continue to do so.”
Potentially carving out musicians did not win support among parliamentarians, either.
The shadow attorney general, Michaelia Cash, claimed such a proposal would “divide the rightsholders”.
“This ham-fisted tactic should be strongly resisted. Everyone who owns property should have the same right for it not to be stolen.”
Pocock also described it as “some sort of divide and conquer strategy”.
“It’s hard to know what [Labor] are actually doing at the moment. The joint select committee hasn’t even given its report to the government, and we’re hearing all sorts of whispers about what the government is planning.”
The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young urged the government not to meet copyright demands requested by big tech.
“What they’re asking Australia to do actually is to undermine copyright the world over,” she told News 24. “Australia will become known as the Cayman Islands for AI if we allow this loophole to happen.
“I say, don’t be that stupid. Stand up to them.”
summary: Reported proposal to give musicians special treatment is ‘unworkable’, Aria chief executive says Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The music industry has declared it will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”. The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens. British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that EU students would pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line.
The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.
As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement on Friday.
The EU-UK reset talks went down “down to the wire”, sources said, as both sides battled over the nature of the UK’s role in shaping future European food and farming rules.
But on the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.
There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.
The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards but France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start.
Instead, the UK will be consulted on new food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.
Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.
It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.
The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.
With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some central sticking points.
Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”
A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP, including the a highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.
Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”
According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules.
An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.
In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK.
“Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.
The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.
The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state.
The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.
Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.
The UK has prioritised seeking commitments on Britain’s position relating to the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. The trade defence policy will include tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles but will also affect British manufacturing. The sides are believed to be close to an agreement to language at the summit that would point towards UK inclusion, but nothing can be formalised until the EU passes its own legislation.
Burnham’s spokesperson said: “[The UK is] engaging constructively with the EU on that, and we’ve been clear about the challenges it could represent for British industries. We have deeply integrated supply chains with Europe, and we want to keep working together to boost growth and open up trade.
“The UK and Europe have shared economic challenges, and we believe shared challenges are best met with a collective approach that is in Britain’s best interests, and in Europe’s too.”
summary: Britain makes concessions on youth mobility scheme as negotiations on food and farming go down to the wire British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme. It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that EU students would pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a last minute concession to get the deal over the line. Continue reading...
title: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches

body:
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.
A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.
Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.
It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.
The document states: “The EU and UK … will establish a structured dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel action plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathway.”
In May, the UK and 45 other European countries signed an agreement that explicitly endorsed plans to send unwanted asylum seekers to third-country hubs.
A political declaration from the 46 members of the Council of Europe, the body that oversees the European convention on human rights (ECHR), said states had an “undeniable sovereign right” to control their borders.
It is understood that the UK has been seeking a deal with an unnamed third country, similar to the Italy-Albania agreement that allowed Rome to place detention centres in Albania. Albania has ruled out a bilateral agreement on a return hub with the UK.
Previous discussions have reportedly centred on 11 countries: Armenia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Libya, Mauritania, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Uganda and Uzbekistan. Montenegro has denied reports that it is considering housing refused asylum seekers.
Starmer scrapped a Tory plan to forcibly send small-boat arrivals to Rwanda where their asylum claims would have been processed.
Before the election, the Conservative government had spent £700m on its Rwanda returns policy, which was meant to deter Channel crossings. The scheme hit legal and political obstacles from the start, with the UK supreme court eventually ruling it illegal.
Under Burnham, the Home Office has refused to close down the possibility of sending asylum seekers to Rwanda. This week, when asked if the UK might ever send asylum seekers to Rwanda, a Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK, like other European countries, is exploring innovative approaches including returns hubs to tackle illegal migration.”
The UK has been looking for years to strengthen cooperation with France and other EU member states to tackle small boats carrying asylum seekers across the Channel.
But sources say it is only in recent months that there has been a change of mood in the EU, with member states realising that the intensity of criminal trafficking across the Channel is “proving [to be] a pull factor” to enter the EU. Those that fail to make it to British shores remain in the EU’s migrant support system.
Responding to the planned cooperation on migrant hubs, Madeleine Sumption, the head of the Migration Observatory at Oxford University, said: “Its inclusion in the statement would confirm the now relatively widespread interest in ‘third country’ options.”
In response, Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said return hubs were likely to be difficult and costly to run.
“Removing people to places they have never stepped foot will be difficult and distressing,” he said.
“The last decade has shown that working with people to support their return to their countries is far more successful.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we are not part of this EU member state initiative, there is widespread international agreement on the need to have practical and workable solutions to deal with the global challenge of illegal migration.
“We continue to explore innovative approaches, including returns hubs, to build on the 80,000 people with no right to be in the UK returned or deported since July 2024. We have consistently made clear that we support the principle of returns hubs.”
summary: Two sides to commit to discussing third-country hubs as part of reset pact after five-country deal with Rwanda The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document. A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”. Continue reading...
title: UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries

body:
'A Yalta format will not bring about peace,' Merz warns
Merz is the first to speak.
He says the leaders want “a peace for Ukraine that is both just and lasting,” with “more, not less, security for Europe and the world.”
“We will continue to support Kyiv for as long as is necessary. Should peace negotiations take place, we will be involved. Negotiations can only succeed if Ukraine and Europe are part of the process together. A “Yalta-style” format will not bring about peace.”
He says that as a gift he gave each of the guests a piece of the Berlin Wall, as an example of “what the Yalta arrangement represented for Berlin.”
“You may recall that in 1987, President Reagan stood here in Berlin and said: ‘Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!’ Today, we say to President Putin: ‘end the war in Ukraine, and let us work together to find diplomatic solutions.’ We never again want to live in a divided Europe. We want to live in freedom and in peace – together.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
European leaders showed a united and defiant front as they repeated their backing for Ukraine “for as long as it takes” at the latest summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, declaring no decisions on Ukraine and Europe can be made without their participation (17:58, 18:06, 18:11).
Their comments appeared to play down the importance of Donald Trump’s summit with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen (16:34), with German chancellor Friedrich Merz saying “a Yalta format will not bring about peace,” in a reference to secretive discussions between superpowers above the heads of those most affected (17:45, 17:50).
European leaders and US peace envoys insisted that some progress has been made in discussions on ending the Russian war of aggression in Ukraine, although they struck a cautious note about Putin’s intentions in the coming months (15:46, 18:38, 18:44).
US envoy Jared Kushner claimed that Russia’s leadership appears to be “comfortable” with the concept of Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine in any postwar settlement (18:29).
Meanwhile, Russia’s Putin struck an uncompromising tone at his press briefing in Shenzhen, vowing “painful” response to Ukraine’s attacks on Kerch bridge and defending his maximalist demands (13:09, 13:34).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Is Europe now in the shadow of a Trump, Putin and Xi alliance? – podcast
Andy Burnham is meeting western leaders in Berlin and Brussels this week, to discuss Ukraine and closer ties to the EU. Meanwhile, Donald Trump,Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have met at the Apec summit in China.
Is this the start of a global shift of power away from Europe, or was it just a hyped-up photo opportunity?
Here is our latest “Politics Weekly” podcast on this if you want to catch up on today’s events:
Separately, Poland’s Donald Tusk also told reporters on his way back to Poland that Trump’s comments after his meeting with Putin and Xi sounded “quite optimistic.”
But Tusk quickly added that Trump’s “faith in Putin’s good will is probably unshakeable,” and he was a bit more sceptical about it.
“It would be good if indeed sooner or later it turned out that Russia is seriously ready to undertake peace talks,” he said.
But he warned:
“I don’t think it’s likely that Russia will sit down at the negotiating table in any serious way before the winter is over.”
'Some grounds for optimism' that talks can progress, Burnham says
The European leaders also get asked about Welt/Politico’s report earlier and the tone of Trump’s comments.
Burnham says that Trump’s comments focused on “horrific” loss of life during the war, saying “he spoke quite passionately about that subject.”
He stresses “nobody is winning this war,” and stresses that in his view there has been “huge progress” in now consensus that “there is no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine in the room and no decision about European security without Europe represented in the room.”
He says “there is a greater degree of alignment.”
“I would say for the first time in my period as prime minister of the United Kingdom, I see alignment; I see people saying the same thing; I see solidarity across the board in Europe; a strong, united European position.
And that gives some grounds for optimism that there can now be progress. But obviously, there is one person who can determine that more than anybody else, and that is president Putin.”
Witkoff jumps in there to say that Trump has “adamantly supported a peaceful end to this war,” with clear instructions to engage with the coalition of the willing and work in all formats that can be helpful to end the war.
“What I heard from him on the call today was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders who he was meeting with [Xi and Putin], so he made Ukraine, and a peaceful end to this war, a principal part of that trilateral today, and I think he’s to be commended for that.”
Russia 'comfortable' with Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine, Kushner says
Kushner says that the US managed to get Moscow comfortable with the concept that any security agreement for Ukraine would be based on Article 5-type arrangement, like in Nato.
(Not sure the Russians would say the same.)
He says “I know that there’s a lot of, scepticism and disbelief on that concept in Russia, but that’s why it’s important to restart the dialogue between Europe and Russia.”
He says:
“I will say from America’s perspective, giving an Article Five like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to. but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that and … we have to make sure it is part of a broader security package.”
Merz gets a question on potential multilateral talks with Ukraine, Russia, Europe and the US, and confirms that’s the plan and adds that finding the right place for it shouldn’t be too difficult.
He also goes back to his Yalta reference earlier, saying Europe was “parcelled up” by powers, and “we will not allow anything like that to happen again.”
Macron says the focus is on safeguarding Europe’s security.
He said that a peace declaration agreed by Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China “does not lead to a reorganisation of the world”.
“Today, if there is one critical factor in Europe’s reorganisation, its security, it is precisely the meeting that took place in Berlin,” he said.
Trump comes away from China talks thinking peace is achievable, Kushner says
US Kushner is up next.
He says the meeting was “very substantive and successful,” and “essential in helping us shape our point of views,” as he confirms that Trump dialled in for parts of the talks.
He pointedly praises Italy’s Meloni, Poland’s Tusk, European Commission’s von der Leyen, Nato’s Rutte, Finnish president and Norwegian PMs, Stubb and Gahr Støre.
He says Europe is “very united, and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine,” which he and Witkoff “relayed to president Trump.”
He says, without revealing details, that Trump came away from the trilateral China meeting thinking “peace is achievable”.
“For us, success in an outcome would be to have a sovereign, secure, prosperous and free Ukraine at the end of the war,” he says.
He says the talks have been making “a lot of progress” on postwar prosperity plan, security guarantees, and a plan to exchange prisoners of war.
On postwar security, he says that “Nato will be a central pillar” of proposals, with the right structures to avoid accidental escalations.
Kushner also says that Russians appear to be “willing to trust” the US suggestion that Europeans need to be included in the process to make sure that whatever agreement is struck will be respected.
The US envoys will be meeting with national security advisers next to agree on the detail of their proposals.
“President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” he insists..
“Our goal is really to end this war and to really help build a durable peace. We are very committed. President Trump, will do whatever it takes to do that. He’s instructed us to commit as much time as possible, and we will continue to do that in full coordination, and unity with our European partners.”
'Not for the aggressor to set out wide raging and unrealistic security demands' Burnham says
UK’s Burnham speaks next.
He says today’s meeting “has put on a huge show of support” for Kyiv, and “the mood was stronger, more united, more determined.”
“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position. It’s not for the aggressor in this conflict to set out wide ranging and unrealistic security demands. That much we are all absolutely clear about.”
He says the coalition is ready for discussions on European security, but only “if there is a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”
He says the UK’s support for Ukraine will continue for “as long as it takes.”
“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position. It’s not for the aggressor in this conflict to set out wide ranging and unrealistic security demands. That much we are all absolutely clear about.
And I hope that message is heard very clearly, in Moscow: for as long as it takes.”
“If we want to be credible in peace negotiations, then it is important that Ukraine defends itself and goes into these negotiations in a good position, and Ukraine can only do so if we continue supporting Ukraine.”
He adds:
“Everyone who is here today have to do everything in their power so that Ukraine has everything it needs in order to resist and to defend herself …”
He says that faced with Russia’s maximalist demands, it’s time it is “the right point in time to discuss [Ukraine’s] Nato membership.”
Commenting on the current state of talks, he says Russia “did not submit any concrete and tangible proposals for peace.”
He acknowledges that “the coming weeks will be critical” for Ukraine, and so the coalition gathered at the right moment.
He says there was every attempt made to “make this meeting as concrete as possible.”
He thanks all partners for helping Ukraine and highlights “active efforts to ensure that we stand firm.”
He thanks the EU for its “very substantial” proposed loan of £45bn.
He also highlights some of the priority areas for Ukraine, including the move to stop daily drone attacks (which he confirms hit the Austrian and the Dutch embassies), and deploy more air defence systems.
He also says the next round of talks should include European leaders, and highlights the importance of security guarantees and Ukraine’s future membership in the EU.
summary: Berlin meeting of the ‘coalition of the willing’ comes after Trump declared Putin a ‘friend’ during trilateral meeting with Xi in China For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media , includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever. There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues: “The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.” Continue reading...
title: Ukraine allies warn ‘Yalta format’ will not bring about peace – as it happened
