body:
The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
The gathering, which follows up last year’s inaugural EU-UK summit in London, was scheduled for July but postponed when Keir Starmer resigned.
What is on the table?
The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government.
First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports.
A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.
The third deal has proved the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-31 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – which is bad news for anyone in their late 20s.
With less than 24 hours before the summit, the two sides were closing in on a deal. EU negotiators gave up a demand that EU students pay UK rates of university tuition, although they will get a discount on steep international rates. The UK also made a concession, agreeing to allow in 100,000 young EU citizens a year, having previously wanted fewer to keep the numbers down.
To maximise its leverage on tuition fees, the EU is linking the three agreements, warning they must come into force together.
EU negotiators want their students to pay tuition fees at UK levels instead of the much higher international rate. Photograph: Chris Ison/PA
Will the UK be included in Made in Europe?
Not on Friday. The UK has been pushing for inclusion in the EU’s Made in Europe plan, a protectionist scheme to favour EU companies when public money is being spent on goods such as electric cars, renewable energy and nuclear technology. Inclusion in Made in Europe is a big priority for the Burnham government, which has dangled major concessions on tuition fees to make sure British firms are not shut out.
The problem for London is that the EU lawmakers have not finalised the Made in Europe law, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act. Many EU member states want to include the UK, but France and the European parliament take a stricter position.
The EU law is not expected to be agreed until spring 2027. To help the British government, which has linked a generous offer on youth mobility with Made in Europe, the European Commission proposed delaying agreement on tuition fees by six months. But member states want precise guarantees now about equal treatment for EU students.
Another problem is that British inclusion in Made in Europe requires the UK to sign up to EU trade-defence policies. The EU, for instance, has imposed high tariffs on “unfairly subsidised” Chinese electric cars and fears the UK, which has not followed suit, could become an alternative route into the EU if Chinese companies set up in Britain and sell into the bloc. The EU is calling on the UK to align with its trade-defence policies, but the UK insists it can guard against circumvention without copying the EU.
In a sign of possible tensions, an earlier summit text proposing a trusted partnership on economic security has been downgraded to a partnership.
An agreement expected next year will bring the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. Photograph: CW Images/Alamy
What happens next?
Beyond the headline deals, the EU-UK draft summit statement opens the door to British integration in European policies on energy, crime-fighting, educational exchange, tech and foreign policy cooperation.
The next major agreement, targeted for next year, is bringing the UK back into the EU’s internal electricity market. This is a priority for five EU member states: Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Luxembourg. They argue that Britain’s inclusion in the EU electricity market is essential to take advantage of the nascent green power boom in the North Sea. In return for market access, the UK will be required to contribute to the EU budget to aid the development of poorer EU regions.
Beyond that, the two sides will “explore opportunities” for the UK to join the Erasmus student exchange programme after 2027; the current arrangement applies only for the 2027-8 academic year.
In a win for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects. The sides will sign a digital partnership, which includes joint work on AI safety, and examine how to share data on law enforcement and border management.
Is this joining the EU by the back door?
Far from it. A lot of diplomatic plates are spinning, but the UK remains outside the EU’s biggest economic clubs: the single market and the customs union. It also has no decision-making powers inside the EU.
Burnham says he will set out the long-term options for the future relationship after this week’s summit. “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain,” he said on Monday in a major speech. But amid concerns among some cabinet ministers about reopening Brexit divides, the prime minister appears to be taking a more cautious approach. He said the process would take time and insisted that “at every stage the British people will be the boss”.
The EU has welcomed Britain’s interest in rejoining but is wary of a protracted negotiation that could be reversed by an anti-EU British government.
In an echo of the Brexit years, EU insiders say, once again, that it is up to Britain to define what it wants.
summary: Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility UK politics live – latest updates The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc. It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa. Continue reading...
title: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?

body:
The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.
In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.
“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”
Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.
“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”
There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.
The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.
The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.
Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.
The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.
In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.
Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.
In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.
In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.
The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.
Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.
“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”
The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.
summary: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states. In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent. Continue reading...
title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel

body:
The Israeli military crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza on Wednesday in its first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed last October, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Israeli tanks rolled along the Salah al-Din road, Gaza’s main north-south route, a day after the US-backed Board of Peace, a body overseeing the ceasefire, accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities.
An Israeli military spokesperson said troops were carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of the yellow line in central Gaza.
The operation lasted about 24 hours and on Thursday the military said it had been “completed”.
The IDF has not commented extensively on the operation, which came as the Israeli opposition politician, Gadi Eisenkot, has been seeking to form a government without the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his political reputation on promises to keep Israel safe.
A Gaza security source told AFP there was “intense Israeli artillery shelling” north of Nuseirat refugee camp and reported Israeli military vehicles in central Gaza “amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes since midday”.
Hamas condemned the Israeli raid and the forced displacement of Palestinians as “a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement” and a dangerous escalation. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Hamas’s statement.
Residents reported hearing tank fire in the area. Palestinian medics said one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the site of the raid.
After the statement from the IDF that it had concluded the tank raid to dismantle a suspected Hamas tunnel, the defence ministry’s body in charge of civilian affairs in Palestinian territories, Cogat, said Palestinians would again be free to move in the targeted areas near al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps.
In separate incidents on Wednesday, Palestinian medics said two people were killed by Israeli fire, one in Deir al-Balah and the other in Gaza City. The Israeli military said it was unaware of any incident in Deir al-Balah and had struck a militant in Gaza City.
Israel has stepped up its attacks on Hamas, which it says has been regrouping and rearming. Hamas has accused Israel of trying to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025.
Israeli strikes have continued since the ceasefire, and Hamas remains armed.
Last week, an Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.
The body overseeing Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza has accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, leaving Palestinians in dire conditions and the ceasefire at risk of collapse.
In its second report to the UN security council since the truce began 13 months ago, the Trump-led Board of Peace said the gap between what was agreed and what was happening on the ground remained the biggest threat to the deal. The report, seen by Reuters, warned that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.
Gaza’s health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Israel launched its military campaign in response to the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed.
In June, an independent UN inquiry determined that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children. A previous report by the commission in September 2025 found that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, and Israeli officials, including the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, incited those acts. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) for war crimes.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report

Eight people were injured on Wednesday evening when a driver struck Palestinian residents at four separate locations in Kafr Qasim, a city in central Israel.
Footage shared on social media appears to show the car accelerating towards people, all Palestinians, at several locations in the city, striking them before driving away. Three of those injured were in moderate condition, and several of the victims were women leaving a nearby wedding, the Times of Israel reported.
Haaretz has reported that investigators are examining whether the driver struck people deliberately. Avi Levy, a police district commander, said the incident appeared to be a hit-and-run and that the driver had tested positive for drugs. He said the Shin Bet security service was taking part in the investigation and said: “As of this moment, nothing is coming up. The suspect has no criminal record.”
The incident prompted Arab lawmakers and activists to accuse Israeli politicians of fuelling hostility towards Arab citizens. Benjamin Netanyahu has called Arab parties “terror supporters” and said partnering with them would put Israel’s security at risk. The parties won a record 19 seats in the Knesset in the country’s recent election.
Yousef Jabareen, the chair of the Joint List, said the incident “raises difficult questions about the claim that the driver lost control”. He said: “I’ve been warning for weeks that the incitement against Arab citizens will turn into assaults and even assassinations.”
Said Issa, a community activist in Kafr Qasim, described the incident as an “act of terror”. “Someone who loses control of his vehicle might hit one or two vehicles, but not multiple people in several different places,” Issa said. “The attacker struck at four locations, one after the other.”
In a separate incident in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian foreign ministry called on Monday for an Israeli settler to be held accountable after eight Palestinians were run over and injured in Tuqu, south-east of Bethlehem. Local sources told the Anadolu news agency that the driver had first struck three young men, then returned and ran over five others who had gathered to help them.

body:
Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.
Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.
She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.
The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.
Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”
The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.
Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.
The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.
Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.
Bennett said: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”
Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism.
If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.
The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing.
Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an important step, but the struggle is not over yet.”
summary: Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area. Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street . Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed. A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said.
Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran, sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found.
Suleimani, the head of Iran’s foreign military operations, was killed in a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. Iranian officials have repeatedly vowed to avenge his killing.
Merchant had testified that he was forced into the plot to protect his family in the Iranian capital Tehran from the Guards, adding that he thought he would get caught before anyone was killed, multiple media outlets reported.
He said he was never ordered to kill a specific person but noted his Iranian contact had mentioned three people in connection with the plot – Trump, the former US president Joe Biden and former UN ambassador Nikki Haley.
But Todd Blanche, the United States attorney general, insisted on Tuesday that the plot was against Trump.
“An Iranian agent who came to the United States to coordinate an assassination attempt against President Trump has been justly sentenced for his criminal conduct,” Blanche said after Merchant was sentenced to 330 months’ imprisonment.
“The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable.”
US officials previously said Merchant had “close ties to Iran” and described his alleged plot as “straight out of the Iranian regime’s playbook”.
Merchant was arrested on 12 July 2024 as he planned to leave the country.
summary: Asif Merchant, allegedly linked to Iran, found by court to have sought retribution over Qassem Suleimani death A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison on Tuesday for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani, the Department of Justice said. Asif Merchant, who had alleged ties to Iran , sought to hire a hitman to assassinate a politician or a government official in the United States, a Brooklyn court found. Continue reading...

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.
For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.
Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”
Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.
“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.
“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”
In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.
They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.
“Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.
She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”
The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.
Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.
The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.
The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.
There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.
With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.
But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.
“We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.
summary: Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them. For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh. Continue reading...
title: ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling

body:
Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision.
The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.
The ICJ president, Yuji Iwasawa, said a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court found that “the Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya”.
The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang-rapes and burned-down villages.
Nearly a decade later, in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, crowds of Rohingya people watching on outdoor TV screens leaped up in celebration and applause as the final verdict was read out.
One Rohingya survivor, Yousuf Ali, had travelled to the court to hear the verdict. “Today, we have finally been heard, and it is a profound relief,” he said. “This judgment gives hope to our children and the next generation of Rohingya. But our fight is not over.”
Governments had been anxiously awaiting the decision handed down in the Netherlands, where the UN-run court is based, in part because the ruling will set a precedent for genocide claims, notably a high-profile case against Israel.
In what could become a crucial factor for the Gaza case, where Israel claims its mass killings are part of a counter-terrorism operation, judges dismissed Myanmar’s claims of carrying out legitimate military operations against insurgents.
Genocide, defined after the Nazi Holocaust by a 1948 UN convention, is harder to prove than war crimes because it requires evidence of specific “intent” to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Iwasawa said during the reading of the decision that the court was “fully convinced that Myanmar committed acts falling under … the genocide convention with an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in Myanmar”.
After the ruling, Britain’s foreign minister, Ed Miliband, said the government was expelling Myanmar’s defence attaché and called “urgently” for a session at the UN security council, the body that has the power to enforce ICJ rulings.
The case was raised by the Gambia, a Muslim-majority state, on behalf of Myanmar survivors. It rested on claims of genocidal statements and “patterns of conduct” that showed attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state, including gunning down people as they fled and blocking their return.
In January, the ICJ held closed-door sessions to hear from survivors who had travelled from camps in Bangladesh. More than a million Rohingya still live there, in the world’s largest refugee settlement, and fewer than 600,000 are estimated to remain in Buddhist-majority Myanmar.
Refugees who had fled to Bangladesh told the Guardian in 2017 of a massacre in the village of Tula Toli, where survivors described systematic shooting of civilians, mass graves and the drowning of children in a river. That village, which satellite footage later showed had been burned down, was one of several analysed by rights investigators and built a case for genocide.
During hearings, the Gambian justice minister, Dawda Jallow, told the court the case was not “about esoteric issues of international law”. “It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow. “The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction.”
Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to “prevent births”. Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.
The court appeared to back that assessment, accusing the military of using sexual violence to “physically and mentally impair the willingness and ability of the [Rohingya] population to procreate”, referring to cultural stigma for rape survivors. Myanmar had also imposed other measures to restrict births, the court ruled, such as limits of two children per Rohingya family.
Myanmar has denied carrying out a genocide, claiming its actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted guerrilla-style attacks. Its military responded with massive “clearance operations”.
However, judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the international criminal court (ICC), which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states, on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
During a reading of the decision that lasted more than two hours in a packed Great Hall of Justice in The Hague, Iwasawa called for Myanmar to provide reparations and restitution. This included allowing the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, returning or replacing their property, and providing physical and mental rehabilitation.
The ruling was also significant as it formally classified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group under international law, something they have been denied by Myanmar, which refers to them as Bengalis or foreign migrants.
Reached by phone shortly after he left the courtroom, the lead counsel for the case against Myanmar told the Guardian the mood had been emotional in the room as the judgment was read out in front of his legal team, which included Rohingya.
“This is the ICJ recognising their history of discrimination, recognising them as a group, recognising the horrific violence they endured and suffered,” said Arsalan Suleman. “It was a really emotional moment for them and the whole team. We felt the weight of the court’s judgment.”
Israel and its chief ally, the US, have been closely following the Myanmar case, as the decision provides the strongest hint of how judges could assess the Gaza case, brought by South Africa. UN independent investigations, as well as genocide scholars, have already said Israel has committed acts of genocide in Gaza.
A judgment finding Myanmar had breached the convention has been predicted to lead to the US imposing sanctions on ICJ judges, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay.
Washington had considered the Rohingya crisis to be a genocide, based on a decision by the Biden administration. However, the administration of Donald Trump has been on the offensive against international rights bodies, including imposing sanctions on the ICC.
The US state department said in a statement that it would study the ICJ’s decision “to fully assess its implications” and that “the proper interpretation of the genocide convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicisation of the ICJ”.
It reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”.
The Trump administration of has been implacably opposed to international legal organisations. On Thursday, the president used a trilateral meeting with Russia and China on Thursday to condemn “rogue globalist organisations”. But Trump’s ire has been directed most towards the ICC, a separate body which the administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick”, rather than the ICJ.
Two other ICJ cases dealing with atrocities in the 1990s Balkan wars fell short of finding states directly responsible for genocide, although Serbia was found legally responsible for failing to prevent or punish genocide committed by Bosnian Serb troops at the Srebrenica massacre.
Other UN tribunals have established genocide in only a handful of cases since the Holocaust, including Cambodia’s Khmer Rouge rule in the 1970s and the 1994 mass killings in Rwanda.
summary: Judgment finds ‘intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population’ after case seen as critical test for dealing with most serious of state crimes Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 military campaign, the world’s highest court has ruled, in a historic and unprecedented decision. The judgment from the international court of justice (ICJ) – which has never previously found a state responsible for genocide – ends a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes. Continue reading...
title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, world’s top court rules

Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.
Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on Thursday.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, was set on fire late on Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.
Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.
During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.
On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses were set on fire, authorities said.
Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.
At least 37 branches and offices of Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires since 10 November, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday, the bank said.
On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

body:
The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
71
Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.
Get in touch
Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

- Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan
- Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall
Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.
In 2022, I was living in an area that had less risk of flooding. I had a small child and my PhD thesis was just a few weeks away. I tried to avoid flood news on social media until I saw a picture of a two-year-old girl who was buried in mud. It was probably her last breath. She died after that. That was the turning point.
I immediately called my friends, six to seven people, in a mosque. I talked to them: “We don’t know what to do, but at least we can start from somewhere.” Initially, it was food. We hired some commercial cooks.
We planned to work only in villages close to our city. A lot of people were taking refuge in nearby high places, high enough that the water did not reach them. On the first day we went with some food to the nearest village.
When the rain is over, the sun comes out. Usually, it’s a good sign. But, in those areas, it didn’t feel good. It felt like it opened a scar. The pain that was hiding somehow had become open. It was like being naked. I could see trolleys, tractors, vehicles and homes all drowned in the flood. There was nothing from the government, nothing from any development sector. There was no camp. People were just living under open skies.
Men felt that their women being in an open place was a kind of emotional damage for them. It was not normal for most of the people here. Many women never came out. They came out for their work, the agriculture work, but not sitting that openly among the public. Their hair was full of dust and dry mud. Their clothes had a heavy layer of dry mud; no shoes on their feet. Mothers were not breastfeeding. Babies crying for milk, and the milk was not there. Mothers trying to soothe them with fake sounds.
The cows did not have feed and were not giving milk. Many of the animals were lost, their bodies wide open, decomposed. Then the water, which stayed there for a week, started to smell very bad. There was no good smell.
We prepared food in the morning. Then we prepared food at lunchtime. We generally finished distributing food around 8pm. One night it was 11pm and we thought some people might not have food. So we just cooked some food late at night and went to every camp.
One old woman started to laugh. I was surprised. I asked her: “It’s OK, we have food, but why are you laughing?” And she said: “I was just complaining, ‘Lord, that you left me with an empty stomach today.’ And suddenly you appeared.”
It was a very strange experience for her. For us also. People, when they are in tough conditions, are attached to their beliefs. And, when things like that come up, they establish a spiritual connection with the people who are helping out.
We posted on social media. We tried to mobilise. A lot of people contacted us who were from other parts of Pakistan. Money poured in and we kept expanding the team. From two or three villages, we started to cover the entire district, and then almost the entire region.
The government protocols were to not go into certain areas that looked dangerous or were not safe for a boat. Families were trapped, many, many kilometres into the water. There was no land in one village. Small wooden cupboards were hung on trees so stuff could be saved from the water. The immediate shelter was a big tree near them. The whole family was in the tree. The elders were lying on the branches. They somehow made a swing for the kids. They spent days in those trees.
A few villages were completely destroyed. Not a single home was standing. Everything was in shock, even the trees. One old woman who was living with her married kids was not ready to leave that rubble. She was so attached to that home that she felt like there was no life after it. She had a small cupboard in which she kept some small things to sell, for her independence. She was so concerned about that small cupboard. When I reached there, that cupboard was all broken.
One day I had a fever and my wife stopped me: “Don’t go out – you are not well enough to help other people.” But I still went out to a village to help people. When we reached there, I got news that the city we were living in – which I thought was safe – suddenly was a source of threat. There was water coming toward the city. Within hours, the water would be in the city. My family was there. And I was almost 100km away.
So I rushed back. But the road toward the city was cut off by the flood. There was no way I could go back to my family. I called my wife and I asked them to stay vigilant and look out for water in the city. I gave them some suggestions: how they could save themselves and evacuate. That was a very, very tough call.
Eventually, the city was saved. Next day, we took a boat to get past the road that was cut off. Sitting in that boat, I was thinking about my family. Once I reached the other side, I called some people to take me home.
When I reached home, I had a very strong fever and I spent that day at home. I tried to behave normally, but everybody knew I was not feeling well. I took one day off from community work.
The next day I wanted to stop. But the problem was, I was in the middle of that network. If I stop, this whole process will stop. This whole network of relief work will stop.
The next day, even with a high fever, I left for the field because I didn’t want that to stop. When I grew up, the community fabric was very strong. It was common practice that whenever people got sick, got in an accident, hospitalised, people would visit the person and share some money.
This was the kind of culture I observed happening around me.
I went back to those areas where the flood came. There was still some water standing so there were remains of that devastation. But there’s a very common sweet in that area we call jalebi. I can smell that sweet in those villages. I see shops open. I see farmers, labourers. I felt good watching people working again. It looked like life was coming back.
There was an annual poetry event happening three months after the flood. Saraiki culture is very rich, one of the oldest. I was consulted by one of my friends who is the organiser of that event. Should we suspend this year’s events or not?
I said you should never suspend the event. Let people believe the normalisation, let people believe in the spirit of survival. They organised the poetry event.

summary: When the floods hit Pakistan he went out to help. Then the water reached his own family. This is Imran Lodhi’s story Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development . The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan , a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan . Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense . Continue reading...

An expert has determined that Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is mentally competent to face charges of keeping child sexual abuse material in storage in California, a judge said on Thursday.
Markle’s defense lawyer said they would not contest the finding by Dr Amie Gerodimos. The exam was ordered after his arrest at a senior care center in Lakeland, Florida, on 6 November.
Investigators seized approximately 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, according to the FBI.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle is in custody while the case remains in federal court in Tampa. It will eventually shift to a similar court in southern California.
Markle was initially released on bond but was arrested again when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor on 10 November.
He had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the US and settle in Florida.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half-brother found child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. The discovery led to a search of the two US storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute images. The Women and Children Protection Center, a branch of the Philippine national police, filed a formal criminal complaint against Markle on Monday, police spokesperson Brig Gen Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.
The complaint was filed with the prosecutor’s office following an investigation into digital devices found at Markle’s former home in Cebu City, the statement said. The prosecutor’s office will assess the case for possible charges.
Markle did not attend his daughter Meghan’s 2018 wedding to Prince Harry at Windsor Castle. She said at the time he needed to tend to his health. Meghan is an American citizen who starred in the US television drama Suits.

Markle’s defense lawyer said they would not contest the finding by Dr Amie Gerodimos. The exam was ordered after his arrest at a senior care center in Lakeland, Florida, on 6 November. Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived.
GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait.
The hype around the release led to schools encouraging pupils not to miss lessons in anticipation of “GTA flu”, a term coined for the swathe of absences when GTA V was released in 2013, which is expected to recur over the coming weeks. The human resources platform Remote said there had been a 32% increase in leave requests worldwide on Thursday.
Birchgrove comprehensive school in Swansea, south Wales, had warned parents and carers that despite the “considerable excitement”, studies should remain a priority.
The Sandon secondary school in Essex entered students into a raffle for £10 Amazon vouchers, a lunchtime queue-jump pass and free Christmas dinners as incentives to stop them bunking off to play as the game’s dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia.
Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, took a different approach in a country with an estimated 550 million gamers. Modi posted 10 images on X modelled on the game’s artwork that compared India today with the time of GTA V’s release.
The Indian politician, who has stepped up efforts to appeal to younger voters since youth-led protests over jobs and education, wrote: “India is playing a whole new game!”
Downing Street said Andy Burnham would not be playing the new instalment. Asked whether the UK prime minister would be exploring Vice City, the Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar’s fictional take on Miami, a spokesperson said: “His diary is very full.”
The launch of GTA VI generated more than 2.6m posts on social media in 24 hours, according to social media monitor Visibrain.
Approximately 1,850 messages about the game were published per minute – 7% more than the number of posts at the start of the 2026 men’s Fifa World Cup.
Among the game’s fans is Sean Little, a self-employed painter and decorator. He persuaded his wife and daughter to sign a “non-interference contract”, giving him a week off dad duties to play in peace in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland.
Myles_Away, a UK-based streamer on the Twitch platform, told the BBC he planned to play for “13 or 14 hours” on Thursday.
He said: “I played all last night, and then I slept, woke up, and [came] right into this interview,” adding: “Obviously not everybody is able to drop the money required. [Consoles] are very expensive at the moment, so they are able to experience the story through streamers.”
Jacob Joel, a 30-year-old IT professional in Bengaluru, southern India, took the day off to play in a gaming cafe. “We waited around 13 long years to get into GTA VI,” he said. “That is a nostalgic feeling.”
In Bangkok, British tourists Kyle McKee and Emily Todd reserved a PS5 console, TV and a sofa at a gaming centre. McKee, 27, told the AFP news agency: “It’s the fear of missing out, honestly.”
The launch also surpassed broadband records in the UK. Virgin Media O2 said its evening traffic between 8pm and 10pm on Wednesday was 9.4% higher than the previous record, set last week by “pre-loading” for GTA VI.
BT and EE networks also recorded their highest-ever home broadband traffic peak in the lead-up to the release.
Data from the two brands found that Fort Augustus, in Loch Ness, Scotland, recorded the biggest percentage uplift in gaming download traffic anywhere in the UK since the start of the pre-downloads last week.
Sony’s shares were up 2.92% on the Tokyo stock exchange after the global launch, with the analytics firm Omdia estimating that GTA VI could generate $3.2bn (£2.4bn) in sales by the end of the year.
summary: Hotly anticipated Bonnie and Clyde-inspired adventure GTA VI has gamers glued to their screens around the world Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived. GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait. Continue reading...

It has been a memorable few days for Wales. At the weekend, the men’s rugby team secured a historic win against New Zealand – their first victory over the All Blacks in more than 70 years. Then on Thursday evening came another culturally significant moment when Cardiff rolled out the red carpet to celebrate the first Welsh-language dub of the Star Wars franchise.
Stars of stage and screen who voiced the words of Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, C-3PO et al in Welsh (Cymraeg) over the original 1977 Star Wars film took the plaudits at the Cineworld Cardiff screening.
Among those on the red carpet was Mark Lewis Jones, who has appeared in shows ranging from The Crown to Game of Thrones and had a role in the 2017 Star Wars film The Last Jedi. In this version of Star Wars, he is a Welsh Darth Vader.
He said he thought Welsh was a good language for Vader. “It has an ancient, poetic sense. It gives him that status, that authority,” said Jones, who hails from the Wrexham area in north-east Wales. “I give all my characters north-east Wales accents,” he said.
Also taking a bow was Osian Morgan – well known in Wales for his appearances in the Welsh-language soap opera Pobol y Cwm – who voices Luke Skywalker.
“There’s so much excitement about this project and the cast is unbelievable,” Morgan said. “I think in Wales we’re on an upward trajectory and this instils a lot of hope. The future is exciting for Wales, particularly in the creative arts. The talent is vast.”
Asked if he felt the pressure of being Luke Skywalker, he said he was thrilled rather than nervous. “He’s had such an important impact on my life,” he said. Morgan was also pleased that his 10-year-old brother’s first experience of Star Wars would be in the medium of Welsh. “The fact that Luke tonight in the Welsh language can have that impact on kids here is fantastic.”
Rhys Ifans, who has appeared in Harry Potter and Spider-Man films, had the tough job of standing in for Alec Guinness as the Jedi master Obi-Wan Kenobi. Sadly, he did not make it to Cardiff for the event.
His brother, Llŷr Ifans, the Welsh voice of the droid C-3PO, was present, however, which was apposite as C-3PO is “fluent in over 6 million forms of communication” – including, clearly, Welsh.
Ifans said: “When I first heard about it, I thought: wow, what are we doing – Star Wars in Welsh? The idea has settled. C-3PO is a genius who speaks over 6 million languages. Now he speaks 6 million and one. He speaks the best language in the world.”
Asked what accent he used for his C-3PO, Ifans said: “There are no accents in space. But it’s more about the character. He lives on his nerves and speaks staccato. I had to bring in those aspects.”
The Welsh-language version of the 1977 film (subsequently retitled Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope) has been produced by Lucasfilm and Disney in collaboration with the Welsh-language broadcaster S4C and the Welsh government via its Creative Wales agency.
Its Welsh title is Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd (New Hope). Those not lucky enough to be at the screening in Cardiff will be able to hear the immortal line “May the Force be with you” in Welsh (“A boed i’r Grym fod gyda chi”) when the version is broadcast on S4C platforms on Christmas Day.
Thursday’s screening wasn’t as glitzy as a London or Los Angeles premiere, but it had charm. Côr Bechgyn Glantaf, a schoolboys’ choir from Cardiff, performed as the crowds – including many children – arrived and made their way up the escalators of the multiplex to screens eight and nine. Band Pres Llareggub, which bills itself as a Bronx hip-hop-inspired, New Orleans-tinged brass band with attitude from north Wales, also provided a musical backdrop.
S4C’s chief executive, Geraint Evans, described the screening as a “hugely proud moment”. He said: “Most importantly, it will give Welsh-speaking children the thrill of hearing some of cinema’s most beloved characters speak their language for the very first time, showing that Welsh can tell any story.”
There are a few connections linking Wales and Star Wars, not least that a version of the Millennium Falcon was built in south-west Wales.
Mark Williams, who oversaw an exhibition about the Millennium Falcon, said he felt the Welsh-language version of the film was long overdue. “I’ve been saying for years it should be done, especially with the ties that Wales has with the franchise,” he said.
Also at the screening was the cabinet minister for enterprise, connectivity and energy in the Welsh government, Adam Price, who said it was an excellent opportunity for Welsh actors and production staff to work with a major Hollywood studio.
“Seeing one of the most iconic films of all time in Welsh is a great way to make the language more accessible and introduces it to new audiences beyond our shores,” he said.
The Welsh government is aiming to have a million people speaking Cymraeg by 2050. A spokesperson for the Welsh language commissioner’s office said one of its key aims was to increase the use of the language on a community level.
The spokesperson said: “In order to do this, the language must be seen and heard in all aspects of our daily lives. The use of Welsh in such a high-profile film as Star Wars has the potential to attract new audiences and raise awareness of the language.”
summary: Actors Mark Lewis Jones and Osian Morgan, who voiced characters in dub of 1977 film, among guests on red carpet It has been a memorable few days for Wales. At the weekend, the men’s rugby team secured a historic win against New Zealand – their first victory over the All Blacks in more than 70 years. Then on Thursday evening came another culturally significant moment when Cardiff rolled out the red carpet to celebrate the first Welsh-language dub of the Star Wars franchise. Stars of stage and screen who voiced the words of Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, C-3PO et al in Welsh (Cymraeg) over the original 1977 Star Wars film took the plaudits at the Cineworld Cardiff screening. title: ‘Welsh can tell any story’: Cymraeg dub of Star Wars premieres in Cardiff

The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault.
After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime.
Other factors that will help to decide whether he has broken a rule include the “notoriety” of the crimes and the length of time between the verdict and the statement.
A video in which Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, read out a message from the jailed sex offender protesting he was not guilty has remained on YouTube days after ministers asked for it to be removed.
Brand is serving a 10-and-a-half-year term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.
On Thursday night, the UK prime minister said he “wouldn’t leap” to changing the law to force social media companies to take down the content. But he added: “I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down.
“You know, why are we having to hear from from him? We shouldn’t be, and certainly [the victims] shouldn’t be hearing from him.”
According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that “serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner’s crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific.”
The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast “must not contain material about the prisoner’s own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence”.
It is understood that the inquiry is taking into account the right of prisoners to protest their innocence. However, there is a strict protocol governing the way such statements are issued and whether permission has been sought beforehand.
Recent reports have claimed that Brand, who is jailed in the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, is likely to be moved to a category A or B prison instead after protesting his innocence.
It is understood that there has been no such proposal, and he is likely to remain in Littlehey, a specialist prison for sex offenders.
The government has no power to compel YouTube’s direct owner, Google, to remove the video, but has been in “dialogue” with the tech firm over it.
“We trust that they will do the right thing,” a Downing Street spokesperson said when asked about the standoff. They said: “The prime minister’s position on this is that Russell Brand’s victims deserve peace, and we’ve heard enough from him.
“We’ve asked YouTube to remove the content. I would also just point out that they acted before when they suspended Brand’s account from making money. Given he has been convicted of rape by a jury of his peers, we trust that they will act again.”
No 10 was repeatedly asked whether Burnham would personally welcome the video being removed, as well as Brand’s YouTube channel being disabled. It told reporters: “Removal ultimately depends on YouTube and the platform’s terms and conditions.”
A spokesperson for Google said: “We’re aware of the new content and our teams are investigating. We suspended Russell Brand’s channel from the YouTube partner programme in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then.”
Kemi Badenoch said if she was in power she would not immediately demand Google remove the video.
The Conservative leader told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “My personal opinion is that Russell Brand has been convicted. He is guilty under the law. His wife is a separate person. She can make the protestations that she likes.
“I think that immediately demanding the private platforms take things down without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from. If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that.”
summary: Ministry of Justice weighs up comments issued through rapist’s wife as PM asks: ‘Why are we having to hear from him?’ The prison authorities are weighing up whether Russell Brand harassed his victims by issuing comments through his wife insisting he was not guilty of rape and sexual assault. After Andy Burnham called on Google to take down the statement from YouTube, a continuing Ministry of Justice inquiry is focusing on whether Brand has broken rules that are supposed to prevent “serious distress” to the victims of crime. Continue reading...
title: Prison authorities consider whether Russell Brand harassed victims with YouTube message
