Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”, after a man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg.
West Yorkshire police said there was nothing to suggest the incident was politically motivated, although the investigation was at an early stage.
Jim McMahon, the MP for Oldham West, described the attack as “horrific” and said: “Our thoughts are with [Ali], his family, councillors in Bradford and, of course, our members of parliament too.
“Our thoughts are very much with you all at this time.”
Imran Hussain, the MP for Bradford East, said: “This horrific attack is deeply disturbing. My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family.
“No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community. I am receiving regular updates from the police as they deal with this extremely serious incident, and I understand a suspect is in police custody.”
Officers were called just after 11am to reports that a 52-year-old man, a serving Bradford councillor, had been found seriously injured on Manse Street.
Police said: “The man is believed to have first been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to Manse Street where emergency services attended. He was taken to hospital where his condition is described as serious but not life-threatening.”
A 32-year-old man fled to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue but was brought down some time later and arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.
He remains in custody.
Sharon Taylor, a local government minister, named Ali in the House of Lords. Lady Taylor said: “I am afraid I have to mention a very tragic incident that’s occurred in Bradford … where an independent councillor who was out canvassing has been stabbed.
“I would want to send the wishes, that I’m sure noble lords would agree, of the whole house to councillor Ibrar Ali for a speedy recovery, and our thoughts are with all of those in Bradford who are affected by this awful incident.”
Police cordons were in place on Manse Street, Leeds Road and Thornbury Avenue while inquiries are carried out.
Adam, who works in the area and did not want to give his surname, said: “I know the councillor on a personal level and it’s shocking. I just know he’s a very kind, warm-hearted man whose goal is to serve, his life is to help out everyone.
“He just wants everyone to succeed. He definitely didn’t deserve what’s happened.
“The world’s not a nice place.”
Chris Herd, the lord mayor of Bradford, said: “It is deeply distressing that this incident has occurred.
“Councillors work tirelessly on behalf of residents across the district and should be able to carry out their duties safely.
“We will continue to work closely with our colleagues at West Yorkshire police as they investigate this matter and seek to bring those responsible to justice, and would like to thank those who provided aid and support at the time.”
Press Association contributed to this report
summary: Politicians call attack on independent councillor Ibrar Ali canvassing in Bradford Moor ward ‘deeply disturbing’ Politicians have described an attack on a councillor who was canvassing in Bradford as “horrific” and “deeply disturbing”, after a man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. A 32-year-old man is in custody suspected of attacking Ibrar Ali at about 11am on Thursday as the independent councillor was door-knocking in his Bradford Moor ward, leaving him with a stab wound in the leg. California attorney general opens investigation into Nvidia and co-founder Jensen Huang
California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, said on Thursday that his office has “served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia” that is related to reports that the chip-maker’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors. My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Bonta said in a statement. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
Rapping Republican congressman-elect Anthony Constantino skips orientation to dine with Roger Stone
Anthony Constantino, an incoming Republican congressman who called for Donald Trump to pardon Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs in a foul-mouthed victory speech, confirmed a report on Thursday that he skipped orientation this week to dine with former Trump adviser Roger Stone in Florida instead.
“I let my staff pick the office so I can work on more important things such as eating Chicken Parmesan with Roger Stone while planning how to defend us from Radical Democrats,” Constantino said in a statement to the congressional news outlet Punchbowl.
Stone was seen with Constantino earlier this month at a rally in Rome, New York, when JD Vance endorsed him in a speech late in the campaign.
Constantino, a Trump-endorsed sticker magnet from northern New York, narrowly won the race to represent New York’s 21st congressional district, defeating Democrat Blake Gendebien just 1.5 points in a district former Republican congresswoman Elise Stefanik won by over 24 points in 2024.
Constantino was spotted in Washington DC last week, when he told a TMZ reporter that his call for Trump to free Combs from federal prison after his conviction on prostitution-related crimes, “caught attention.”
“I’m the most talked about person entering Congress right now,” he added.
The newly elected congressman is already facing calls from local Republican officials to focus on his work, instead of promoting his sideline as a right-wing rapper best known for a music video attacking Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, which is over 200 miles south of his district along Canadian border.
“The City of Plattsburgh Republican Committee is calling on Congressman-elect Anthony Constantino, to immediately change course, and put the urgent needs of NY-21 first, or face a formal call for his expulsion from Congress,” a local party official said in a statement on Thursday.
“We do not care about your rap career. We do not care about anything that does not directly serve the people of NY-21,” David Souliere, the chairman of the Plattsburgh Republican Committee said. “The residents of this district are counting on real results … if this is not your singular priority, then it is time for you to seriously question whether you belong in this role at all.”

California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, said on Thursday that his office has “served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia” that is related to reports that the chip-maker’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors. My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” Bonta said in a statement. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
An appeals court decided on Thursday that Democratic New Jersey representative LaMonica McIver will continue to face charges related to a skirmish outside an immigration detention center last year when she attempted to conduct an oversight visit there.
The court’s decision to decline McIver’s request to overturn the court’s earlier ruling comes just a day after she pressed the homeland security secretary for the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement operations, telling the secretary: “You are killing people.”
Now, with the court’s decision, she is facing a likely trial for the May 2025 incident.
“Because of a weaponized Department of Justice, and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in a statement on Thursday. “Now, due to the disappointing decision by the third circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”
McIver was charged last year with assaulting, resisting, impeding and interfering with federal officers. The prosecution led to a lengthy legal battle, with McIver claiming the prosecution represented a political attack by the Trump administration.
Democratic US senator Adam Schiff has penned an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal warning about “the systemic risk to the economy” posed by the AI industry – and demanding that Congress rule out a taxpayer-funded bailout should the sector collapse.
Highlighting the turmoil surrounding Nvidia since the spectacular exit of its CEO Jensen Huang, Schiff writes:
This technology [artificial intelligence] has boundless potential to enhance our lives and expand our individual and collective capacity. But as the turmoil around Nvidia reminds us, this swift and massive investment also carries significant risk that an industry downturn or a bubble could destabilize the American economy. In the first six days of the scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO, the sector lost $500bn in value.
Given the risks to our economy and investors, Congress must make sure that industry understands this:No company is too big to fail, and in the event of a financial collapse of the tech sector, there will be no taxpayer-funded bailout.
The AI industry, after less than five years of market power, is already estimated to represent 3.6% of our nation’s economy. But much of its explosive build-out is financed by an opaque debt structure and expectations of increasing profitability. This may be the biggest economic gamble in American history, and policymakers should make clear that Congress and American taxpayers won’t act as its fail-safe should this industry falter under its own immense weight.
Republican congressman Brad Finstad requests hand recount in Minnesota House race after final count shows him losing by 324 votes
In one of the last US House races to be decided, congressman Brad Finstad, a Minnesota Republican, asked for a publicly funded recount after the state canvassing board’s final count showed him losing his seat to Democrat Jake Johnson by 324 votes, the CBS News affiliate WCCO-TV reported.
Nik Marda, Johnson’s campaign manager, told the outlet that the hand recount in 21 southern Minnesota counties, would take place “likely right after Thanksgiving.”
“What we know from history is over the last 40 years, no full recount in a US House race has moved the vote total by this amount,” Marda said. “Nowhere close to it.”
Trump's nominee to lead cybersecurity agency says January 6 2021 storming of US Capitol was not 'an attack'
Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the US homeland security department’s cybersecurity and infrastructure security agency (Cisa), said on Thursday that the US Capitol was not attacked on January 6 2021.
At his Senate confirmation hearing, the nominee, Michael LoSapio, was asked by senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, “Was there an attack on the Capitol of January 6 2021?”
After initially replying, “I don’t know,” LoSapio said, “No, I don’t believe it was an attack.”
LoSapio, the chief information security officer for Palantir, a technology firm founded by JD Vance’s mentor, Peter Thiel, also refused to admit that Joe Biden had won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio told Blumenthal. The senator noted that since election security is a central part of the agency’s mandate, by refusing to accept the fact that Trump lost the 2020 election, LoSapio was “disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill”.
The week after the 2020 election, as Trump falsely claimed that count had been rigged, Cisa was one of a number of federal agencies with oversight of election infrastructure to issue a statement calling the election “the most secure in American history” and noting that there was “no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes, or was in any way compromised.”
After he returned to the White House last year, Trump signed an April 2025 presidential memorandum directing executive offices to take steps to address supposed “risks from Chris Krebs,” who lead Cisa in 2020. “Krebs, through CISA, falsely and baselessly denied that the 2020 election was rigged and stolen, including by inappropriately and categorically dismissing widespread election malfeasance and serious vulnerabilities with voting machines,” Trump’s memorandum claimed.
Lawmakers in the Senate failed to advance another war powers resolution to limit military action in Iran. The vote, 48-51, largely fell along party lines. However, three GOP senators – Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky – crossed the aisle to support the resolution. While John Fetterman of Pennsylvania voted “no”.
Earlier today, Fetterman, who frequently breaks with his party to side with Republicans in Congress, underscored his unequivocal support for Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader in the next Congress. Fetterman said that Senator Chris Van Hollen, from Maryland, will probably lose his bid for the top position. “No one’s ever heard of this guy, and then he started going after Israel, and then he flew to go hold hands with the guy that beats his wife, and he really endeared himself to the progressives,” Fetterman said, referencing Van Hollen’s trip to El Salvador Kilmar Ábrego García, a man who lives in his state but was sent to a mega-prison by the Trump administration last year despite an immigration court order preventing his deportation.
Fetterman also said he was “considering things” when asked about a potential 2028 re-election bid. When asked by MS Now whether he fears a potential primary challenge in the next election cycle, Fetterman feigned fear. “Oh, oh, that could happen. How about the guy that loves Hamas?” the senator said, referring to Ahmed Moor, the writer and activist who was born in Gaza and announced he would compete in 2028.
Donald Trump said that he will hold a press conference at the White House on Fridayat 12pm ET following a“great and highly consequential trip” to the Philippines and China, which included a trilateral summit with Xi Jinping andVladimir Putin. The president announced the briefing on Truth Social, and also said he would discuss the trade deals he signed on his trip.
A federal judge in Florida ruled Thursday that Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and Penguin Random House can move forward, handing the president a legal victory in his ongoing fights with major media organizations. The suit centers on a book by two Times reporters and a series of articles that Trump alleges were “false, malicious, defamatory, and disparaging” and intended to undermine his 2024 presidential campaign, which he ultimately won. The complaint also targets reporting by longtime Times White House correspondent Peter Baker.
Senate fails to advance war powers resolution to curb military action in Iran
Lawmakers in the Senate failed to advance another war powers resolution to limit military action in Iran.
The vote, 48-51, largely fell along party lines. However, three GOP senators – Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky – crossed the aisle to support the resolution. While John Fetterman of Pennsylvania voted “no”.
Chris Murphy, a Democratic senator, missed the vote, after recently suffering a stroke.
John Cornyn of Texas, who is leaving the US Senate after nearly 24 years following his primary loss to a Trump-backed challenger, told the Associated Press he would not support T Elliot Gaiser, a 37-year-old official in the justice department, to serve on a district court in northern Texas.
“He’s not from Texas. He hasn’t been vetted. And this is a lifetime job, and there’s better-qualified people to hold that job,” Cornyn said on Wednesday.
Cornyn’s refusal to support Gaiser came a day after he got into a heated verbal argument with a fellow Texas Republican senator, Ted Cruz, on the Senate floor over Gaiser’s nomination, according to the Washington Sun.
The two men’s yelling match was reportedly so loud that those in the press gallery could hear Cornyn tell Cruz: “I don’t find you credible. I’m mad at you.”
At one point, Cornyn told Cruz he was upset at someone “for ending my career”, though it is unclear whether Cornyn was referring to Trump or Cruz.
House lawmakers announce formation of bipartisan AI safety caucus
Three House lawmakers announced the formation of a bipartisan group focused on artificial intelligence safety, the first of its kind. Republican congressman Nathaniel Moran of Texas and Democrats, George Whitesides of California and Don Beyer of Virginia, unveiled the the House AI Safety and Innovation caucus, which will also focus on the “security risks posed by increasingly advanced AI systems while ensuring the United States remains a global leader in innovative AI technologies”.
“We don’t have to choose between innovation and safety. We can, and we should, do both. Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan issue,” Moran said in a statement.
Meanwhile, Whitesides added: “Now is the time to build bipartisan consensus and advance commonsense guardrails we know will reduce the most serious risks. Americans are rightly concerned about where this technology is heading, but too often the debate in Washington is framed as a choice between doing nothing and banning AI altogether. That’s a false choice.”
The caucus will, among other things, develop legislative proposals and endorse existing bipartisan bills that create guardrails against the most serious AI risks, as well as meeting with AI developers and technical experts when safety incidents occur.
Democratic lawmakers targeted by Trump for video reminding troops to refuse 'illegal orders' address reporters one year later
The six Democratic members of Congress who Donald Trump accused of “sedition, punishable by death” after they posted a 90-second long video reminding active-duty US service members to refuse “illegal orders”, are speaking to reporters a year after they drew the president’s wrath.
A reminder that senators Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin and congressional representatives Maggie Goodlander, Jason Crow, Chris DeLuzio and Chrissy Houlahan all posted a video on social media saying that the Trump administration “is pitting our uniformed military and intelligence professionals against American citizens”.
They added: “You must refuse illegal orders.”
Trump said that “each one of these traitors to our Country should be arrested and put on trial.” He also reposted a message from another user reading: “Hang them George Washington would!”
Federal prosecutors had sought an indictment against the Democrats who participated in the video, but a grand jury in Washington DC declined to indict the six lawmakers, all of whom have military or intelligence backgrounds.
In February a US judge also blocked the Pentagon’s effort to reduce Kelly’s retired military rank and pension pay for his role in the video.
“I think it was important for us to come together a year later to say, number one, we stand behind the video we made. Number two, we won’t be intimidated out of calling out threats to our democracy,” Slotkin told reporters today on Capitol Hill. “We stand behind our men and women in uniform for the amazing work that they do, and I think we feel strongly that if this is the thing we need to do to stand up for the country we love, we have no problem doing that.”
Kelly added: “I will tell you that none of us are backing down. Last year, I said we were the first ones through the breach, and we’re seeing that now. Trump is threatening more members of Congress with prosecution for doing their jobs, and asking for asking questions that he just doesn’t want to answer.”
summary: State’s attorney general Rob Bonta says ‘conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags’ as he opens investigation Sign up for the Breaking News US email The National Security Agency is seeing a third day of disruptions to its internal network, NSA Net, which allows staff to share highly classified information with each other , according to the New York Times. The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors. A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed. The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role. The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December . Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race. Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. In the Senate, Republicans unanimously backed John Thune to continue leading the conference. Continue reading...

Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to put a man to death for the killing of a Houston jeweler during a $3.6m diamond heist.
Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was scheduled to receive a three-drug injection at 6pm at Florida state prison in Raiford. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, was set to receive a lethal injection about an hour later at a prison in Texas and become the ninth person executed by that state this year. The planned executions of the two septuagenarians in one day reflect the ageing of the US death row population.
Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his office in January 1996.
On Thursday, Overton woke up at 5am and remained compliant, a Florida department of corrections spokesperson, Jordan Kirkland, said during a news conference. He did not meet with any visitors or a spiritual adviser.
Florida has carried out more than half the nation’s 37 executions this year under Ron DeSantis, the state’s outgoing Republican governor who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. Thursday’s scheduled executions come amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US after Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in October.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
On Thursday, the US supreme court denied a final appeal in the Florida case while an appeal remained pending in the Texas case.
Overton was convicted in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder and received a death sentence for each. Defense attorneys had argued that investigators had planted the DNA evidence.
The MacIvors were found dead in their Tavernier, Florida, home in August 1991, according to court records. Autopsies determined both were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.
Investigators collected DNA evidence from the scene but initially found no match with samples in the state’s database. But Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996. Authorities said a sample taken from him matched the sample collected at the MacIvors’ home, and he was charged with their killings.
In the Texas case, Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes had arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours. According to court records, she opened the door for him and his brother the night of the shooting and also distracted the security guard at Dennes’s request.
The guard, who was shot twice but recovered, identified Dennes as his attacker.
Police found the jeweler’s body upon entering his office, according to court filings. The documents said officers found the jeweler’s safe empty with no sign of the diamonds or the $200,000 in cash he was supposed to have on hand. The diamonds have never been recovered.
Dennes’s attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove that he killed Szucs.
Prosecutors noted in a recent court filing that Dennes admitted guilt during a Spanish-language interview with Telemundo in 2022.
“I did those things, so I am guilty,” Dennes told Telemundo, adding that he regretted taking a man’s life, the prosecutor’s filing said.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.
summary: State to execute man convicted of two counts of first-degree murder while Texas also plans to put a man to death Florida is set Thursday to carry out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas plans to put a man to death for the killing of a Houston jeweler during a $3.6m diamond heist. Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was scheduled to receive a three-drug injection at 6pm at Florida state prison in Raiford. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, was set to receive a lethal injection about an hour later at a prison in Texas and become the ninth person executed by that state this year. The planned executions of the two septuagenarians in one day reflect the ageing of the US death row population. Continue reading...

Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media.
With surgery too risky for full-grown hippos such as Fiona, who weighed in the region of 2,500lb (1,113kg), veterinarians tried an alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.
The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to the Cincinnati zoo tossed it in the air, after which it bounced off a ceiling fan and fell into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press. Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.
Days later, however, she began to lose appetite and staff at the zoo were forced to feed Fiona more in the hope that she would eventually get the hat through her digestive system.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo statement said.
The zoo announced on Wednesday that the animal care team was using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move things along, according to the Associated Press.
Fiona was sedated a second time on Tuesday for evaluation. After an ultrasound, veterinarians could see her intestines still trying to push the hat through. They also used a 9ft scope colonoscopy to view her intestines.
“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo had said on social media. Fiona remained out of her enclosure while she was receiving treatment.
Footage from the procedure released by the zoo on Wednesday shows her snorting and moving around her enclosure, which vets said was a sign of progress. Her hydration levels were being monitored.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond. Thank you for your continued love and concern for Fiona and her dedicated care team,” the zoo said.
This wasn’t the first time Fiona’s health had been at risk. She became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017, when she couldn’t stand on her own.
Hopes for Fiona’s recovery had garnered support from across the country including, apparently, from Timothy, another hippo at the San Antonio zoo. Timothy had sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
Zoo staff published a message on social media reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
Fiona was born six weeks premature at just 29lb (13.2kgs), falling below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time. Because she was initially too weak to nurse, Cincinnati Zoo staff hand-milked her mother while documenting Fiona’s recovery through photos and videos that captivated the internet.
Her survival then offered a much-needed positive chapter for the zoo following months of intense public backlash over the fatal shooting of Harambe, the silverback gorilla killed after a child breached his enclosure.
Wildlife facilities have long warned of the dangers posed by foreign objects dropped or blown into animal habitats. Past incidents have demonstrated the fatal risks involved, including a rare antelope that choked to death on a plastic cap of a snack pouch at a Tennessee zoo two years ago, and a polar bear at a German zoo that died in 2014 after swallowing a visitor’s dropped jacket.
summary: Zoo staff tried a colonoscopy, vibration plate and other procedures to aid the hippo in passing the hat to no avail Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful. “It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media . Continue reading...
title: Fiona the hippo dies after ingesting knitted hat at Cincinnati zoo

An appeals court decided on Thursday that the Democratic New Jersey representative LaMonica McIver will continue to face charges related to a skirmish outside an immigration detention center last year when she attempted to conduct an oversight visit there.
The court’s decision to decline McIver’s request to overturn the court’s earlier ruling comes just a day after she pressed the homeland security secretary for the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement operations, telling the secretary: “You are killing people.”
Now, with the court’s decision, she is facing a likely trial for the May 2025 incident.
“Because of a weaponized Department of Justice, and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in a statement on Thursday. “Now, due to the disappointing decision by the third circuit, we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”
McIver was charged last year with assaulting, resisting, impeding and interfering with federal officers. The prosecution led to a lengthy legal battle, with McIver claiming the prosecution represented a political attack by the Trump administration.
McIver has attempted to have the case dismissed on various grounds, including by arguing the constitution protects her from prosecution. The third circuit court of appeals rejected her arguments in August and on Thursday declined her request to have an “en banc” hearing, meaning the full bench of active judges refused to reconsider the three-judge panel’s decision.
“This result is frustrating, but my lawyers and I are looking at every possible option for what comes next,” McIver added.
The case stems from a heated oversight visit to a contentious immigration detention center in her state.
Last May, McIver arrived at the Delaney Hall detention center, a large Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in New Jersey, for a congressional oversight visit. She arrived with two other members of Congress and Newark’s mayor, Ras Baraka.
McIver and the other officials were barred access into the detention center. While standing outside Delaney Hall, a federal agent attempted to arrest Baraka for refusing to depart the premises. According to a homeland security agent’s declaration, McIver intervened, attempting to prevent Baraka from being arrested.
Federal officials claim that during the pandemonium, McIver “slammed her forearm” into the homeland security agent and “forcibly” struck another deportation officer with her forearms.
“I hope that everyone who feels that way will stand with me in my fight against these unjust charges, because while I am the first lawmaker they have tried to jail, I will surely not be the last,” McIver said.
The court’s decision came a day after McIver got into a heated exchange with the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, for leading the agencies in charge of the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown.
The Delaney Hall facility has fallen under repeated scrutiny since it began detaining immigrants arrested by ICE again in 2025. At least three people detained at Delaney Hall have died. And the facility was the site of major clashes with ICE earlier this year during protests outside the facility in support of a hunger strike by detained immigrants.
McIver brought up conditions inside Delaney Hall and the number of who have died in ICE custody during Wednesday’s House committee hearing with Mullin.
“As you know, I am facing 17 years in prison, from this Trump administration, for my work at Delaney,” McIver said on Wednesday, then asked Mullin: “Do you even understand why I have been sounding the alarm about Delaney for so long?”
Mullin quipped that he had visited Delaney and said the facility was in “very good condition”.
McIver challenged Mullin’s claims, telling him: “History is going to judge you for what you are doing.”
“You are killing people. You are killing people,” McIver added during the exchange with Mullin, who told her those claims were false.
McIver is the only elected representative facing charges for last year’s Delaney Hall scuffle. The charges against Baraka were dropped.
summary: New Jersey congresswoman, charged with interfering with immigration arrest, set to face trial over May 2025 incident An appeals court decided on Thursday that the Democratic New Jersey representative LaMonica McIver will continue to face charges related to a skirmish outside an immigration detention center last year when she attempted to conduct an oversight visit there. The court’s decision to decline McIver’s request to overturn the court’s earlier ruling comes just a day after she pressed the homeland security secretary for the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement operations, telling the secretary: “You are killing people.” Continue reading...
title: Appeals court rejects Democrat LaMonica McIver’s bid to toss charges over ICE protest

As the artificial intelligence startup Anthropic debuted on the US stock market at an eye-popping $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters from anti-AI groups rallied in front of the Nasdaq exchange at its New York City headquarters in Times Square and several were arrested. Similar demonstrations took place outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters.
“I think people are starting to get that there’s something wrong,” Jose Gonzalez, 46, one of roughly 30 protesters in New York City, said. Protesters carried flags reading “STOP TECH OLIGARCHS” and “FREEZE AI: END ICE, END WAR”.
Anthropic, founded in 2021, completed the largest initial public offering in history this week, raising about $81bn to continue developing its Claude family of generative AI models.
The Times Square rally featured a series of speeches from several community leaders, including Aber Kawas, a New York state senator, who said: “Investing in AI also comes at the direct cost of investing in people.”
Gonzalez took off work to rally in Times Square on Thursday morning. He works as a policy researcher for New York Communities for Change, a non-profit community organizing group that helped rally outside the Nasdaq building. He believes stricter regulations on AI progression nationwide are needed before people are more comfortable with AI research.
Environmental safety, national security, Flock cameras and AI’s connection to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and law enforcement were among the largest concerns for protesters.
“It’s all connected,” Jes Vesconte, 30, said after wrapping up the New York rally. “The same capitalist imperialism is causing the affordability crisis and the climate emergency and atrocities that ICE is doing.”
Vesconte works for a local worker agency in New York. He said he’s encouraging his peers not participate in the stock trading for Anthropic.
“If we did not have the profit motive, we wouldn’t be having these issues,” he said. “This is the epitome of that with the largest IPO ever.”
The scene in San Francisco
Outside Anthropic’s headquarters in downtown San Francisco, about three dozen protesters from two different groups gathered before 11am. One activist held a fake stock certificate for a single share of “Misanthropic”.
Sydney Von Arx with the group Ban RSI said she was there to draw attention to the dangers she sees with “recursive self-improvement”, a technical process in which AI trains itself to become more advanced. Von Arx thinks Anthropic’s IPO is “a time to reflect on how these AI companies that started as small startups with lofty goals have turned into giant corporations that have put profit before safety and security”.
She wants a global ban on recursive self-improvement. “We should not have AI building AIs,” she said. “It’s going to go too fast at a pace that no humans can keep up with.” Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, previously warned that recursive self-improvement could outrun human’s ability to control the systems.
Adam Kaufman, who works at an AI safety non-profit, held a sign saying: “The only winning move is not to RACE,” with the “A” rendered to mimic the Anthropic logo. Kaufman said the sign was a reference to the movie WarGames, in which a nuclear strategy computer, after simulating numerous nuclear wars, concludes the only winning move is not to play.
summary: Anti-AI groups gather in front of Nasdaq exchange in Times Square and Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco As the artificial intelligence startup Anthropic debuted on the US stock market at an eye-popping $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters from anti-AI groups rallied in front of the Nasdaq exchange at its New York City headquarters in Times Square and several were arrested. Similar demonstrations took place outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters. “I think people are starting to get that there’s something wrong,” Jose Gonzalez, 46, one of roughly 30 protesters in New York City, said. Protesters carried flags reading “STOP TECH OLIGARCHS” and “FREEZE AI: END ICE, END WAR”. Continue reading...
title: Protesters rally against Anthropic in New York and San Francisco after $2tn stock market debut

Attempted murder arrest after councillor stabbed
- Published
A councillor has been seriously injured after being stabbed while undertaking his duties in Bradford.
Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Manse Street, according to the deputy leader of Your Bradford Independent Group, councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed.
West Yorkshire Police said a 32-year-old man had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and was being held in custody.
The force added there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".
Ali is believed to have been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to the nearby Manse Street where emergency services attended, according to police.
A force spokesperson previously said the suspect had climbed on to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue following the incident and was later brought down.
Ahmed said Ali was undergoing emergency surgery at Leeds General Infirmary after being stabbed in the leg. He said Ali was in a stable condition but had lost a lot of blood.
"My thoughts are with him and his family and loved ones. It's an extremely distressing time," said Ahmed.
"We shouldn't have to fear for our personal safety because we have chosen to serve the public.
"There should be no normalisation of violence in our democratic life."
Responding to the incident in his Bradford East constituency, Labour MP Imran Hussain described the incident as "horrific" and "deeply disturbing".
"My thoughts and prayers are with councillor Ibrar Ali and his family," said Hussain.
"No elected politician should feel under threat or fear for their safety while carrying out their duties and serving their community."
Ch Supt Richard Padwell urged anyone with information to contact police.
"This is a serious incident where a local councillor has been stabbed in the street and our thoughts are with him, his family and colleagues at this difficult time," he said.
"Whilst the investigation is in the early stages, there is nothing to suggest that this incident is politically motivated at this time."
Ali is a community development manager at charity The Leap.
He has worked with community organisations Bradford Moor Pass and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.
He was first elected as a councillor in the May local election, replacing the previous Labour representatives.

summary: Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali is in hospital with serious injuries.
title: Attempted murder arrest after councillor stabbed in Bradford

Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish
- Published
Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
But doctors stress it is a long way from knowing how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.
Incredibly exciting
Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.
The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.
"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.
Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.
Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.
Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.
The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.
Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.
In the trial:
- tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients
- just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear
- for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans
Longer survival
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.
"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.
Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US. It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS, external, found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.
Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.
Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."
He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."
Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."
There are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease in Britain each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.
Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.
Symptoms can include, external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.
summary: Daily pill daraxonrasib appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest cancers.
title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish

Girls as young as five targeted for upskirting as charges continue to rise
- Published
Girls as young as five have been targeted for upskirting, new police figures show.
Over the past three years, Wales' four forces received 219 complaints from females up to the age of 87, with 18 people charged, results of Freedom of Information (FOI) requests, external reveal.
Upskirting involves taking a photo or video, external beneath someone's clothing - without their knowledge - with the intention of viewing their genitals, buttocks or underwear.
It was made a criminal offence under the Voyeurism (Offences) Act 2019, external and carries a maximum sentence of two years in prison.
The Crown Prosecution Service, external urged people to report incidents immediately, saying those that led to charges almost doubled between 2022 and 2026.
"As well as being an extremely damaging offence in its own right, our prosecutors often see upskirting forming part of a wider pattern of sexual offending," said national lead for sexual offence prosecutions Siobhan Blake.
Between January 2023 and June 2026, Wales' four police forces received 219 complaints, with the highest being 159 in the Dyfed-Powys area and the lowest, six in Gwent, according to the FOI figures.
Where ages were recorded, 11 involved under-10s, 67 came from girls aged 11 to 17, 35 from those 18 to 24, and 12 from over-55s.
From these 219 complaints, nine people were charged in the north Wales force area, six in Dyfed-Powys, three in south Wales, while Gwent had no data.
A previous FOI to Greater Manchester Police, external showed it received 146 reports between 2019 and 2025, leading to 41 arrests and 10 people being charged.
West Midlands Police received 75 reports between 2022 and 2026, with 23 charged, according to another FOI, external.
"I think a lot of the time [boys] think it's a joke or banter, but it's not funny," said student Rowan Stanger, 21.
"Whilst it is illegal, I don't think a lot of people take it seriously."
She was in secondary school when it was made a criminal offence in Wales and England in 2019, and as a teenager, heard about lots of cases of it happening to friends.
"I was wearing shorts under skirts in school, I think that's what was kind of expected even before I really knew why," she added.
"That is still ingrained in me. I'll rarely wear one without."
Rowan is part of a student-led Time to Act, which fights against sexual violence in higher education.
Emily Hasling, 23, is also part of the Cardiff-based campaign group, and said she remembers when she was in university and going to nightclubs, she would only wear jeans.
"Young boys don't see it as sexual assault or sexual violence, because it's not a physical kind of touching element, it's a photo," she said.
"So that's how they see it 'just a photo'."
Another group member Freya Price, 22, described feeling wary on public transport.
"Obviously trains are quite crowded so if I can't stand in a corner I'll feel quite anxious, because I can't guarantee that someone's not going to violate my privacy," she said.
In September 2020, Dominique Pelicot was caught after a supermarket security guard saw him filming under women's skirts.
It prompted a police search of his electronic devices, which uncovered thousands of files revealing a decade-long scheme to drug and sexually abuse his wife, Gisele.
A former North Wales Police detective is also due to be sentenced later this year after admitting taking pictures beneath the clothing of a child without consent.
Lee Harshey-Jones, 45, was a detective constable and lead investigator in the case of two-year-old Ethan Ives-Griffiths, whose grandparents were jailed for murder last year, and has given evidence in other high-profile murder trials in north Wales.
He pleaded guilty to one charge of voyeurism and one of perverting the course of justice by applying a factory reset to his mobile phone to conceal evidence.
Last month a former supply teacher was jailed for six years after taking more than 100 upskirt photographs of schoolgirls, including in his classroom, across Greater Manchester.
Recently the operator of the popular amusement ride at the Munich Oktoberfest took proactive measures and handed out free cycling shorts to women, after thousands of voyeuristic videos emerged on social media.
Olivia (not her real name), a teenager from south Wales, said she loves wearing skirts but from an early age has been made to feel uncomfortable in them.
She described how boys in primary school had an obsession with "flipping up girls' skirts", which led to them either wearing shorts underneath or switching to trousers.
This was her first experience of feeling unsafe in them, while she was then upskirted on a night out while at university.
"There was a little stage area and I'm dancing, having a great time," Olivia said.
"I look over to my right and someone has got a camera with the flash on underneath my skirt.
"We made eye contact and he walked off. I was frozen and I didn't know if I was imagining it. I didn't know if I could tell someone or who to tell."
She has not felt comfortable enough to wear the same dress again until recently, describing her head as being "on a swivel" every time she was in a club, and feeling like she could not get too drunk.
In 2019, Libby Squire, 21, was raped and murdered by Pawel Relowicz, who was found to have previous convictions for voyeurism and public sex acts.
Libby's mother Lisa Squire has spent the past five years trying to increase the reporting of non-contact sexual offences, launching the It Does Matter campaign in 2024.
"I know first hand how harmful behaviours that are too often dismissed as 'minor' can build into something catastrophic, and I am committed to ensuring no other family experiences what we have," she said.
The NSPCC said its Childline service, external has heard from young people who have had indecent images of them taken and shared.
"They tell us how devastating the abuse can be on their mental and emotional wellbeing, leaving them afraid, ashamed and unsure where to turn," a spokesperson said.
One 16-year-old described how the same boy tripped her up on the way to her seat every day in her tutor group, laughing and looking up her skirt.
"It just freaks me out and I don't know what to do about it," she said.
A mum called to say her daughter, also 16, had heard a rumour a boy in her year had taken a photograph up her skirt, and shared it with his friends.
She added: "The thought alone is incredibly upsetting for her."
The Children's Commissioner for England said Children's Commissioner Dame Rachel de Souza said: "The fact a number of teachers have admitted or been found guilty of upskirting offences, some in their own classrooms, is particularly shocking.
"Teachers and other school professionals have a clear responsibility to keep children safe, so staff must be alert to the signs of sexual harassment and abuse and ensure all children know where they can turn for help and support if an incident occurs."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC Action Line
Related topics
More top stories

  - Published3 hours ago
summary: Police forces have received complaints involving girls as young as five and women as old as 87.
title: Girls as young as five targeted for upskirting as charges continue to rise

Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO
AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Shares in the artificial intelligence giant Anthropic soared in their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering and private placement that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old AI company, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.
The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
Anthropic's shares opened trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT at $111.50, a whopping 34% above the IPO price. They eased over the trading day to end 17% higher at $97.17.
A breakaway beginning
Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.
Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.
Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.
They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Opportunities and risks
The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.
"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."
There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.
"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"
Conflict with the Pentagon, and "pacing the frontier"
Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.
And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks. In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to "pace the frontier," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.
On Thursday, Amodei said the company's principles would not change.
"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control," he said at the opening bell ceremony to start the Nasdaq exchange's trading day. "We will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."
That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies, setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents. This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
Anthropic's IPO prospectus dedicated dozens of pages to potential risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI, or that AI could take harmful actions on its own.
The company also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash. Indeed, the IPO comes just weeks after midterm elections in the United States, which analysts say likely herald a period of elevated scrutiny and oversight for AI firms. Data centers became a hot-button issue this election cycle, and tech stocks sank after the election as investors anticipated that the incoming Congress would crack down on the industry.
Still, Anthropic's prospectus was bullish about the development and spread of AI. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.
OpenAI had been on track to also list shares this year, but CEO Sam Altman postponed those plans, likely to next year, after the Hugging Face incident. At the Semafor conference on Monday Altman promised: "We will go public at some point."
"The world as a whole would like exposure to this," he continued. "And I think that's, you know, directionally a good thing to do."
Meanwhile, shares in SpaceX, the first of this year's AI mega-IPOs, are trading near their initial price of $135. After the company's June listing, the stock leapt to more than $200, then slid to as low as about $108 before recovering ground.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
Editor's note: This story was updated with the share price after the start of trading on the Nasdaq exchange, and to add a quote from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Nov. 19, 2026
summary: Shares in the maker of the popular Claude artificial intelligence model leapt in first day of trading on the Nasdaq Thursday.
title: Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO

Religion should be removed from Australia’s terrorism definition and making bomb threats should not result in life imprisonment, the country’s national security laws watchdog has said.
The highly anticipated report from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor (INSLM), released Thursday, reviewed how terrorism has been defined in Australia over the past 25 years after a suite of laws were introduced following the September 11 attacks in the United States.
It comes as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation (Asio) warn the rise of extremist, violent nationalism has changed the threat landscape and the motivations behind some terrorist attacks cannot be categorised into single ideologies.
Among the recommendations are suggested changes to the definition of terrorism to remove religion, which the INSLM head, Jake Blight, said gives accused terrorists “false credibility” and has a detrimental impact on religious minorities.
“Having a law that requires proof that terrorists were advancing a ‘religious’ cause gives these terrorists false credibility and reinforces their narrative that they are doing holy work,” the report said. “The same individuals will still be able to be prosecuted, but should be described as violent ideologues.
“Reference to religion in the definition of terrorism has also, in practice, contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities, especially Muslim Australians. This has a negative impact on social cohesion.”
The current definition of terrorism under the federal criminal code requires agencies to prove an act intends to cause serious harm to people or property in order to advance a political, religious or ideological cause.
A change in terrorism laws to remove religion as a primary motivation and place it as an example of a broader “ideology” category is in line with international best practice, Blight’s report said.
The INSLM noted the UN special rapporteur’s report earlier this year recommended defining terrorism acts by political and ideological causes and omitting religious motives, as references to religion have “discriminatory and stigmatizing effects that outweigh the benefits of criminally denouncing them”.
In his submission to the INSLM, Australia’s special envoy to combat Islamophobia, Aftab Malik, said keeping religion in as a terrorism motivation created a “climate of suspicion” around Muslims and “provided ammunition for far-right extremist narratives”.
Eleven Muslim advocacy and community groups, including the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network, welcomed the report’s recommendations and urged the Australian government to amend the laws.
“Every time someone in authority says that a motivation is ‘religious’, it uplifts ISIS, far-right and harmful media narratives all at once, by officially perpetuating the false premise that Islam encourages terrorism,” their joint statement said.
“This makes all Muslims feel under siege.”
The Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Australia’s peak Jewish body, described the report as “high-quality” but said removing religion as a motivating factor made “little sense when so many notorious terrorist acts have featured motifs, words and images that unmistakably refer to religious doctrines and beliefs”.
“The inclusion of ‘faith’ as a type of ideology does not solve the problem. Faith is not the same as religion and religion is more than an ideology,” the organisation’s co-chief executive, Peter Wertheim, said.
“It is clearly not appropriate for Australian law to decide which beliefs are an authentic expression of a religion and which are not. Even the adherents of a religion may have divergent views about such matters.”
The INSLM’s report made six other recommendations, including separating credible threats of terrorism from actual acts.
Under existing laws, a person found guilty of making a credible terrorist threat can be sentenced to life imprisonment with a mandatory minimum sentence of six years.
The report said the punishment was “disproportionate, unnecessarily complex and out of step with international standards” and recommended terrorism threats be treated as a separate charge with a maximum sentence of no more than five years.
The legislation monitor also recommended raising the bar on designating damage to property and electronic system as acts of terrorism while excluding advocacy, protest, dissent and industrial action.
Asio’s director-general, Mike Burgess, has warned of the rise in violent nationalist extremism in recent years. In an October submission to a parliamentary inquiry into radicalisation, Asio said around 65% of its counter-terrorism caseload related to religiously-motivated violent extremism while 35% related to ideologically-motivated extremism.
summary: Independent National Security Legislation Monitor says reference to religion has ‘contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Religion should be removed from Australia’s terrorism definition and making bomb threats should not result in life imprisonment, the country’s national security laws watchdog has said. The highly anticipated report from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor (INSLM), released Thursday, reviewed how terrorism has been defined in Australia over the past 25 years after a suite of laws were introduced following the September 11 attacks in the United States. title: Religion should be removed from terrorism definition under Australian law as it gives ‘false credibility’, watchdog says

Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China.
The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that the transfer of any Virginia-class submarine to Australia “has not been factored into the plan”, the report says.
But the Congressional Budget Office has evaluated the impact of Aukus, releasing detailed analysis on Friday morning, finding “the US submarine industrial base is currently struggling to meet the Navy’s demand for submarines”.
“Increasing production further to replace SSNs [attack submarines] sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the Navy and the shipyards are facing,” the report found.
“The sale of SSNs to Australia would reduce the number of attack submarines available to the Navy for many years.”
Under the so-called “Pillar One” of Aukus, the US has agreed to sell between three and five in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032.
The CBO analysis questioned whether any submarines transferred to Australia could be utilised in the event of a US conflict with China.
“Would China be less deterred if the United States reduced the number of its attack submarines to help Australia develop its own submarine force?”
The report argued that because of the longstanding, and robust, alliance between the US and Australia, boosting the Australian navy’s submarine fleet could help offset the US Navy’s “potential loss of capability”.
“That loss might even be more than offset because the Australian submarines would be based in the Western Pacific region and therefore could respond more quickly to any conflict with China over Taiwan or other issues in the South China Sea.
“However, Australia would control its own submarines, and their participation in any particular conflict would not be guaranteed.”
In 2023, Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said Australia would make no promises it would deploy its submarines in support of any US conflict with China, and that any future Australian submarines would be “under the complete control of the Australian government of the day”.
Submarine-building rates in the US have been tenaciously laggard. The country’s shipyards are currently producing Virginia-class submarines at a rate of 1.13 a year: that rate needs to lift that to two submarines a year to service America’s own needs, and 2.33 a year to have additional boats to transfer to Australia.
The CBO report said submarine-building rates had slowed over the past two decades, and Virginia-class submarines were delayed between 24 and 36 months.
“Building … submarines took five to six years in the 2000s but now takes an average of 10 to 11 years, according to current schedules.”
The US legislation governing Aukus states that the president of the US can only transfer a submarine to Australia if losing that submarine from US service “will not degrade the United States undersea capabilities”.
The US can refuse to transfer any submarines to Australia without penalty, under the terms of the Aukus agreement.
Critics of Aukus have said there is vanishingly little chance the US will have the capacity to sell any of its in-service submarines to Australia.
The former foreign affairs minister Bob Carr told Guardian Australia both countries were “living a lie” in upholding the fiction that the submarine deal would happen. “It’s now conventional wisdom in Washington as well as in Canberra that we’re not going to get the subs.”
But the deal has avowed, bipartisan broad political support across both the US and Australia. Marles said earlier this month: “Aukus is happening, our alliance is happening, and all of that continues unimpeded.”
Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, affirmed his support for the Aukus agreement, and the two countries’ commitment “to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific” at a meeting with Marles in September.
The US Congressional Research Service has openly countenanced an “alternative division of labour” under which no Virginia-class submarines are ever transferred to Australian control.
The research service’s latest report on Aukus, issued in January, considered a revision of the Aukus deal under which the submarines earmarked for sale to Australia were instead retained under US command to be sailed out of Australian bases.
The report argued both for and against the US selling three Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032. But it makes the case that, in the event of a “conflict or crisis” with China over Taiwan, submarines under Australian command could not be ordered into operation, whereas US-commanded vessels, operated out of Australian bases, could be immediately deployed.
summary: Congressional Budget Office also questions whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into a conflict with China under Aukus deal Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China. The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that the transfer of any Virginia-class submarine to Australia “has not been factored into the plan”, the report says. Continue reading...
title: US warned supplying nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish its own fleet for ‘many years’
