'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
- Published
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.
The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.
He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.
"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.
When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor

summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.
title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC

body:
Next round of BBC cuts will be more noticeable to audiences, report warns
- Published
Further job losses and programme cuts at the BBC will be more noticeable to audiences than previous savings measures, a new report has warned.
The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach its £500m target.
In its report, the National Audit Office (NAO) anticipated the BBC's next round of cost-cutting measures will be more difficult to deliver and more perceptible to audiences.
The BBC welcomed the report and said it has "consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform".
The NAO's report also said the BBC's current measures are expected to reduce the BBC's workforce by 11% over three years.
Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "As the BBC approaches charter renewal in just over a year's time, there is no doubt that there are difficult choices ahead."
The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.
The organisation has so far achieved savings by reducing staffing levels, rationalising its estate, modernising technology, simplifying processes and changing the mix and scope of content and services, the public spending watchdog said.
The NAO found the BBC's licence fee income fell by 26% in real terms over the last decade, due in part to the significant changes in audience habits.
The proportion of UK adults using BBC television, iPlayer, radio or online services on an average week also fell from 90% in 2021-22 to 81% in 2025-26, the NAO said.
The report noted the corporation's public service broadcasting operating defecit reached £209m in the last financial year.
The BBC has already announced plans to reduce spending by about 10%, including cuts to programming across its news, nations and content divisions.
Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank, Live At The Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and RuPaul's Drag Race UK are among the TV programmes to have been cut so far.
Radio programmes are also being dropped from the schedules, such as You and Yours and The World Tonight on BBC Radio 4.
The corporation has also announced plans to close the linear broadcast services of BBC Radio 4 Extra, BBC Three and BBC Scotland, with the latter two becoming online-only services.
'Reinventing for a changing world'
The NAO said the BBC expects to face difficult choices about the scale and scope of its services as part of its latest savings programme, with further content reductions expected to have a greater impact on audiences.
It warned the corporation was likely to find it harder to identify further savings following its previous cost-cutting programmes.
The NAO also found the broadcaster had not properly monitored the cumulative impact of its previous savings on audiences, service quality and organisational capability.
It also raised concerns about the BBC's risk management and governance arrangements, and said stronger oversight would be needed to deliver the more demanding savings programme.
In response to the report, the BBC said it welcomed the findings, and added that it has had to "make tough decisions due to sustained financial pressures driven by declining licence fee income, changing audience behaviour, increased competition and rising costs".
Berangere Michel, the BBC's group chief financial officer, said: "We welcome this report and are pleased that the NAO has acknowledged the significant savings already delivered by the BBC, with the programme on track to meet its target one year ahead of schedule.
"The BBC must respond to significant cost pressures while reinventing for a changing world. This continues to require tough decisions, while ensuring that the impacts on audiences and colleagues are minimised.
"We accept the NAO's recommendations and have already begun implementing them to strengthen the delivery of our current savings programme, while recognising there are further opportunities to build on this progress.
She added: "We will continue to engage with government to secure a new Charter that provides sufficient, sustainable and universal funding so the BBC can deliver for audiences for generations to come."

summary: The BBC has already cut jobs, programmes and services but has further to go to reach its £500m target.
title: Next round of BBC cuts will be more noticeable to audiences, report warns

body:
Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions.
“And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for,” Rollins wrote in a 5 April email, marking Easter.
US district judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco said the emails violated the first amendment’s establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of Department of Agriculture (USDA) workers.
The USDA did not respond to a request for comment.
Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins’ Christian faith, Thompson ruled.
When disseminating religious messages, Rollins must stop if a colleague asks her to. “Cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates” are commands that were quoted directly from a USDA policy on workplace religious expression that Rollins herself adopted.
Rollins may discuss her faith with interested colleagues, share why her faith is meaningful to her, politely invite co-workers to religious events and express her views in appropriate conversations, Thompson ruled, again quoting directly from Rollins’ policy.
Six USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees, a labor union representing 19,000 USDA workers, brought the suit in May.
summary: A federal judge ruled that messages sent by Brooke Rollins to USDA workers suggest Christianity is a shared faith and violate the first amendment Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday. Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions. Continue reading...
title: Religious messages agriculture secretary emailed to staff deemed unconstitutional

body: 'The bravest woman in Britain' and 'Silence is not an option' Published 6 minutes ago Image caption, Joanne Young is pictured on a number of Friday's front pages. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexually abusing Young after her husband drugged and advertised her for sex online. The Daily Mail calls her "the British Pelicot" and "the bravest woman in Britain" after she waived her right to anonymity to "condemn the 'horrific betrayal'". Her ex-husband - 50-year-old former Conservative councillor Philip Young - has already pleaded guilty to a number of rape charges, and another man pleaded guilty to rape and sexual assault at a previous hearing. Image caption, "You are not alone" is the Daily Mirror's front page headline - words spoken by Young as she appealed to other survivors outside court after the verdicts were delivered. "Joanne Young faced the whole world as she described the impact 13 years of rape and abuse had on her life," the paper writes. It also pictures US President Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who held trilateral talks with China's Xi Jinping on Thursday, and describes their relationship as a "bromance". Image caption, "Bravery beyond all measure" is how the Daily Express describes Young, whom it reports has "called for a change to the law on consent". Separately, the paper reports that Reform UK leader Nigel Farage says "our PM does not believe in Britain like me". Andy Burnham will attend a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where he has said a "win-win" deal can be struck with the bloc. Image caption, Negotiators have "provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the Britain every year under a new mobility scheme" ahead of the summit, according to the Guardian. The paper describes the number as a "concession" from the UK side, who are said to have previously sought a lower cap of 50,000-80,000. Downing Street has not commented on the details, which would also allow young Britons to live in Europe. Also on its front page are Joanne Young's remarks, and the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling that Myanmar was guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority. Image caption, Young has said her case raises "serious questions" about how the law deals with consent, writes the Times, "after the defendants claimed they had been 'duped' by Young into believing his wife was a willing participant". The Times also covers reaction from European leaders to the historic talks between Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzen on Thursday - "dismissing it as a 'photo-op'". Image caption, Trump told European leaders to withhold funding for Ukraine in a "phone call 'tirade'" after the talks, the Daily Telegraph reports. It also writes that the Speaker of the House of Lords has warned peers that the "soaring cost of refurbishing Parliament risks drawing cash away from priorities like defence", and that pubs "could be allowed to serve pints before 06:00 under plans to relax drinking laws for the Rugby World Cup", which will be held in Australia in 2027. Image caption, "Anthropic surges on Wall St debut" is the Financial Times' Friday headline, after the AI firm became one of the most valuable public companies in the world as it began trading on the stock market on Thursday. The "blockbuster listing caps a stunning ascent" for Anthropic, the paper reports. In other news, the FT covers Trump, Xi and Putin's meeting - where it writes nuclear weapons were the main talking point - and reports that the UK Treasury is resisting Alan Milburn's proposal to tackle youth unemployment by cutting employer National Insurance costs. The department declined to comment but pointed to Burnham's previous remarks that tax decisions would wait until next year's Budget. Image caption, Anthropic's "stock market bonanza" hits close to home for the Metro, which dedicates its front page to co-founder Jack Clark - a former journalist who "worked weekends as a sub-editor on our website". "Clark says much of his success is due to his career in news," the Metro reports. Image caption, "Andrew dossier sent to police" is the Daily Star's headline, as it reports 80 pages of files "said to concern misconduct in public office" have been submitted "amid calls for a new probe" into Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. The evidence has been handed over by the campaign group Republic, which said details had not been made public following legal advice. The former Prince Andrew was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the US. Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein. Image caption, The Sun meanwhile splashes on Grand Theft Auto 6's UK release. "Grandular fever" is its headline, as it reports that a "sickie frenzy" saw 1m gamers skip school or work to play the highly anticipated game. "Some schools offered pupils rewards just for coming in," according to the Sun. Image caption, The i Paper reports that an alzheimer's test that "gives diagnosis in days" will be made available in the UK next year. The paper reports that this could cut diagnosis time "from years to days after first visit to a memory clinic". Sign up for our morning newsletter and get BBC News in your inbox. Related Internet Links Daily Express Daily Mail Daily Mirror Daily Star Daily Telegraph Financial Times Guardian Independent Metro Sun The i Times
summary: Joanne Young, whose husband drugged and advertised her for sex online, is pictured on a number of front pages.
title: 'The bravest woman in Britain' and 'Silence is not an option'

body:
Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
- Published
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.
Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.
Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".
But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.
The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.
Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.
Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.
Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.
If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".
Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.
But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.
Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.
There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.
Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.
She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.
The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.
She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.
"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.
The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.
Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.
Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.
Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.
summary: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.
title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force

body:
Does our ethnicity change how we experience dying?
- Published
We're all going to die - and whether we think about it consciously or not, we generally hope that it will be as smooth as possible for ourselves and our loved ones.
But a study published earlier this year by King's College London and the University of Sheffield suggests that your ethnicity could play a role in how likely this is to be the case.
The research found that people from minority ethnic backgrounds experiencing end-of-life care and grief often struggled to access culturally and religiously appropriate support.
One woman told researchers a hospital sent an Imam - a Muslim religious leader - to her father's bedside when he was dying, even though their family were Hindu.
That lack of culturally appropriate resources or training is exacerbating an "incredibly difficult time in their lives where they were really vulnerable", says Sabrina Bajwah, one of the study's co-authors.
So how can our ethnic or cultural background shape what kind of death we have? And what kind of support is available?
Culturally appropriate care
Bajwah told the BBC researchers discovered different types of inequality in their research.
"There was the structural racism that people talked about, which was the 'treating everybody equally' - and by treating everybody equally, services weren't meeting the needs of these communities," she said. "Then there was the other, direct form of racism."
A study last year from the NHS Race and Health Observatory, set up in 2021 to try and tackle racial inequalities within the wider healthcare system, found there was an "alarming" lack of trust among some ethnic minority groups in the care or service they receive.
For example, just over half of participants said they had experienced some form of discrimination from their healthcare providers.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care, which commissioned this year's study, told the BBC that "ethnicity or background should never be a barrier to accessing bereavement support and everyone has the right to the same level of care".
"We will consider the findings of this research project carefully as part of future policy making," they said.
Pravin Navekar's wife Gita started experiencing chronic pain in her back and legs in 2010, but despite multiple GP visits over a two-year period, was repeatedly sent home with pain relief and no further investigations.
In the end the couple, from Leicester, paid to see a consultant privately, at which point Gita was referred for a CT scan. This picked up a rare cancer, a synovial sarcoma, in her pelvis.
Though she was given a prognosis of under five years when she was first diagnosed, Gita lived for another 11, before passing away in April 2021.
Pravin felt culturally appropriate care was "lacking" at times when Gita was in hospital.
"We're all individuals and we have individual needs and wants, and they're tied in with your faith, your culture, your beliefs," he said.
"If she was in hospital for Diwali, then it was another normal day. But when you have Christmas they do all sorts of things and make people really comfortable… [for Diwali] they don't even acknowledge it. There's nothing wrong with a nurse or a doctor coming up to you and saying, 'Good morning, and happy Diwali to you'.
"It's about recognising a person as a whole person, rather than somebody in a bed who needs care."
Support group
When Marwa Soliman's father died in 2013, she had just moved from Egypt to Nottingham and was pregnant with her third child. She didn't know anyone, and had struggled to find a community.
"I just remember crumbling on the floor and crying, not knowing what to do and feeling alone and afraid," she said.
Six years later, Marwa set up a support group for Muslim, Arabic-speaking women called Heya - meaning "she" in Arabic.
It's grown from 50 women at the start to more than 700. If there's a death in the community, they all rally around to support each other.
"People send condolences and speak to each other, read the Quran together, we can send out timings if they'd like people to visit," she said.
Marwa has since lost three other close family members, including her mother - but she says having Heya made the experience completely different.
"When the other deaths happened, I had hot food, people coming over, people calling… It's a beautiful thing," she said.
But she worries that other communities won't have the same support, and that funding is scarce for the groups that do exist.
"I think there should be more research, and a clear support and referral path with information about where to go and who to speak to," she said.
Marwa's experience, and the group she set up because of it, could be an example to the Department of Health and Social Care, Catriona Mayland, one of the study's co-authors from Sheffield University, told the BBC.
"Services shouldn't look to replace what's already there," she said. "There's some real strengths within communities that we've seen, and [we should think] actually, how can we build on that and work together?"
Related topics

  - Published9 November
  - Published16 October
summary: Death is the one certainty we all share - but could our ethnicity change how we go through it?
title: Does our ethnicity change how we experience dying?

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was ousted from his job, a person close to the White House told Reuters on Thursday, days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking and national security systems.
Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross declined to comment on his departure.
Axios first reported Cairncross’s departure from the White House, citing anonymous officials claiming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller pushed for the personnel change because Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job”.
Technology-related outages have hit regularly over the last week, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services and a temporary disruption to the US National Security Agency’s network.
The Trump administration has faced criticism over its response to the outages. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions to critical systems over the past week were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

body:
The US army has delayed its plan to detonate a stash of bomb-making chemicals in south-eastern Iowa as questions swirl about the public health risks.
The army was set to blow up about 5 tons of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, at noon on Friday, a move it described as the safest way to dispose of the highly sensitive compound.
During the controlled explosion, barrels of the material would be stored inside concrete structures and surrounded by sand-filled Hesco barriers reaching up two stories high.
Army officials advised certain residents of Middletown to evacuate between 8am and 2pm local time, due to the potential for window damage. The vibrations from the two blasts would not last long but could break old windows in town, and the resulting dust was expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said.
The detonation is also expected to produce a plume containing lead particles.
Officials have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north. Updated maps showed the plume’s shift, and the army will continue to update the map based on weather. Some schools in the path of the plume have already canceled classes.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the path of the plume.
While the army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces after the detonation, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.
Iowa’s top leaders appeared to learn about the plan along with the public. The office of the Iowa governor, Kim Reynolds, was first briefed on Monday about the public advisory, her office said.
“An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation,” governor-elect Rob Sand wrote on X on Thursday. “The public deserves to know, if this is the safest option, why other options were worse.”
Adam Telle, the acting secretary of the US army, alluded to the criticism in his Thursday announcement about the delayed detonation.
“Public communication is essential to public trust,” he wrote on X, adding that he was engaging state officials.
The plan is now expected to proceed on Monday. According to Telle, it’s the “latest possible moment”, before temperatures drop, which could risk destabilizing the material.
Middletown residents learned in March that the army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered.
“The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable,” Lt Col Daniel Nosse, the commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production.
The army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on 13 November approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday’s detonation.
That permit required the army to track specific rates of potential air and dust dispersion and notify the public five days in advance, prompting Sunday’s original advisory to communities as far as 100 miles (160km) away.
Just a few miles north-west, the Danville community school district will close on Friday, the superintendent said in an announcement on Tuesday. Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but there were enough uncertainties that made canceling “the most responsible decision”.
“I am not suggesting that the detonation will result in unsafe conditions,” he wrote. “The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon.”
In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles (32km) north-east of the ammunition plant, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure on Sunday, when the initial map put them dead-center in the dust exposure area. Schools and the public library will close on Friday and the local fire department planned to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles.
The city of nearly 2,000 residents was no longer in the plume in an updated map.
“This is probably a first for me. I believe it’s a first for a lot of our citizens,” the deputy city clerk, Amy Stucker, said on Wednesday. “The biggest issue we’re having is the lack of information.”
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s department of occupational and environmental health, said it was encouraging to see that the army and the EPA were doing all they could to minimize the dust, but it was still unknown how much would end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.
Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth.
According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.
summary: The controlled detonation can lead to a plume containing lead particles, worrying residents and state officials The US army has delayed its plan to detonate a stash of bomb-making chemicals in south-eastern Iowa as questions swirl about the public health risks. The army was set to blow up about 5 tons of lead azide in Middletown, Iowa, at noon on Friday, a move it described as the safest way to dispose of the highly sensitive compound. Continue reading...
title: US army postpones plan to detonate bomb-making chemical amid outcry

body:
In a legal filing on Thursday, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to dismiss the lawsuit it filed before the midterm elections seeking to block the certification of the US Senate race in Alaska should Democrat Mary Peltola win.
The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The Alaska supreme court already ruled that the second Sullivan’s candidacy was legal and that he could be on the ballot.
Peltola did win the election, with 50.13% of the vote, giving her more than the combined vote totals of all other candidates, including the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, and a second Daniel Sullivan, who was reportedly recruited to enter the race by Democrats to siphon votes away from the sitting senator.
The suit was filed at the direction of Donald Trump saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot.
The administration moved on Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided.
Peltola faced significant controversy on the campaign trail, after the New York Times reported that her staffers were involved in a scheme to recruit the “decoy” Dan Sullivan.
Peltola denied any involvement in encouraging the second Sullivan’s run.
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, will join the Minnesota senator-elect Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth band of Ojibwe, as the first two Native American women to serve in the US Senate.
The legal filing came a day after Alaska concluded its vote-count and used ranked-choice tabulation to decide races where no candidate got more then 50% of the votes cast, including the election for the state’s sole representative in Congress.
One of those candidates, Eric Hafner, was apparently also included on the ballot in an attempt to confuse voters. Hafner, who was allowed to contest the race as a Democrat, over the objections of the state’s Democratic party, and despite having no connection to the state and currently being incarcerated in federal prison in New York, got 22,715 votes.
Had all of his ballots been cast for Hill, who was backed by the state’s Democratic party, Hill would have defeated Begich.
summary: President had sought to block results if Democrat won race that featured two candidates named Dan Sullivan In a legal filing on Thursday, the Trump administration asked a federal appeals court to dismiss the lawsuit it filed before the midterm elections seeking to block the certification of the US Senate race in Alaska should Democrat Mary Peltola win. The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican senator Dan Sullivan. The Alaska supreme court already ruled that the second Sullivan’s candidacy was legal and that he could be on the ballot. Continue reading...
title: Trump DoJ moves to drop legal challenge to Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win

body:
GTA 6 breaks records as sales top $2.3bn - industry estimate
- Published
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's launch on Thursday, after a 13-year wait.
The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure saw pre-orders and first day sales total more than 24.5 million units, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.
In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas.
GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.
The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.
At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.
The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.
GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.
The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.
Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.
Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.
That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.
Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.
The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.
If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.
Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.
GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.
The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play.
Its launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles.
The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China.

summary: Rockstar Games ended a 13-year wait with what is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch ever.
title: GTA 6 breaks records as sales top $2.3bn - industry estimate

Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
- Published
The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona has died just days after swallowing a knitted hat that slipped into her enclosure.
"It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said on Thursday afternoon.
Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017, swallowed the hat about 10 days ago and required emergency care.
The vet staff "tried everything they could to help her" but "it was ultimately too much to overcome", the zoo said.
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".
The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm.
"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.
Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Her death is also very premature, with hippos normally living up to 50 years in human care, according to the zoo.
"Although this was not an intentional incident, of which, regrettably, there are many, Fiona's painful death is a tragic reminder that everyone should behave carefully and respectfully around animals," Debbie Metzler, the Managing Director of Captive Wildlife for the animal rights group Peta.
"Peta expects that the zoo will review its protocols to help prevent anything like this from happening again, and we urge every visitor to secure their belongings and never toss objects near an animal's enclosure."
As well as being famous online, Fiona's story inspired an ice cream flavour and a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval said Fiona "was a symbol of perseverance and joy" in the city.
"She brought smiles to so many faces, from kids to parents to visitors from around the world," he wrote on X. "Our city is heartbroken, but we couldn't be more grateful that she was part of our lives and our community as a whole."
Related topics
  - Published8 hours ago
summary: Fiona, who became an internet star after her premature birth in 2017, "fought until she couldn’t anymore", the zoo says.
title: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo

A jury has convicted a diabetic woman of murdering both her elderly parents with insulin after a marathon criminal trial.
Raelene Polymiadis, 66, will face two mandatory life sentences after jurors on Friday delivered unanimous verdicts after a four-month South Australian supreme court trial.
She clutched the dock as the first verdict was read out, then dabbed at her eyes with a tissue after the second guilty verdict was announced, repeatedly shaking her head and blinking rapidly.
Polymiadis’s bail was revoked and she was remanded in custody ahead of sentence.
After a trial that began on June 15 and blew through its 12-week estimate due to illnesses and other delays, the jury needed less than five hours before returning verdicts on Friday morning.
They accepted Polymiaidis, who has type 1 diabetes, injected Brenda and Lynton Anderson with fatal doses of insulin in separate incidents in March 2022 and April 2023 respectively.
Both were aged 94 at the time of their deaths.
Each had faced declining health and both were strongly opposed to being moved into aged care.
One potential motive raised by prosecutors was a misplaced idea that killing her parents would spare them from entering a nursing home.
After Brenda had a fall in February 2022, she was admitted to Noarlunga hospital with a fractured vertebra, complicated by pneumonia and another fall.
She had been recovering and had a discharge plan in place, but after Polymiadis visited her mother on March 12, nursing staff found Brenda “largely unresponsive”.
The prosecution alleged Polymiadis administered insulin to her mother on two occasions – on 12 March and between 13 March and 15 March.
Lynton continued to live at home after his wife’s death, but became more frail and his four children began staying there at night on a shift basis.
Polymiadis left the house on 30 April, 2023, after staying with her father for the weekend.
Two hours later, a carer found Lynton unconscious. He died on 1 May as a result of insulin toxicity.
Polymiadis’s former boyfriend Ian Edward Willcourt told the court she had told him that “insulin was the perfect murder weapon because it’s natural in the body and it can’t be detected”.
In other key evidence, a police listening device captured Polymiadis alone in her car allegedly confessing to God that she had killed her parents.
Police also seized notes written by Polymiadis, including one which read: “What they will do is wait for a few weeks, months, year to see if I ‘think I got away with it’ and I get cocky and slip up.
“Hang on buddy, it could be a long ride, otherwise the suspect would be arrested now.”
Polymiadis’ husband, Michael, and her son, who had accompanied his mother to court throughout the trial, did not comment as they left the courthouse.
Justice Sandi McDonald thanked the jury for their service during the “long and difficult trial”.
Polymiadis will reappear in court on 16 December for a directions hearing.

Anger, disgust, shame. In the last couple of weeks, as news of famous older men being convicted and accused of crimes against very young women and girls has emerged, the public mood has shifted.
The conversation has moved from “how did society let this happen?” to “how do we stop it from happening again?”. In that space, a campaign has grown for the consent gap to be closed.
The government is seriously considering the move, which is backed by two women who have made allegations against Russell Brand and David Walliams.
They’re fighting to change UK law to introduce a staggered age of consent under which 16- and 17-year-olds would still legally be able to have sex, but only with people no more than three years older than them.
Nosheen Iqbal speaks to the Guardian columnist Polly Hudson about why the culture and the law has left girls vulnerable to exploitation by older men for so long. And the educator Michael Conroy explains what needs to be done to ensure change is made.

Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the company engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes.
The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of new 22-metre power poles amid community protest.
The share price has since recovered to over $9 a share, but not before rival Goodman Group bought a nearly 10% stake in the business.
Shareholders revolted against the company at the AGM, issuing a second strike against executive pay, but the resulting motion on whether to spill the board was resoundingly defeated on Friday.
The chief executive, Craig Scroggie, said it was his “hardest AGM” in 15 years, and that he ultimately took responsibility for “delivery, power, planning, approvals, construction and community support”.
“At M3, we needed to work more closely with our power and construction partners, and with the community,” he said. “We are now doing that.”
Scroggie said the community deserved to be heard earlier than they had been during the Jemena construction works, and it was NextDC’s job to do that.
“M3 has certainly changed how we plan, build and operate alongside our neighbours,” he said.
“For more than 15 years we’ve built datacentres right across the country, and what earned trust then is not enough now. Community expectations have moved in the age of artificial intelligence and we must move with them.”
In addition to a new community consultative committee, including a standing forum for residents and local stakeholders, NextDC has said it will have a dedicated project website and contact channels with defined response times for complaints and inquiries.
NextDC’s chair, Doug Flynn, also revealed that the company would change where it builds in future.
“Given community sensitivities, we do not intend to pursue new development opportunities that are near residential properties,” Flynn said.
“The pushback against datacentres is very different right now than it was … six or so years ago.”
Flynn said that the M3 site in inner Melbourne had been an industrial site for 100 years, and had petrochemical works on it before NextDC built the datacentre.
After the blowback to taller power poles led to a delayed expansion, Flynn said the Jemena employee overseeing community engagement left the business.
“They recognise that they were just charging ahead regardless of community,” he said. “And they got a bloody nose.
“Unfortunately, we did as well.”
A spokesperson for Jemena declined to comment, but pointed to a September statement announcing its general manager for electricity networks had decided to step down.
summary: Public expectations around datacentres have changed in the age of AI, chief executive Craig Scroggie says Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the company engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes. The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of new 22m power poles amid community protest . Continue reading...
title: NextDC vows to keep future datacentres away from homes after community backlash in Melbourne

Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
- Published
"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.
But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.
The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.
A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.
The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.
About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.
The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.
Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.
While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support.
Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.
We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.
Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.
Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".
The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.
'Total dishonesty' in marketing
Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.
Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.
Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.
Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.
Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.
The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.
But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.
He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.
"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."
Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.
Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.
Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.
We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.
There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.
According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.
But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".
In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.
It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.
However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.
Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."
'No-one is directly accountable'
While there are doubts about what kind of housing Nurture has been providing, the BBC also found other flats sold to investors overseas with tenants who were in supported exempt accommodation.
The web of companies involved in providing this housing and cross-border ownership means it can be difficult for vulnerable tenants to get help when there are problems with properties.
"The way that the current system works is there's different levels of involvement by different organisations and companies and no-one is directly accountable," Abena Oppong-Asare, the housing committee chairwoman, told us.
Mo, who has mental health issues, was housed in a studio flat in Cricklewood, north London, after he became homeless. The converted house containing his flat was bought by Gemelli London 2 Limited, a company run by French nationals living in the Czech Republic, for £1.83m in January last year.
He says his supported housing provider, Windrush Alliance, receives nearly £2,000 a month via Barnet Council for the flat. Mo says he receives £340 in universal credit for living expenses every month - but he is expected to pay Windrush a monthly £120 service charge out of that.
Last year his ceiling collapsed after a leak went unrepaired for more than a year and Mo was temporarily housed in another flat in the property.
Mo says his weekly visits from a Windrush support worker feel like a tick-box exercise and do not help him with the mental health issues which have been keeping him out of work.
Gemelli's director Stephane Boussier told the BBC that when the company bought the property "no complaints from residents were disclosed". It was made aware of issues in August 2025, he said, and since then has "raised them with Windrush in writing, inspected the property and pressed for them to be resolved".
He added that Gemelli London 2 Limited receives about £1,365 per flat per month from Windrush and does not receive any of the extra housing benefit that would be used for vulnerable tenants.
Windrush said it was aware of issues at Mo's property and was "working with the building owner to put them right". According to Gemelli, the ceiling was repaired after the BBC contacted the two companies.
Windrush has previously been criticised by the Regulator for Social Housing for a "failure to meet the standards" of the regulator, including failing to ensure "tenants are safe in their homes".
It acknowledged that it "fell short in the past". It wrote off £1.8m in "funds to former directors and companies under their control", saying the company's financial position had been "compromised" by their actions. The company now has a new board in place.
Windrush told us its "priority is residents, not investors" and the rates it charges "are agreed with the relevant local authorities" and "any surplus is reinvested in our homes and services".
'The worst kind of exploitation'
In Bradford, the BBC visited City Exchange and Colonnade House, two former office blocks which Lee Jones has converted into housing - with Nurture Housing Association managing many of the flats.
Many of the properties there were advertised as supported housing investments. Residents showed us cockroach infestations, faulty fire alarms, broken lifts, leaks through the ceiling and black mould.
Nurture Housing said it was only responsible for the individual homes that it manages and does not manage communal areas or "wider building infrastructure".
"Nurture Housing and its managing agents regularly raise these concerns with the block manager," the company said.
The freeholder for Phil's block, Castleview House, and City Exchange, blamed "defects" by the developer Lee Jones for the problems with the buildings and said it was taking legal action. Colonnade House has had several building management companies in recent years and the latest said it was addressing the problems.
None of these companies or individuals are breaking the law, but critics say they are exploiting a lack of regulation in the sector.
Three years after the Supported Housing Act was passed in England, which would put in place a licensing regime for supported housing providers and give local councils more powers to shut down providers that failed to meet the standards, it still has not been implemented.
"It's taken too long," said Jasmine Basran, head of policy and campaigns at housing charity Crisis. "In the meantime, this an area where we've seen the worst kind of exploitation."
Additional reporting by Lorna Acquah and Abi Smitton
Get in touch
Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? Share your experiences.
summary: The properties are marketed at premium prices with claims of “government-backed” returns, the BBC finds.
title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad

body:
Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
- Published
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.
It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.
"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.
"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The BepiColombo mission blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.
So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform an 11-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.
"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."
Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.
Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.
A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.
A European Space Agency (ESA) craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), will view the planet from a distance.
A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.
Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.
The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.
"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.
"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gently… As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."
With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.
Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.
  - Published9 January 2025
  - Published19 October 2018
summary: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
title: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage

body:
New Hunger Games cast say joining the franchise is 'nerve-racking'
- Published
It's been 14 years since the release of the first Hunger Games movie, which helped establish the careers of talented young actors Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler.
This latest instalment, prequel film Sunrise on the Reaping, looks to do the same with its leading trio: 21-year-old Joseph Zada, 20-year-old Mckenna Grace and 23-year-old Whitney Peak.
Sitting down with BBC News at the start of a gruelling press run, the group were buzzing with a mixture of anticipation, nerves and excitement ahead of the release of the much-talked-about film.
Zada, who is taking on his first major role as lead Haymitch Abernathy, said they had been "clinging together" and "using each other, making sure we all feel supported".
'Nothing like anything I've experienced'
Grace is the most experienced of the three, having grown up as a child star with appearances in TV series The Handmaid's Tale, The Haunting of Hill House and two of the recent Ghostbusters films.
Even then, she said joining The Hunger Games franchise is "so nerve-racking", adding "I don't think anything can prepare you for working on it - this is nothing like anything I've experienced."
Peak, who starred in Netflix's Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, jokes that she and Zada have sought out Grace every time they have felt "stuck or confused about what's happening" while promoting the film, and Zada says she has been a "mentor" to the new actors.
Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the series, which to date is one of the highest-grossing film franchises of all time, bringing in more than $3.3bn (£2.51bn) worldwide since 2012.
It is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film and is based on the 2025 book of the same name by author Suzanne Collins.
Zada takes on the role of a teenage Haymitch, who is played by Woody Harrelson in the original films - a District 12 tribute in the games, chosen alongside Grace's character Donner.
Peak plays Lenore Dove, Haymitch's girlfriend.
'I'm a bit traumatised'
Reviews of the latest film have been generally positive, with several outlets praising Zada's performance, noting the difficulty of stepping into Harrelson's shoes.
Zada says he spent months "completely invested" in Harrelson's performances in the first four The Hunger Games films, "watching everything I could find and then making notes" which he used "as a base layer to colour with my own ideas".
He didn't meet the Oscar-nominated actor until halfway through filming, but says his advice was to watch two films - Cool Hand Luke and Harold and Maud, with the former "helping a lot to ground my performance" and the latter serving as "a fun watch".
Jesse Plemons, who plays a games producer in the film, told the BBC he knew Zada's role would be "a massive undertaking" after reading the script but says he was "amazed by his stamina and grace".
This was echoed by Glenn Close, who plays an over-the-top representative from the ruling Capitol, who said she "loved working with" Zada.
"When I met them [Zada, Grace and Peak] for the first time, they'd done all the games and been through it all.
"The first thing Joe said to me was 'I'm a bit traumatised' and he wasn't even done - there was still so much to go," she added.
The film, which includes an ensemble cast of Ralph Fiennes, Maya Hawke, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning, is set during the 50th edition of The Hunger Games - with most elements of the brutal dystopian universe that fans have come to recognise from the previous films returning in this iteration.
Adapted from Collins' novels, the series is set in a post-apocalyptic North America, which is known as Panem, with the first trilogy focusing on a teenage Katniss Everdeen, who was played by Lawrence in the films.
Panem has 12 districts that participate in the yearly Hunger Games, produced and run by the governing area, the Capitol, as a punishment for rebellion.
Peak notes that being on set was an intense experience for the young cast and could "get overwhelming very quickly" on set, so they had to make sure to "keep it light between all the hard stuff".
"I don't think people realise how intensely bonding an experience like this is because we all spend days doing extremely physical and deeply emotional things," Grace says.
"It's like a little family on set; we've all been thankful to have each other," she added.
The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is in cinemas now.
Related topics
  - Published1 day ago
  - Published11 December 2025
summary: The prequel, which is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film, is released today.
title: New Hunger Games cast say joining the franchise is 'nerve-racking'

body:
How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, closed 17% higher on its first day as a publicly traded company. Shares closed at $97.17, giving the company a market valuation of around $1.77 trillion, after briefly surpassing $2 trillion during trading.
The debut came as the wider technology sector fell 2.4%, raising questions about investor confidence in the AI boom.
The BBC's Samira Hussain breaks down Anthropic's first day on the stock market.
