body:
Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain
- Published
Mercedes driver George Russell topped a second practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix run on a wet but slowly drying track.
Russell, competing with Red Bull's Max Verstappen for second in the championship in the final three races of the year, set his time right at the end of the session.
The same applied to Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who went second, 0.071 seconds behind Russell, with a lap even later the Briton's.
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, the main pace-setter throughout the session, was third fastest ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.
The Frenchman had a faster lap ruined when he was blocked by Haas' Oliver Bearman at the end of the Strip.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth, ahead of of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and the second McLaren of Lando Norris, who was fastest in the wettest early part of the session.
New world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest, ahead of Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.
Las Vegas Grand Prix
20-22 November
Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live and 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app
Verstappen did not run until late in the session but was complaining about a problem with his engine.
Piastri will have a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance this season.
The new internal combustion engine the Australian needs as a result of a failure at the Mexico City Grand Prix two races ago is his fifth of the season - only four are permitted.
Piastri and team-mate Norris will also use the latest turbo Mercedes have produced under F1's engine upgrade scheme but that comes penalty-free.
That is not the case for Williams' Carlos Sainz, who will take the new turbo but it is his fifth of the season, so he also has a 10-place penalty which team-mate Alex Albon avoids despite also fitting the new turbo.
At the factory team, only Antonelli will use the new turbo. The team decided it was not worth Russell having it as it would have given him a 15-place grid penalty.
The turbo provides only a small performance upgrade and is more aimed at expanding the engine's useability for the 2027 season.
Bearman also has a grid penalty for engine changes and is set to start from the back of the grid.

Sutton's predictions v world champion boxer Lauren Price
- Published
Manchester United start life under new boss Mauricio Pochettino on Sunday but will they get their first Premier League win since August when they face Liverpool at Anfield?
"My worry for United is that they have one of the worst back fours in the Premier League," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.
"Their defensive record is something Pochettino will try to address but, whoever he picks, they are just not very good."
Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers anad a variety of guests.
For week 11, he takes on boxer Lauren Price, who is an Arsenal fan.
She will defend her unified welterweight titles against Michaela Kotaskova on Friday, and has a shot at becoming Wales' first undisputed world champion after the vacant WBO welterweight title was added to the fight.
Price returns to home soil at the Utilita Arena in Cardiff for a fight that will be shown live on BBC Two and BBC iPlayer, from 21:00 GMT.
Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.
The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.
A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.
Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.
Before turning to boxing, Price was a world kickboxing champion and international footballer - she captained the Wales Under-19 side, and played for the senior team as well as Cardiff City.
"My football days have helped me massively to get where I am in the ring today," the 32-year-old told BBC Sport.
"I honestly believe my footwork, and how fast my feet are, comes from when I played football.
"I am really proud of everything I achieved in football, especially playing for my country. It is the same now in boxing - to get in the ring and represent Wales is always an honour."
Price said the support of her grandparents helped her become successful at so many sports - and she followed her grandad, Derek, by becoming an Arsenal fan too.
"When I was a kid I was absolutely besotted with football and Arsenal were THE team when I was growing up," she explained.
"It was just the way they played under Arsene Wenger, and how they passed the ball - it was incredible. I loved Robin van Persie but Thierry Henry was my icon, my hero."
Chris Sutton and Lauren Price were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.
The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.
Premier League predictions
Saturday, 21 November
- Etihad Stadium, 12:30 GMT
The wheels have come off for Enzo Maresca at Manchester City with three Premier League defeats in a row.
It's not just City's results which have been alarming, either - they were well beaten by Nottingham Forest last time out, and their performance would have been the biggest concern for their manager.
In contrast, Fulham's results have improved of late and they are unbeaten in four league games. They've done all right whenever I've seen them this season, so I'm not surprised to see them picking up points.
Still, the international break probably came at a good time for Maresca to sort things out. Erling Haaland is scoring again too - not that he ever really stopped for very long - and I'm expecting City to be much better here.
I'm even going for them to keep a clean sheet, for the first time in eight games. I'm always brave... which is why I am bottom of the predictions table.
Sutton's prediction: 2-0
Lauren's prediction: City are having a tricky time of it at the moment but they should still win this. 2-0
AI's prediction: 3-1
- Villa Park, 15:00
I was at Sunderland's win over Chelsea and they thoroughly deserved it. They had been on a dreadful run of results before then, but it was a reminder of what they are about.
Brian Brobbey was just phenomenal for the Black Cats in that game but, like his captain Granit Xhaka, he is injured and will miss out here.
That just makes me think Aston Villa will have the edge. I always fancy them at home anyway with the way they go after teams, although I don't think this will be easy for them.
Villa boss Unai Emery was fuming after his side threw away a two-goal lead twice in their 4-4 draw at Manchester United, but they will hold on this time while Sunderland go down fighting.
Sutton's prediction: 2-1
Lauren's prediction: Villa are going really well. 2-1
AI's prediction: 2-0
- Vitality Stadium, 15:00
Bournemouth have won eight games in a row in all competitions and it is incredible how Marco Rose has turned things around after a slow start.
The Cherries were absolutely flying before the international break - but will the two weeks off affect their momentum?
Forest did not need the break either, after their brilliant win over Manchester City.
That was such an important result for their manager Oliver Glasner but I think they will find it difficult to follow it up at Bournemouth.
Sutton's prediction: 2-1
Lauren's prediction: Forest shocked City last time out but I am going with Bournemouth here, they are on a brilliant run. 2-1
AI's prediction: 1-1
- Stamford Bridge, 15:00
Chelsea were so lethargic when I watched them lose against Sunderland, and I don't think they were hard done by in that game - they looked flimsy at the back, and were deservedly beaten.
I had a bit of a pile-on from some Chelsea fans for saying that after the game, but then Xabi Alonso came out and was also heavily critical of the way they had defended - so he and I are on the same page there.
If Joao Pedro is fit then they will at least have more physicality up front this week, but I still have a feeling Leeds will get something out of this.
Daniel Farke's side got a great win over Tottenham last time out and they do not give much away - Arsenal and Brighton are the only top-flight teams to have conceded fewer league goals this season.
Leeds have definitely benefited from signing keeper James Trafford and what a move it has been for him personally as well.
I admire him for that, because he could have hung around at Manchester City as Gianluigi Donnarumma's number two, but he wanted first-team football. Now he is battling it out with Jordan Pickford to be England's number one.
Sutton's prediction: 1-1
Lauren's prediction: I don't think Leeds will keep Chelsea quiet. 3-1
AI's prediction: 2-1
- Coventry Building Society Arena, 15:00
This is the battle of the Franks... Lampard versus Thomas.
Thomas Frank's first conundrum as Crystal Palace's new manager is to stop them leaking so many goals - they have conceded 24 in their first 10 games, which is concerning.
I still think Palace have got some really good players, like Ismaila Sarr, Jorgen Strand Larsen and Jean-Philippe Mateta, and it's just a case of them getting fit and finding some form.
The way Coventry play, the Eagles are going to get some chances - but can they take them?
Frank Lampard's side counter-attack with such vigour, so I definitely think they will score... but I can see Palace's forward players having some joy too.
Sutton's prediction: 2-2
Lauren's prediction: I'm standing next to a Palace fan now, Ed from Boxxer, so I've got to go with them here! 0-2
AI's prediction: 1-1
- Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, 15:00
We've seen Palace change their manager after making a disastrous start but they are still only four points below Ipswich and they will certainly see that as retrievable.
The Tractor Boys are not in the relegation zone but they are still in a relegation fight so, it is important for them to keep picking points up here and there. The trouble for them is that I don't see them getting anything at Tottenham.
Spurs lost to Leeds last time out but I still think they have turned a corner with their performances before that defeat.
I actually think this will be a routine win for Roberto de Zerbi's side, and I'm going for them to keep a clean sheet too.
Sutton's prediction: 2-0
Lauren's prediction: Spurs will take this one. 2-1
AI's prediction: 3-1
- St James' Park, 17:30
I am covering this game and I think it is a huge one for Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle.
The Magpies have picked up as many points - 12 - in their first 10 games under Jaissle as they did when Eddie Howe was in charge last season, but I still don't think their fans are overly convinced by him.
Some of their unease is because Newcastle don't seem to have a defined style of play, and can be a bit kamikaze going forward.
Because of that, I just think Arsenal will pick them off, and win comfortably.
The Gunners have conceded only five league goals so far and have made an incredible start to their title defence with nine wins out of 10.
The worry for their rivals is that it feels to me Mikel Arteta's side have not even got going yet, but I still don't see anyone being close to them.
Sutton's prediction: 0-2
Lauren's prediction: No problems for Arsenal here! 0-4
AI's prediction: 1-1
Sunday, 22 November
- MKM Stadium, 14:00
Hull are going to scrap and fight - they have not won for eight games now, but they have still picked up some points because of their battling approach.
You know they will get in Brighton's faces but I don't think it will bother the Seagulls too much.
I want to apologise to Hull fans because I keep writing the Tigers off every week, but I am going to do it again here because Brighton are such a good team going forward and defensively.
Sutton's prediction: 0-3
Lauren's prediction: Brighton to edge this one. 0-1
AI's prediction: 1-2
- Anfield, 16:30
Good luck to Pochettino. I like him as a manager and he seems a decent guy too.
He will need some luck as well, because it is going to be incredibly difficult for him to succeed at Old Trafford.
The constant for Manchester United is their managers keep getting the sack, when the club's problems seem to be deeper-lying than that.
Pochettino will get time because of what he has taken over, but it is amazing and also alarming to think United are in the bottom three, and could be bottom by the time this game is played.
As well as being so poor at the back, they have a midfield without any great athleticism and, stylistically, they did not really have an identity under Michael Carrick.
If you are Pochettino, you are probably going into the dressing room and putting your arm arm around Bruno Fernandes, to get the old sulker onside.
He really needs to, because Fernandes is an outstanding player and played a key role in the club's form with his numbers last season.
United need to see that version of him more than ever now, because so far this season he has not got going at all.
As for Liverpool, well I think they will get there under Andoni Iraola. It is just taking a bit of time for his players to adapt to his style.
They are not particularly fluid most of the time, and it feels like Iraola is not quite sure what his best midfield is.
Liverpool are still a work in progress, and United have picked up some results at Anfield recently - two draws and a win in their past three visits - but I can only see one result here, and it is a home victory.
Pochettino will probably look to defend and play on the counter-attack, and they might get some chances that way, but Liverpool are going to win. The only question is how many they will score.
Carrick began by beating Manchester City and Arsenal in his first two games in January. Pochettino might start by being on the wrong end of a pummelling.
Sutton's prediction: 4-0
Lauren's prediction: Liverpool are at home and I am going with them to win it. 2-1
AI's prediction: 2-1
Monday, 23 November
- Gtech Community Stadium, 20:00
Brentford beat Everton 4-2 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium last season but, in three of their past four meetings, the points have been shared.
This has got a draw written all over it, too.
Everton are so solid under David Moyes, and so well organised, that I just don't see them losing. Brentford will keep things tight as well.
Sutton's prediction: 1-1
Lauren's prediction: Both these teams are doing well and this should be pretty even - I haven't gone for a draw yet, so let's finish with one. 1-1
AI's prediction: 1-1
How did Sutton do last time?
Before the international break, Chris got four correct results with no exact scores from the 10 games in week 10, giving him 40 points.
His guests were the computer game Football Manager 27 and Miles Jacobson, the studio director of Sports Interactive, the company behind it.
Miles managed five correct results with no exact scores, giving him 50 points, while FM 27 got six correct results with three exact scores, to end up on 150 points.
Their individual totals will be shown on the guest leaderboard below - with FM 27 going top - but they have been combined, giving them an average of 100 points, for the guest score for the BBC predictions league table.
That means they miss out on the weekly win, which ended up in a tie between the BBC readers and AI. They both got six correct results with no exact scores, for a tally of 120 points.
There was only one game where everyone picked the right outcome - Liverpool's 3-1 win over Crystal Palace.
Chris, FM 27, Miles, AI and the BBC readers all backed the Reds to win, but AI was the only one to get the score spot on.
There were two games where no-one got the correct result - Nottingham Forest's win over Manchester City, and Sunderland's victory against Chelsea.
Out of more than 25,000 predictions, fewer than 1,500 people thought Forest would beat City and only 36 of them got the 3-1 scoreline right too.
Related topics
  - Published28 August
summary: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on world champion boxer Lauren Price, plus the BBC readers and AI, with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
title: Sutton's predictions v world champion boxer Lauren Price

The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.
Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.
Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.
The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.
Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.
A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.
Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.
In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.
Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.
Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.
But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.
It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.
Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.
The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.
In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.
In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.
Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.
Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.
summary: Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations. Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate. Continue reading...
title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers

Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
On Friday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.
The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.
But Hatfield told the New South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.
The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.
“The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield said.
“His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.
“His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”
Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.
Hatfield said the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.
“His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he said.
Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.
The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.
Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.
Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.
His decisions to go to Sushi Train for dinner with his friend and undergo a minor elective surgery in the aftermath of the alleged murders showed Lamarre-Condon was calm and at points “completely relaxed”, Hatfield alleged.
But within days, the accused must have been “feeling the world closing in”, the prosecutor said.
“He wants credit for handing himself in to police … but even in his last hours he’s there going to Bunnings, buying paint and painting the inside of the van … still trying to cover up what happened,” Hatfield told the court.
Lamarre-Condon eventually helped police locate the bodies, but only after being told about the state’s no body, no parole laws.
“The bodies were left … for a further four days after he’s arrested,” Hatfield said. “Evidence all the while being destroyed.
“Imagine the grief [of the families] on those four days.”
The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.
Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but says this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.
“It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer said.
Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.
summary: Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard. Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024. The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.
As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.
The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.
Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.
“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.
Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”
The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.
Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.
An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.
Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.
An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.
“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.
“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.
Produced in collaboration with Jummar, an independent Iraqi media platform
summary: Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy. As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators. Continue reading...
title: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests

An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school.
The school, part of Lion Academy Trust, has issued a formal apology after it sent letters to the children’s parents saying they might be referred to the counter-extremism programme or to local hate crime teams.
The issue dates back to November 2023 when the children’s school, Barclay primary school in Leyton, east London, held a non-uniform fundraising day for Children in Need.
The four children, all British Muslims aged between six and 10 at the time, attended wearing items displaying Palestinian colours or the Palestinian flag, in memory of children who had been killed in Gaza and those who continued to suffer during the conflict, which was ongoing at the time.
One child wore a Children in Need Pudsey sticker featuring a bow tie in Palestinian colours. Another wore a homemade badge bearing the Palestinian flag and colours.
Parents of the four children said they had repeatedly asked the school to apologise for their treatment of the children and had launched a legal challenge when none was forthcoming.
At a hearing at Central London county court on Thursday, the court heard that the academy trust had now made a formal apology to the children and their families and would pay them substantial compensation.
Lawyers for the children alleged direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment on grounds including race, ethnicity, religion and belief, together with breaches of their rights to freedom of expression and freedom of thought, conscience and belief.
Shahid Achhala, the father of one of the children, said: “What happened to our son was deeply disturbing and should never have happened to any child. He was just eight years old, expressing compassion and solidarity with children suffering in Gaza, including members of his own extended family. Instead of being supported and protected by the school entrusted with his care, he was deliberately subjected to mistreatment that caused him considerable emotional distress.
“For almost three years, we have had to fight legally for accountability and an acknowledgment of the wrongs we believe were committed. While we welcome Lion Academy Trust’s apology, we cannot overlook the distress caused to our son and our family, or the fact that this matter could have been resolved long time ago.”
The families were represented by law firm Leigh Day and supported in their legal claim by Prevent Watch, which provides casework support to individuals and families affected by the Prevent duty.
Layla Aitlhadj, a director at Prevent Watch, said: “In this case, parents who were protecting their children’s rights were told that their concerns were ‘false and malicious’. They held firm through three years of pressure. Today the families, and the wider community who stood with them, have been vindicated.”
The academy trust has been approached for comment.
summary: Lion Academy Trust apologises after threatening four pupils in east London with referral to counter-extremism scheme An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school. The school, part of Lion Academy Trust, has issued a formal apology after it sent letters to the children’s parents saying they might be referred to the counter-extremism programme or to local hate crime teams. Continue reading...
title: Academy trust pays out after Prevent threat over children’s Palestine badges

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation after a patient was “horrified” to discover that notes of sensitive discussions with her psychotherapist had been shared with more than 100,000 NHS workers.
Rosanna (not her real name) found out that her detailed therapist’s notes, including about her grief and trauma, had been uploaded to her patient records when she saw them on a computer screen during a visit to her GP.
Inquiries made by Rosanna under freedom of information laws revealed that her therapy notes had been accessed by staff who did not work at the hospital trust where she was being treated.
Her discovery led to her stopping the treatment she was receiving for bipolar disorder with South London and Maudsley NHS trust (SLaM). It meant she had no mental health support during a close family bereavement.
Rosanna’s case has prompted questions in parliament, and suggests many other patients’ psychotherapy notes, including those of children, could have been shared without their knowledge or consent. This week the ICO confirmed it would investigate the case after a request to expedite it by the former Labour minister Philip Hunt.
Her case also raises questions about whether the new single patient record, proposed under the health bill, will include intimate details from any psychotherapy sessions provided by the NHS.
SLaM said it was reviewing how it documented psychotherapy on electronic patient records and how it communicated how data was shared.
Rosanna’s psychotherapy notes were uploaded to the London Care Record (LCR), an electronic patient record accessible to up 140,000 NHS staff, at a time of increasing concern about health workers snooping on patients.
She said: “I felt horrified looking over my GP’s shoulder as they checked what I had told them about my therapy records being available on the LCR. It’s like discovering that your personal diary has been photocopied and placed in a library.”
SLaM said “no intimate details” from therapy sessions had been shared, but in a response to Rosanna it admitted that “key session content” from therapeutic discussions was automatically uploaded. It also told her: “Very private material can be shared in the context of treatment.”.
In September Rosanna attempted to clarify exactly what had been shared on her medical notes by submitting a subject access request to SLaM. So far SLaM has failed to respond to that request.
She is concerned that sharing therapy notes, including those of children, could present a danger to patients.
She said: “Where trauma is involved, it can create a safety risk. You don’t want the most intimate parts of your life getting into the hands of the wrong person. SLaM’s own list of what it shares includes all events from its child and adolescent mental health services.”
She added: “When I asked what was being shared, a senior therapist told me he didn’t know all the answers. SLaM now accepts staff and patients may not have been given enough information.”
Rosanna said there should have been a choice to opt out of such information being shared, but SLaM had failed to inform her that her therapy notes would be available to tens of thousands of staff.
Her MP, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, asked the government what guidance had been issued to mental health trusts on sharing therapy notes. James Frith, a junior health minister, replied that all records “relating to direct care are shared on a basis of implied consent”.
Rosanna said: “It’s implicit that therapy is confidential unless you’re told otherwise, within the normal safeguarding limits. Patients should be told where their data is going. You can’t object to something if you don’t know it’s happening and you haven’t been told.
“I paused my psychotherapy because I couldn’t be confident where what I said in treatment would end up. I’ve been without mental health secondary care support since, including while a parent was seriously ill and after they died.
“I am concerned other people receiving therapy from SLaM will see this and, like me, pause treatment. I would urge you not to, and to learn about your data rights instead.”
Rosanna supports the new planned single patient record, but thinks the focus should be on sharing medical details, not the contents of therapy sessions. “Transparency over what will be on the shared record and the option to opt out is essential,” she said.
Prof Derek Tracy, SLaM’s chief medical officer executive, said: “We apologise again to the patient for the delays in responding to her concerns.
“We put the utmost importance on patient confidentiality and the trust placed in us by our patients and service users. We have clear guidance on limiting the information recorded. This includes any significant changes or themes, risks and agreed actions.
“Clinicians also have the option to limit access to information to local teams in the trust without it being shared more widely and mask parts of the record as appropriate to balance sharing relevant information and respect privacy.”
Andy Bell, the chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health, said: “Normally when you start therapy there’s a discussion about confidentiality. The therapist will say ‘If you tell me something that creates a safeguarding risk to yourself or others I will have to tell x y and z’. Not everything can remain confidential.
“A situation like this does raise issues about the boundaries of what is shareable and what isn’t, and what is appropriate to go on someone’s notes and what absolutely shouldn’t.
“If a patient is finding out information about themselves on the system that they didn’t expect, that suggests that the system isn’t working properly.”
summary: Exclusive: Investigation launched after details of grief and trauma uploaded, raising questions over extent of issue The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) has launched an investigation after a patient was “horrified” to discover that notes of sensitive discussions with her psychotherapist had been shared with more than 100,000 NHS workers. Rosanna (not her real name) found out that her detailed therapist’s notes, including about her grief and trauma, had been uploaded to her patient records when she saw them on a computer screen during a visit to her GP. Continue reading...
title: Patient ‘horrified’ to find her sensitive discussions were shared with more than 100,000 NHS staff

body:
Loneliness & mood swings - what's it like to miss a season through injury?
- Published
"I told my mother. I sat with her and I told her: 'Listen, I don't think I can play any more'," says Dejan Kulusevski in a moving interview about his injury nightmare.
It is 18 months since Tottenham and Sweden winger Kulusevski, 26, last started a competitive match.
Spurs have won the Europa League, sacked both Ange Postecoglou and Thomas Frank, "mutually agreed" to part ways with Igor Tudor and appointed Roberto de Zerbi since the former Juventus player last started a first-team game for his club.
A serious knee injury two weeks from the end of the 2024-25 season forced him to miss the whole of the following campaign, as well as the 2026 World Cup.
"You feel like the whole world has forgotten about you," adds Kulusevski in an interview with Tottenham's in-house media, external about the emotional toll of being out for so long.
Thankfully, the player nicknamed 'Deki' has made a full recovery and is closing in on his first Tottenham start since 11 May 2025.
He is not the only footballer to question their career after having their world turned upside down by injury.
In the women's game, Everton club captain Megan Finnigan recently returned from a cruciate ligament injury after 602 days out., external
"The amount of times the thought of retirement entered my head during rehab was a lot," Finnigan, 28, tells BBC Sport.
Countless hours in the gym away from team-mates, boredom, setbacks and frustration - what is it like for a player at the peak of their game to miss a season because of injury?
- 'I am a different man now' - Kulusevski on return after 526 days 
  - Published20 October
- Kulusevski out for a 'few months' - Postecoglou 
  - Published15 May 2025
'I stared at the wall for hours'
Before Crystal Palace visited Tottenham a fortnight from the end of the 2024-25 campaign, Kulusevski had much to look forward to.
Off the pitch, he was making plans to marry his partner Eldina Ahmic, a former midfielder with Swedish club Brommapojkarna and Bosnia-Herzegovina.
On the pitch, there was a Europa League final against Manchester United coming up.
Everything changed in that match against Palace.
In the early stages, Kulusevski stayed down after a challenge with Marc Guehi. He was able to climb to his feet and walk unaided off the pitch and straight down the tunnel.
But in that moment, his problems were only just starting.
"It was pain, but it didn't hurt that much," Kulusevski says, recalling the patella and cartilage injury in his right knee.
"I could feel that the knee was moving a little bit too much."
The initial diagnosis from Tottenham was that the £25m signing from Juventus, who arrived in the summer of 2023, would be out for "at least a few months".
Due to complications, those months turned into a year and Kulusevski's dream career threatened to turn into a nightmare.
He travelled to Bilbao on crutches to watch his team-mates beat United in the Europa League final.
"That was one of the hardest days of my life," he says. "It was so beautiful to see all the people happy, but for me I was going there with crutches, I couldn't work.
"I couldn't even go and get my medal because it was too slippy to go on that thing [platform].
"Seeing the team celebrating on the bus [outside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] was probably one of the most difficult parts of this journey because you feel so alone.
"You feel like the whole world has forgot about you and what you put in."
As months went by, Kulusevski underwent multiple operations and was even offered a knee transplant as a treatment option, which he rejected.
"You get stressed because nothing works," he says.
Then came another crushing blow delivered in a phone call with Sweden boss Graham Potter. Stockholm-born Kulusevski, who had played for his country since the age of 19, would not be going to the 2026 World Cup.
He had hoped to recover in time to be selected.
"I just stared at the wall for three hours because I really believed I would do it," he says.
It is not just the players who suffer when they are out for so long; the people around them feel the emotional toll as well.
"Seeing him miss the Europa League final and the World Cup, every Premier League game last season, seeing him skipping around on his crutches, those parts were really difficult," Eldina, Kulusevski's wife, says.
As recently as this past summer, Kulusevski wondered whether he would play again.
"It had been one year and two months and I could still not walk up the stairs like a normal guy.
"I wasn't going to give up, but I also had to think if this didn't work out, what am I going to do, because I am 26 and I have to have some sort of plan."
Enormous comfort came from Leonie, Kulusevski's two-year-old daughter, during his bleakest days.
"I said if I cannot play football any more, I will still have fun with her."
Then, after multiple setbacks, came a crucial breakthrough.
His knee had healed sufficiently for specialists to give him permission to train again.
On 19 October, Kulusevski was given a hero's reception by Spurs fans when he made his first appearance in 526 days.
It came in Tottenham's 3-1 win over Coventry City as an 87th-minute substitute.
Waiting for him after the final whistle were Eldina and Leonie, his daughter wearing a Spurs shirt with the number 526 on the back, along with the words 'My Hero'.
He made his Sweden return this month, coming off the bench in a win against Bosnia-Herzegovina.
"Every day is just beautiful now," says Kulusevski, who has made four substitute appearances totalling 42 minutes for his club this season.
"I don't take it for granted any more."
'I wasn't pleasant to be around'
Research suggests female footballers are two to six times more likely to suffer anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries than their male counterparts.
Everton captain Finnigan remembers how she "completely lost my sparkle" as she endured the long road to recovery.
"It's not comfortable to think back how I was," Finnigan tells BBC Radio Merseyside's Giulia Bould.
"Anyone that knows me knows I'm very bubbly, quite loud, I like to be at the centre of things. I completely lost myself in rehab, completely lost my sparkle as my mum says.
"How I was in this building is not nice to think back on. I was always thinking what other people were thinking about me. I was not pleasant to be around as I was struggling so much.
"I was also thinking 'no-one wants to be around me'. I was just miserable. Everyone in this building has seen me cry over the past 18 months."
Finnigan - Everton's longest-serving women's player having joined the Blues at the age of nine - suffered her injury in an FA Cup tie against Tottenham in January 2025. She did not return to competitive action until September of this year.
"I was in quite a difficult place mentally," she adds.
One thing that helped her through her lowest moments was writing down her feelings.
"It was an absolute whirlwind of a rehab, a rollercoaster," she adds.
"Anyone who went through it with me will tell you that. I am really glad I kept a diary as proof I did it and survived it."
'I felt like a ghost'
Former Arsenal and England midfielder Fara Williams points to how some players who suffer serious injuries in the Women's Super League face specific worries.
"While they are going through rehab, there are financial worries, bills to pay; they are on short contracts so you don't have that stability," says Williams.
"While you are managing the injury, mentally you are stressing, wondering where the next contract is coming from. When you are stressed, I imagine that doesn't help with the healing of the injury."
Micah Richards suffered multiple long-term knee and hamstring injuries before he retired in 2019 while at Aston Villa.
A few months later the former Manchester City and England defender opened up to BBC Sport about injuries and the "dark side of football".
"I was in a lonely place for a long time, and I did not know how to get out of it," he said at the time.
"Deep down, I probably knew it was already over, but for most of the two and a half years between my 295th and final game as a professional, against Wolves in October 2016, and the day I announced my retirement in July 2019, I was living in denial.
"I could run and I could jump - but I couldn't twist on my right knee, and it would not get any better. Whatever I tried, it did not make any difference.
"There were times while I was injured at Villa when I felt like I was a ghost.
"They told me to come in three times a week, then two. Then one.
"I would go into the gym and tell myself 'I am all right, I am all right, I am all right' but actually I had no idea how to deal with what was happening to me, and my body."
summary: Not pleasant to be around and staring at a wall for hours after being told you are not going to the World Cup - what's it like for footballers when they miss a season due to serious injury?
title: Loneliness & mood swings - what's it like to miss a season through injury?

body:
Missing fishing boat Kilda recovered from waters off Orkney
- Published
A fishing boat that went missing near the Isle of Lewis a month ago has been recovered after it was spotted semi-submerged in the North Sea off Orkney.
Three men were on board the Kilda when it disappeared on 13 October.
The body of crew member Douglas Craigie was found by search teams the following day but two other men - Norman Murray and Murdo Morrison - remain unaccounted for.
The wreck was spotted about 50 miles (80km) east of Orkney on Wednesday morning, and a specialist vessel recovered it on Thursday before bringing it to Kirkwall.
An HM Coastguard aircraft confirmed the sighting of a semi-submerged boat on Wednesday before ships were sent to the scene, including one equipped to recover the Kilda.
The Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) has started an investigation into the loss of the Kilda.
It is understood it will be kept in a secure yard while investigations are carried out.
Earlier this month, an empty life raft from the Kilda washed up 200 miles away in Shetland.
The Kilda was last known to be operating close to the Port of Ness in Lewis.
Coastguard personnel, lifeboat crews, police and volunteers have been involved in searches since its disappearance.
A specialist Northern Lighthouse Board ship was brought in to carry out surveys of the seabed off north Lewis, and it identified two sites which were searched but nothing was found.
On Wednesday night, a coastguard said it had taken a number of actions off Orkney.
A spokesperson said: "An HM Coastguard aircraft was tasked to the incident, and the aircraft was able to provide a visual report of the wreck which confirmed no further search and rescue activity was required.
"HM Coastguard Counter Pollution is monitoring and a security broadcast has been issued warning vessels to steer clear of the area."
'Devastating impact' in Lewis community
Speaking at the time of the Kilda's disappearance, Duncan Macinnes, secretary of the Western Isles Fishermen's Association, said the incident has had a devastating impact in the local community.
He told BBC Scotland: "It is just an unimaginable tragedy that happened just over a week ago and we have heartfelt sorrow for the grieving families who have suffered such loss and we pray that Tam and Murdo will be found.
"We are thankful for the rescue services that have taken place by the Coastguard, the Marine Accident Investigation Branch, Police Scotland, and all the others that have gone and assisted in any way possible to try and find those that have been lost.
"With a tragedy like this which is one of the worst fishing tragedies that we have experienced in the Western Isles in a generation, it is going to leave broken hearts.
"It is just very difficult and total devastation for the industry and for the community."
Ness is a sparsely populated area on the northern tip of Lewis.
It is an area of rugged coastline, with many of its roughly 1,300 people living in crofting townships - small holdings where families can raise livestock and grow crops while working other jobs.
The parish has one of the highest concentrations of Gaelic speakers in the Western Isles.
A minute's silence was held at the Royal National Mòd, Scotland's annual celebration of Gaelic culture and language, which was taking place in Glasgow at the time.
Flowers were also left on the plinth of the Ness Fishery Memorial at Port of Ness.
  - Published4 November
  - Published22 October
  - Published21 October
summary: The Kilda and its three crew was reported missing near Lewis on 13 October.
title: Missing fishing boat Kilda recovered from waters off Orkney

body:
The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory
- Published
As soft, instrumental opera music plays in the background of a precise temperature-controlled room in northern Italy, Thomaso is using a children's toy ball and hairdryer to perform his meticulous work.
Hugely focused, in a crisp white coat, he moulds a precious sticky black material over and over again for up to six hours.
One day, his fastidiousness may save the life of one of the best athletes in the world.
The room Thomaso works in is called "the magic shop". Its motto? 'One man, one shell.'
Much of what happens inside is top secret. What we can say is the black material Thomaso is working with is a blend of carbon fibre that has to be stored at exactly -16°C. He moulds it into a secret form, layer by layer, after which the entire unit is baked in a vacuum bag at a set pressure at 120C for three-and-a-half hours.
The handmade products he is working on are personally chosen by their clients - for their safety features, as well as comfort, practicality and look.
Thomaso's colleague Sven travels the world between February and December to keep those clients happy. A different country almost every week, with a reliable weather forecast almost as important as a large allowance of hand luggage.
Together with 32 colleagues, Thomaso and Sven work for one of the four leading manufacturers of F1 helmets.
They produce sophisticated engineering masterpieces, and works of art.
"Our philosophy is to make the best product for the best drivers," says chief executive Alberto Dall'Oglio.
From leather caps to life-saving technology
In the early days of grand prix racing, protection was rudimentary. Drivers often wore little more than leather flying caps, goggles and - eventually - relatively basic open-face helmets.
Safety standards were inconsistent, materials primitive and the consequences of an accident frequently devastating.
According to the official F1 website, Giuseppe Farina - the first winner of an F1 race and first world champion - competed wearing nothing more than "his trusty cloth cap, two pairs of goggles (he wore the spare pair round his neck), cotton dungarees, leather boots and leather gloves".
The arrival of the full-face helmet in the late 1960s marked a defining moment. Bell introduced its pioneering Star model in 1966, and Dan Gurney became the first driver to race in a full-face helmet in 1968. The face - previously exposed to flying debris, fire and impact - finally had meaningful protection.
Progress was painfully slow, and motorsport's darkest moments repeatedly exposed the limitations of the technology.
In 1976, Niki Lauda's Ferrari erupted into flames at the Nurburgring. His helmet came loose, leaving his head exposed to the fire. He survived, but suffered severe burns and lifelong injuries. The accident became a defining lesson in the importance of helmet retention, fire resistance and the protection of the driver's entire head.
The tragic deaths of Roland Ratzenberger and Ayrton Senna at Imola in 1994, followed by Jules Bianchi's fatal accident at Suzuka in 2014, demonstrated even increasingly sophisticated helmets could not eliminate every danger.
Ratzenberger suffered a fatal basilar skull fracture; Senna succumbed to multiple fractures of the skull base, after a strut from the suspension pierced his helmet.
Bianchi's accident exposed the vulnerability of drivers' heads to heavy external impacts. Helmets are only one part of a much wider safety system, which now includes stronger survival cells, the Hans device and the halo.
In 2004, the FIA introduced its new helmet safety standard, requiring advanced carbon-fibre construction to deliver greater strength, improved impact protection and reduced weight for F1 drivers.
At Bahrain's Sakhir circuit in 2020, Romain Grosjean's Haas split apart against the barriers and burst into flames. After 28 seconds trapped in the wreckage, he emerged with burns to his hands and ankles. His Bell helmet, fire-resistant equipment and the halo were instrumental in saving his life - a powerful testament to decades of safety innovation and engineering.
"Today's helmets are withstanding up to 30 seconds at 700, even 800, degrees," says Dall'Oglio. "Then they have to self-extinguish within 15 seconds."
Dall'Oglio is the CEO of Schuberth Performance, Thomaso an engineer and Sven a racing service technician, working trackside at more than 400 grands prix, preparing helmets and visors for rain, sun or floodlights.
Needing to avoid any impact on the helmets, he must carry them - sometimes five or six at a time - to races.
German engineering, Italian manufacturing
Schuberth, a German firm, has a long history in head protection. Founded in 1922, the company began making industrial products before moving into helmet linings in the late 1920s, then mining and motorcycle helmets in the 1950s.
With its HQ in Magdeburg and F1 helmet production in Schio, northern Italy, it produces special helmets for military forces - made of Kevlar, and some of a similar carbon - in the same factory as the F1 helmets.
Its motorsport credentials grew considerably around the turn of the millennium.
Following Michael Schumacher's British Grand Prix accident in 1999, Schuberth developed a new generation of racing helmets, subsequently worn by Schumacher and other leading drivers.
Of the current drivers, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is the most prominent to wear a Schuberth helmet. He is joined by Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar, Cadillac's Sergio Perez, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls.
Dall'Oglio's team hand-makes about 250 helmets a year.
'We work hard to remove 20g of weight... then a driver can add decoration of 80g'
An F1 helmet is a remarkable marriage of science and aesthetics.
Constructed using advanced composite materials, including carbon fibre, it must be exceptionally strong while remaining light enough to minimise strain on a driver's neck.
Visors, ventilation systems, fire-resistant linings, communication equipment, a straw-like drinks system and carefully designed retention mechanisms all contribute to its performance.
Today, F1 helmets must withstand a 225g metal projectile fired at 155mph, a 790C flame and substantial impact and crushing tests. It is engineering with virtually no margin for compromise.
Schuberth works closely with motorsport governing body the FIA.
Dall'Oglio says: "There's a constant exchange of information. We are repeating tests on a regular basis. We are also working on the future regulation of the helmets.
"With the tiniest structural or superficial defect, the carbon shell cannot be used. This could be a lamination, a cooking or a tool problem. So it could be over 1,000 euros (£850) in material, and all those hours of work will have become obsolete."
Arai, Bell and Stilo are the three other leading manufacturers of F1 helmets.
Dall'Oglio says: "We all have the same issues, and in the end, we are protecting drivers. So, the responsibility is heavy for all of us.
"It's the fun part to work with the drivers, but it's also a high responsibility."
When I visit, production is paused and the team cluster to solve a problem. Thankfully this happens very rarely - and the majority of helmet shells are taken to the next station: a water-jet cutting system with a "needle" of water slicing through the rock-hard carbon.
It's 4,000 bars of pressure, like a knife through warm butter, to create the narrow visor opening, six centimetres at its highest point.
"It is genius, because you don't use mechanical force on to the helmet," explains Dall'Oglio.
The cut shell is then taken to what they call "the jigsaw" - the assembly point.
Dall'Oglio says: "The outer shell is created of nearly 100 pieces. Now we add another 100 pieces, depending on the type of aerodynamics parts we need to add on. In total, we can say a couple of hundred pieces make a helmet."
Once assembled, the helmet is taken to the driver's designer.
A helmet can be a driver's signature. From Senna's iconic Brazilian colours to Schumacher's Ferrari red, the designs are miniature works of art.
Combining intricate graphics, specialist paintwork and personal touches, each livery tells a story, celebrating a driver's heritage, family or defining moments.
But while fancy designs look fabulous, they can create headaches for the team in Schio.
"A helmet overall weighs about 1.4 kg, depending on the decoration, and aerodynamic specification," says Dall'Oglio.
"We try to work hard to remove like 20, 30 grams from the top-of-the-line helmets, and a driver then adds decoration of 80 or 70 grams. It's always a little bit of a negotiation with the driver and the painter, but in the end, it's their decision."
Dall'Oglio is proud of the company's relationship with Verstappen, who is very good at giving feedback to initiate improvements.
"We continue on cultivating it, of course, but it's like a happy marriage," he says.
The helmets produced by Dall'Oglio, his colleagues, and other firms are extraordinary pieces of design and engineering, but the greatest achievement will never be the paintwork, carbon-fibre finish or name emblazoned across the side.
Thomaso smiles, as he knows. It is the life they help save, and the driver who walks away.
summary: Inside the extraordinary world of Formula 1 helmets, where precision engineering, personal expression and life-saving technology join forces.
title: The art of protection - inside an F1 helmet factory

body:
UK braces for coldest night of autumn so far with temperature of -10C forecast
- Published
The UK will experience the coldest night of autumn so far overnight on Friday, with a widespread frost developing as temperatures plummet below zero.
It will be particularly cold in northern areas, where temperatures of minus 1 (30F) to minus 5C (23F) are widely expected from the Midlands northward.
However, in rural areas of Scotland where there is some lying snow, it could get as low as minus 10C (14F).
It will stay cold with more overnight frost over the weekend, with cold health alerts from the UK's Health Security Agency remaining in force across northern England until Monday morning.
The coldest night of the autumn so far was on 16 November when the temperature got down to minus 7.7C (18F) at Tulloch Bridge, Highland.
Temperatures for many of us have been up and down recently due to cold Arctic air temporarily sweeping southward across the UK.
Southern areas of the UK have mostly held onto milder air from the Atlantic.
During Friday though a northerly wind will once again bring some of the colder air from the Arctic, and bring a colder day for most of the UK.
Any early cloud and rain in southern England will clear and for most of the UK it will be a bright day with some sunshine. A few wintry showers are possible across Scotland.
By night, temperatures will drop with frost expected widely, mostly across the Midlands, northern England, Northern Ireland and Scotland.
Although it is likely to be the coldest night of the autumn so far, with minus 10C predicted in rural Scotland, we are a long way off the coldest November night on record, when a temperature of minus 16.1C was recorded in Cumbria in 1912.
We came closer to that record low temperature in 2025, when the UK experienced the coldest November night in 12 years with minus 12.6C in Moray.
- How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips 
  - Published2 January
- How to look after dogs, cats and other pets in cold weather 
  - Published4 January
- Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed 
  - Published2 January
Frosty start to the weekend
After a cold start on Saturday morning, there will be a lot of dry and mostly sunny weather across the UK.
But milder air will start to move into the south-west of England again along with areas of cloud and rain by the end of the day.
Saturday night will not be as cold for most but frost is still likely to cover large areas of north-east England and much of Scotland with temperatures widely dropping to between zero and minus 5C.
Rain will continue on Sunday in south-west England, south Wales and even into parts of Northern Ireland.
Elsewhere should be mostly dry and while fairly cloudy, there should be some brighter interludes.
Maximum temperatures over the weekend will be on the colder side of average with 4 to 8C expected.
Is the polar vortex behind the cold weather?
The polar vortex is the strong wind that circles high above the Arctic.
Very unusually the winds of the polar vortex weakened last week - the earliest time this has happened on record.
In some situations, the weakening of the polar vortex can lead to colder weather and even snow some weeks later.
But it is too soon for this weakening of the polar vortex to be having an influence on our weather.
Instead this colder snap is just part of the variability of weather in the UK.
The polar vortex has started to strengthen again and should get back to its normal strength in the coming weeks.
Scientists are still unsure how or if the weakening last week will have any influence on our weather in weeks to come.
  - Published9 October
  - Published2 days ago
summary: Friday night is expected to be the coldest of the autumn so far with temperatures dropping as low as minus 10C, as Simon King explains.
title: UK braces for coldest night of autumn so far with temperature of -10C forecast

body:
Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.
Baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.
His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.
The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.
Expert neonatologist, associate professor Nicholas Evans, said on Friday Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.
It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.
Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks said it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.
Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.
“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”
Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.
Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but ultimately, Evans told the court, it was most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.
Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.
“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”
Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.
The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.
But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.
Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid August.
That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the issue.
“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.
Expert midwives earlier told the court they don’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks, because it’s so rare.
A 19 August ultrasound showed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.
Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times that she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.
The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.
Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.
The inquest is ongoing.
summary: Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard. Baby DH , Baby D , Baby R , and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. Continue reading...
title: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears

body:
Calls for consent law change after Joanne Young rape case
- Published
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change to the law on consent.
Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period, using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.
The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials of this nature.
Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse
Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers without her knowledge.
During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.
The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.
In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone.
"We live in a world where someone's partner can consent for them, and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.
"This is simply unacceptable."
Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial.
"No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.
"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."
The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".
"If someone is drugged asleep and unconscious they can't give consent," Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC.
"Someone can't give consent on your behalf.
"[Technology] is quickly evolving but we need to look at where improvements can be made in the legislation."
Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life.
"It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said.
"You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."
Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations.
"The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked.
"So why are they still accessible?" she said.
- If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, support and information is available at BBC Action Line.
Horvath said more needed to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators.
"The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said.
"We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments.
"[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."
Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told LBC that she did not believe it would be the last unless changes were made.
"The ability of these men to find each other on websites that you and I could just log on to now just means that these cases are going to keep on coming," she said.
"The state needs to make sure that its online safety laws and regulations are strong enough to stop this from ever being able to happen," she said.
"I think that every single one of the websites listed in this case should be called on today to answer the questions, can you guarantee this isn't happening today?"
Phillips said there was "absolutely" a case for making it an offence to advertise another person for sex online and that exploitation of adults occurs "all across the internet" with "very little regulation on the safety or the certainty of consent".
The Domestic Abuse Commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, has also called for the case to be a "turning point":
"Ultimately this case again highlights that we need to stop treating drug-facilitated sexual abuse as an isolated incident and recognise it for the form of horrific domestic abuse that it is," she said.
The men who committed crimes against Joanne Young are:
- Philip Young pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife
- Norman Macksoni, 48, from Bedfordshire, and Richard Wilkins, 62, from Swindon, were each found guilty of one count of rape. Wilkins was also found guilty of one count of assault by penetration
- Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, from Swindon, was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration
- Mohammed Hassan, 38, from Swindon, was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching
- A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February
