body:
Three Kyiv bridges hit during major Russian missile attack
- Published
Russia has targeted bridges in Kyiv and killed eight during one of the largest air attacks of the war so far, days after Ukraine inflicted heavy damage on the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Two people were killed in Russian strikes on a railway station in the western city of Lviv.
Ballistic missiles hit three bridges over the Dnipro River, vital routes which people in Kyiv rely on to move around the city, with six deaths confirmed in the capital.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for Ukraine's strike on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.
The three Kyiv bridges targeted overnight - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - have been closed to traffic, adding to disruption created by retaliatory strikes on bridges earlier this week.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary".
He added that an unspecified critical infrastructure facility was also damaged and seven medical personnel were injured during the night's assault.
Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.
Since illegally annexing the Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.
Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".
Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.
Ukraine's air force says almost 100 missiles were launched by Russia in its overnight attack - one of the largest attacks since the invasion began in 2022. It also involved around 400 drones.
The attack was "one of the most powerful" yet, according to Yuriy Ignat, head of communications for the Ukrainian air force.
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said 28 people were injured, with an ambulance hospital in Kharkiv among the targets of an attack which hit nine regions.
Two people were killed in a hit on the Sknyliv railway station in the south-west of Lviv, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.
He shared a picture of the ruined remains of what he said was the station's ticket terminal.
Ten people were injured and a rescue operation at the site is ongoing.
A Russian projectile reportedly landed inside Poland, with the armed forces searching a site 45km (28 miles) from its border with Ukraine.
Polish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued.
The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.
Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.
The US president dialled into the talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
summary: Five people were killed in a wave of strikes which follow Ukraine's successful targeting of the Crimean Bridge.
title: Three Kyiv bridges hit during major Russian missile attack

White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
- Published
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a string of tech outages which hit the National Security Agency (NSA), the US air traffic control system and some banks.
Sean Cairncross had been national cyber director since August 2025.
CBS, the BBC's US news partner, reported he had been fired, external after losing the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.
The AFP news agency and CBS both said sources had told them Cairncross was fired, in a move supported by President Donald Trump.
The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.
Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".
But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.
- Hacks, AI or just overdue updates - why have there been so many outages? 
  - Published1 day ago
Cairncross was previously a lawyer in the Republican Party, before becoming the chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee.
In the first Trump administration, he was part of the team of the White House chief of staff.
He later worked in the private sector, before returning to government in August 2025.
The White House has not publicly confirmed the departure or given a reason to why Cairncross left his role.

body:
Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of the lunch break
- Published
There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.
Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.
From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.
"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.
She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".
'Suss out the smelliness'
Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed".
He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk.
But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".
"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".
Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.
"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg."
She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."
Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".
"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.
"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."
Do you take a lunch break?
While what we eat in the office at lunch can cause tension, there's also the question of whether we're even taking the time to enjoy our lunch in the first place.
In a world of back-to-back meetings and overflowing inboxes, it's easy to skip our break and shovel down a sandwich with one hand while replying to emails with the other.
A 2025 report by Just Eat found that the youngest workers, Gen Z, were the most likely to take a full break, with 56% doing so.
However, the next generation up, millennials were more likely than any other to eat lunch at their desk.
"While it can be convenient to eat at your desk, it's not best practice to remain glued to the screen all day," says Alan Price, an employment law and HR expert, and CEO of BrightHR.
"Taking a break isn't just an employment right, there are proven benefits for both physical and mental health."
Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".
"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.
But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".
His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".
"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

summary: What is acceptable to eat at your desk, without annoying your colleagues?
title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of the lunch break

body:
Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
- Published
Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures.
Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.
Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.
The latest official sales figures, external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling.
"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.
"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."
The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the uptick came after a 0.6% decline in September.
As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.
The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers.
Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further".
Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises.
- Sales of tinned food and bottled water jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch 
  - Published10 November
- Why should I stockpile and what will I need? 
  - Published23 October
Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October.
Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said., external
Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn.
Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago.
These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate.
Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.
Get in touch
Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story?
summary: People stocking up on long-life food drove retail sales higher October, according to official data.
title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch

body:
Moore eyes Kane shirt as Spurs' past and future stars meet
- Published
Cologne loanee Mikey Moore says he hopes to exchange shirts with former Tottenham team-mate Harry Kane when they face Bayern Munich in the Bundesliga on Friday.
The 19-year-old England Under-21 international is on a season-long loan from Spurs, while Three Lions captain and Ballon d'Or winner Kane left north London to join Bundesliga giants Bayern in 2023.
"I haven't actually spoken to him. When he was leaving Tottenham I was just coming into the first team so we don't really know each other too well," said Moore.
"But we've got Bayern on Friday so I'm looking forward to hopefully getting a chat with him and maybe his top."
The 19:30 GMT kick-off will be shown live on BBC Sport and iPlayer.
Kane was still at Tottenham when Moore was first invited to train with the senior squad during the 2021-22 season.
"He's been a massive idol of mine since I was really young," Moore told the Euro Leagues podcast last month.
"When I first went up to train with the first team under Antonio Conte, Harry Kane was over there, and [I saw] some finishing that [I have] never seen anything like again.
"It will be a great experience to play against him and share a pitch with him."
The pair may not have crossed paths in Germany yet but Moore did bump into the England skipper while on international duty last month.
"I'll try my best to get my hands on that shirt," Moore added. "I saw him on the last international break, actually, and went and said hello.
"Hopefully, I'll be coming back to Koln with that in my hand."
'I wanted to take myself a little bit out of my comfort zone'
Moore says the success of Jadon Sancho and Jude Bellingham in the Bundesliga influenced his decision to join Cologne on loan.
Moore's move came almost a decade after a 17-year-old Sancho left Manchester City to join Borussia Dortmund.
During his time in Germany, Sancho established himself as one of Europe's most exciting wingers, making more than 150 appearances for Dortmund and helping the club win the DFB-Pokal in 2021. He subsequently secured a £73m move to Manchester United.
Bellingham followed a similar path in 2020, leaving boyhood club Birmingham City to join Dortmund. The midfielder quickly developed into one of the most sought-after players in world football before joining Real Madrid for an initial £88.5m in 2023.
"Over the years you've seen so many young players come out here, and there are good examples of world-class players like Jude Bellingham and Jadon Sancho doing really well," Moore said.
"It's a really attractive place to play football, especially for a young attacker. It's a great platform to play, and that was sold to me by the people at the club and the manager.
"They've put real trust in me, and the amount of game time I've played so quickly in my Koln [Cologne] career has been nice. It's been good to have that trust from all the staff and people at the club.
"I'm already happy with my decision. Now I can really kick on, make my own story and build my own path in German football."
Although Moore only turned 19 in August, he is no stranger to stepping outside his comfort zone.
Last season, he made 47 appearances in all competitions, including the Champions League qualifying rounds, during a loan spell at Scottish Premiership side Rangers.
It was the first time Moore had left his boyhood club Tottenham, and he rose to the challenge, scoring six goals and providing two assists in 28 Scottish Premiership appearances.
The experience offered a different test to the one he now faces in Germany, but it provided valuable exposure to the demands of first-team football.
"I had options to stay in England and maybe stay somewhere a little more comfortable," Moore said.
"But the conversations came down to me picking a team, and I wanted to take myself a little bit out of my comfort zone to test myself in one of the top five leagues.
"When we were speaking, everyone said they thought it would be a really good experience for me to experience this type of football.
"It's really intense, and there are some great teams in the league.
"For me, it was a no-brainer. I made the decision early that I wanted to come out here, and now I just need to push on."
Having now found an apartment close to fellow England youth internationals Reigan Heskey and Jahmai Simpson-Pusey, who also joined the club this summer, the teenager has turned his attention to learning German.
Moore had his first lesson last month and, at his mother's request, is hoping to expand his vocabulary in the language over the coming weeks.
"I wasn't the brightest at school, so I might take a while to learn the language," Moore joked.
"At least I'll be able to learn a few words so I can order my food in German."

summary: Cologne loanee Mikey Moore says he hopes to exchange shirts with former Spurs team-mate Harry Kane when they face Bayern Munich on Friday.
title: Moore eyes Kane shirt as Spurs' past and future stars meet

body:
Rams star Nacua suspended for personal conduct violation
- Published
Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua has been given a three-game suspension by the NFL for violating the league's personal conduct policy.
In March, the 25-year-old was sued for assault and battery by a woman who says he made an antisemitic statement and bit her on the shoulder on New Year's Eve.
Nacua's attorney has denied any statement was made and described the bite as "horseplay".
That incident came two weeks after Nacua performed an antisemitic gesture during a livestream appearance, for which he later apologised.
The NFL has now concluded its investigation and has suspended Nacua while he is already out with knee and toe injuries.
He was placed on injured reserve (IR) last week, meaning he will miss a minimum of four games. He has been suspended without pay so will forfeit $950,000 (£725,000).
According to ESPN, the NFL told Nacua that "any further violation of the personal conduct policy... will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the league."
Shortly before Nacua was sued in March he entered a holistic care facility, external to "improve his overall behavior in every aspect of his life" and completed a rehab programme before attending the start of the Rams' off-season programme in April.
Nacua has been one of the NFL's best wide receivers since being a fifth-round draft pick in 2023. He is in the final year of his rookie contract so is set to receive a lucrative new deal after this season.
Meanwhile, Marlon Humphrey will not play for the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday after being sent home from the team's practice facility for a derogatory comment about the city.
The 30-year-old cornerback said on his podcast that Baltimore was "best at making criminals" and while the mayor Brandon Scott has acknowledged Humphrey's subsequent apology he invited him to "sit down with me, external and some Baltimoreans".

summary: Puka Nacua is given a three-game suspension for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy, although the Los Angeles Rams wide receiver was already out injured.
title: Rams star Nacua suspended for personal conduct violation

body:
How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
Trump's crypto profits raise alarms for transparency advocates
For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.
So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.
"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."
This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.
After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.
From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.
Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.
Trump's meme coin
Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.
Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.
In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.
A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.
Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.
For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.
Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.
A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.
"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
A crypto deal with a U.A.E. firm
But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.
Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024.
The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.
Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.
The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.
Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power.
Democrats have seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures.
"I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," Trump told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat.
But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion.
World Liberty Financial declined to comment.
Another major deal for Trump's crypto venture
Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits.
Using $2 billion of World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year.
The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market.
Months later, Changpeng Zhao — the convicted founder of Binance who no longer runs the crypto exchange — was pardoned by President Trump. CZ, as he's widely known, still has the biggest stake in Binance and weighs in publicly, including when the exchange got hacked earlier this month.
Meanwhile, the relationship between Binance and World Liberty deepened. Binance actively promoted World Liberty Financial's stablecoin to its customers, further elevating the market valuation of the cryptocurrency to $5 billion, according to The New York Times.
While the relationship has come under scrutiny, Binance has strongly defended the acceptance of World Liberty's cryptocurrency as having been done on its own merits.
"Any suggestion that Binance did anything to support World Liberty Financial or USD1 to gain political favour or influence a legal outcome is false," a spokesperson told NPR in an email, referring to World Liberty's stablecoin. A representative for CZ declined to comment.
But transparency advocates are suspicious — and so are top Democrats. In a widely quoted social message, Rep. Robert Garcia posted a social media message for the Trump family and his administration: "Lawyer up."
summary: President Trump has made billions of dollars in his second term — most of it in cryptocurrencies. Democrats are vowing to probe his businesses as they gear up to take over Congress next year.
title: How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain

New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island
New York City officials on Friday unveiled their plan to close the troubled jail complex on Rikers Island, the city's main pre-trial detention center, which has been plagued with reports of abuse and neglect for decades.
"It is long past time to close what's been a moral stain on our city," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NPR. "We cannot simply accept the old approaches to public safety just because they've always been done that way."
Rikers, which sits on a former garbage dump in the East River, has long been infamous for its dismal conditions – including crumbling infrastructure. Inmates have accused guards of excessive force, sexual assault and high rates of violence in multiple lawsuits.
Last year, a federal judge called the amount of violence at Rikers an "unconstitutional danger" for both the people held there and the staff.
Since 2022, more than 50 people have died in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction. Almost all had been held at Rikers. People have been found unresponsive. They have died by suicide and been beaten to death. Federal court records say Rikers is "significantly more violent" than comparable jails.
But now, city officials say they finally have momentum to close the jail for good, and the newly released plan details how they intend to do that.
The plan — which takes on both the conditions inside the jails and the size of the population behind bars — is ambitious. It seeks to transform how the city government thinks about crime prevention and safety overall, says Insha Rahman, president of the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit.
"If New York City can do this at scale, which it will, it is encouragement for places like LA, like Chicago, like Philadelphia, like Houston to do the same," Rahman says.
A goal set by the city years ago
In 2019, the New York City Council approved a plan to close Rikers by 2027, and to build in its place four smaller jails in Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and the Bronx.
Rikers is on an island between Queens and the Bronx, out of sight for many New Yorkers. The borough-based jails will be closer to the courts and to public transit, making it easier for families, lawyers and service providers to visit people inside the facilities.
Since 2019, not a lot of progress has been made toward closing Rikers. City officials acknowledge they won't make the 2027 deadline. But Mamdani says the city is in a new moment.
"We're not the first administration to talk about this. We also know that the last administration had no interest in advancing this," Mamdani told NPR. "And we are also confident that we can be the first administration to deliver on it."
Earlier this year, he appointed a "Close Rikers Czar" dedicated to closing the jail and reducing the jail population. The mayor also appointed Stanley Richards as commissioner of the DOC, the first formerly incarcerated person to lead the department.
Mamdani says his administration has already taken concrete steps: The city revived plans for a housing initiative for New Yorkers released from jail with medical needs, for instance, and it opened a therapeutic housing unit at a public hospital in Manhattan.
'Human dignity at the center of incarceration'
Last year, a federal judge stripped the city of its authority over Rikers. Operations are now controlled by a remediation manager, who released his own initial plan earlier this year for bringing the jail system into legal compliance, independent of the city's plan.
Aspects of that plan took inspiration from carceral systems in Europe, a growing trend among correctional leaders across the U.S. The remediation manager, Nicholas Deml, traveled with Commissioner Richards to Germany earlier this year on a trip organized by the Vera Institute. There, they observed the country's prisons and jails, which are often regarded as an international model.
"While German correctional systems are not directly transferable to New York, they reflect a fundamentally different orientation — one that places human dignity at the center of incarceration," Deml wrote in his plan.
Last month, the Vera Institute took a second group of New Yorkers to Germany to see how jails can look when they're done right, including the Moabit jail in Berlin. Each member of that group had a part to play in reimagining New York City's criminal justice system: a prosecutor, a judge, a city councilmember, the chief who supervises officers at Rikers, among others.
At first glance, the group observed, Moabit looked like a lot of jails in the U.S., but key differences emerged on closer inspection. The jail was quiet. The cells had windows to the outside. In some of them, a door inside connected it to the adjacent cell.
"Some people are afraid of the first night here, and sometimes it really helps just to open the door to have someone to talk to," Katharina Spanaus, a staff member at Moabit, told the group.
There were also televisions in the cells to calm people down, and in the hallway, a vending machine selling cigarettes.
"I'll never forget the cigarette vending machine," says Christopher Watler, who was recently appointed chair of the New York City Board of Correction, which oversees the city's jail system.
What struck him wasn't really the cigarettes, but what the gesture communicates about treating people as human, Watler says.
It also showed him how far New York City has to go.
Just a week earlier, he sat at his first board meeting in New York, where he heard stories that evoked a different image. At the start, the board listened to anonymous phone calls from people held at Rikers.
The callers voiced concerns: A woman reported black mold. A man said he was denied his medications. Another pleaded for a less violent environment.
"New York City's a great city. Our jail system isn't great," Watler says. "It's a broken thing. But how do you repair broken things?"
'The sum of all the efforts will help'
The four new jails won't be fully completed for another six years. Each facility will have more access to natural light and fresh air, and more space for recreation, vocational training and education.
Together, the new jails will hold about 2,000 fewer people than the approximately 6,600 people Rikers holds now.
The city's plan invests more than $250 million across the next several years in efforts to reduce the number of people in jail, for instance, by expanding alternatives to incarceration like diversion programs and electronic monitoring.
It also aims to keep people from committing crimes, by expanding services like supportive housing and mental health treatment.
Another way to lower a jail's population is to shorten how long people stay there. The average length of stay of people in New York City DOC custody was nearly twice as long in 2025 as it was in 2015, according to the policy journal Vital City.
The vast majority of people at Rikers are awaiting trial, and many of their cases take longer to process than national standards dictate. Nearly a quarter have been in jail for more than a year.
Judge Joseph Zayas, chief administrative judge of the New York State Unified Court System, told NPR there are many factors that can lengthen a jail stay, including processing evidence during discovery and administering mental health assessments, for instance.
"The only way to solve this backlog problem is to hit each of these things. The sum of all of the efforts will help," Zayas says.
The city is planning a task force dedicated to speeding up court cases, but the forces affecting that are outside city hall's control. Judges act independently from the mayor, as do district attorneys. City officials say they are investing in those relationships.
'If you are wrong, then you have crowded jails'
Some people, including those with deep knowledge of Rikers, are concerned with what happens if the city doesn't lower the jail population enough.
Vincent Schiraldi, who was DOC commissioner under Mayor Bill de Blasio, says he can understand that.
"It's really hard to have the guts to forecast lower incarceration numbers. Because if you are wrong, then you have crowded jails and you're in trouble," says Schiraldi, who now runs a philanthropic fund to close Rikers.
Other cities have dramatically reduced their jail populations. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, New Orleans reduced its jail population by more than two thirds in the decade after.
Schiraldi pointed out that aside from an increase during the pandemic, crime rates have trended downward for decades.
If crime increases again, Schiraldi says, "Then we deal with it. What is the scenario by which the government spends billions of dollars just in case?"
But Elizabeth Glazer, who led the Office of Criminal Justice under de Blasio, told NPR she hopes the mayor will be pragmatic when it comes to having contingency plans – including the possibility of building again on Rikers Island.
She says it is possible to shrink the jail population, but it's not going to be easy.
"It requires relentless attention, coordination and organization around a common goal to get it done," says Glazer, who is also the founder of Vital City. "Even if you hit that number, the question is, can that be sustained for the decades when all you have is that capacity?"
Still, for some people the city's plan is a crucial opportunity, after years of inaction have left thousands of people held at the jail under inhumane conditions.
"We wait for these perfect plans, and for all the reasons we know, including funding, those perfect plans never come to pass. And so what do we do? We do nothing," says Tina Luongo, who leads the criminal defense practice at the Legal Aid Society, which brought the class action lawsuit that resulted in the remediation manager's appointment.
Changing the culture at Rikers
Officials caution the new jails alone won't solve the systemic problems at Rikers.
Over the last decade, the federal government has documented a "culture of violence" among the guards. In 2023, more than 700 women sued the city alleging they'd been raped or sexually abused by staff at Rikers, according to a Gothamist investigation.
"People talk about culture change and that's really just a euphemism for the extraordinary brutality and violence that has plagued Rikers," Glazer says. "If you're going to move the very same system into the new buildings, you're going to move the problem of violence as well."
In their report, city officials outline plans for more training and mentoring for staff, tighter oversight, and more programming for people in jail.
Commissioner Richards told NPR he wants to see the jail's culture transform and become more like what he saw in Germany, where human dignity is non-negotiable for everyone. That includes staff, who Richards says have been demonized.
"Part of the work that I'm doing is showing value and appreciation to our staff. So they begin to expand their capacity to show that same value and humanity to the people who come to us," Richards says.
But he didn't offer specifics on what exactly will change. That may be in part because he has a more immediate focus: safety and security.
The plan set forth by Deml, the remediation manager, starts with the most basic correctional functions, including protocols for securing doors. Richards, who was incarcerated at Rikers himself 40 years ago, says they need to start somewhere.
"Everybody wants something to happen by tomorrow. And we are in a moment of urgency. But it takes time to turn," he says.
The larger goal remains the same: for the failures of Rikers to not be carried into the next generation of New York City jails.
summary: New York City officials are moving forward with plans to close Rikers, the city's main jail complex, after years of discussion. The jail has been plagued by assaults and inmate deaths.
title: New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island

The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties
BRUSSELS — A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences, and just perhaps, to pave the way for them to get back together.
Burnham is scheduled to hold just under an hour of talks in Brussels with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Then they'll all meet in a plenary session with U.K. government ministers and European commissioners.
Burnham has described the rare EU-U.K. summit — only the second since Britain became the first country to leave the world's biggest trading bloc — as a step toward undoing a decade of damage caused by the divorce.
"The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained," he said this week.
Burnham has said all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc. But he's stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent. It would need the backing not just of British voters, but the unanimous support of a mistrustful EU. Still, he has broken a long political code of silence on the option of rejoining.
Ahead of the meeting, von der Leyen said she wanted it to be "a summit of ambition and concrete results. More opportunities for young people. Easier agrifood trade. And a stronger cooperation on economic security."
Burnham pitched the package of agreements expected to be signed Friday as a way of "cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people."
He said "a closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe."
The deals are set to include an agreement for up to 100,000 young adults from Britain to live and work in EU countries for up to three years, and the same number of Europeans to come to the U.K.
There will also be an emissions trading agreement and a deal to remove checks on food and agricultural products that will make things cheaper and easier for British exporters to Europe. Burnham says the deals could add a modest 0.4% to Britain's economy.
To get the deals, the U.K. must accept some EU rules and standards that it has no role in setting. Supporters of Brexit say that undermines Britain's independence.
"I'm afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again," Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told the BBC. He said "it's perfectly clear that this very, very soon becomes a debate about: do we rejoin or do we stay out?"
The war in Ukraine, and the U.K.'s military strength, are drawing the two back together, and the summit provides the EU with an opportunity to discuss stronger cooperation on security and defense, as well as efforts to restrict irregular migration.
"Our security and prosperity are closely intertwined, making a strong partnership between us essential," Costa said ahead of the meeting. "By deepening our cooperation, we can strengthen our ability to address the challenges of our time, strengthen our resilience and promote stability in Europe and beyond."
Nevertheless, feelings remain raw, and EU officials have been reluctant to encourage talk of the U.K. rejoining. They are weary from the shifting demands of seven British prime ministers over the last decade and want real clarity about the country's intentions.
Ireland's ambassador in London, Sonja Hyland, said that when Britain voted for Brexit, "there was a lack of clarity as to exactly what that meant." If Britain wants to reopen negotiations, she said, it must "make a clear decision as to what it wants."
summary: A decade after the people of Britain voted to leave the European Union, top EU officials are meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday, looking to mend more fences.
title: The U.K. and EU hold a rare summit to strengthen ties

Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an 'antique' network
Rossana D'Antonio was at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, just about to board a plane back to Los Angeles, when the Federal Aviation Administration declared a nationwide ground stop.
D'Antonio's flight was canceled last Friday, along with thousands of others. She was lucky, and got a seat on a flight Saturday morning.
"By then, of course, the hotels were all booked. And so I spent the night at JFK," she said with a rueful laugh.
D'Antonio is not just a frequent flier. She also is the president-elect of the American Society of Civil Engineers. So her mind went right to infrastructure.
"The very first thing I thought of was, 'We told you so,'" D'Antonio told NPR. "We are reliant on a system that was considered to be state of the art back in the 1980s. This is common knowledge. We've known about it, and we simply haven't acted swiftly enough."
Last week's nationwide ground stop was an unwelcome reminder that the U.S.' air traffic control system runs on antiquated technology.
"We have a patchwork, archaic federal telephone network," the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, Bryan Bedford, said Thursday at Honeywell Aerospace's American Aviation Leadership Summit in Washington. "Which is why we gotta get off [of] it as fast as humanly possible, while maintaining safety."
The FAA is still unsure exactly what caused the telecommunications meltdown that led to the nationwide ground stop, just the second since 9/11. But the agency says it started with work to install a router at a remote facility in Arkansas -- part of an ongoing effort to replace outdated copper wiring with modern fiber-optic cables.
No one disputes that the old equipment is a problem, or that updates now underway should have happened a long time ago. So why is the world's busiest and most complex airspace still running on network technology from the 1980s?
Former FAA and DOT officials say the answer starts with decades of underfunding.
"At its core, it's a money problem," Michael Huerta, a former FAA administrator during the Obama administration, said in an interview last year. "The FAA has been asked to do more with less."
The agency has tried to invest in new technology. But at the same time, Huerta said, the older systems must stay running to keep planes in the air 365 days a year, 24 hours a day.
The older networks are fragile, and expensive to maintain because they're obsolete, former FAA officials say. And it's challenging to connect them with modern equipment designed to run on fiber-optic networks.
"This should have been taken on earlier," said William Voss, a former FAA executive involved in previous modernization efforts back in the 1990s. "It's effectively been eating all the money up trying to run this antique store in the biggest air traffic system in the world."
The FAA got an influx of money last year when Congress allocated $12.5 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. But Voss warned the task is complicated and daunting.
"There's not a lot of people that have done that in one big leap," he said.
Voss worries the Trump administration is moving too quickly, without allowing enough time for planning and coordination. And he wonders why the failed network upgrade that crippled the nation's airspace was scheduled during a busy Friday afternoon.
"I can't imagine why you do that unless you are just under tremendous schedule pressure," Voss said.
The timing also seems questionable to Dave Spero. He's the national president of Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, the union that represents technicians at the FAA.
"No, I wouldn't do that on a Friday afternoon," he said. "To be safe, I would probably want to schedule it on a midnight shift."
The Government Accountability Office also raised concerns about the speed of modernization work. In a report published in September, the GAO said the administration has been accelerating the timeline of modernization work already underway -- including the telecommunications network that failed on Friday.
"They are basically buying speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and the potential for disruptions in the national airspace," said Kevin Walsh, the director of the GAO's Information Technology and Cybersecurity team, who was the lead on the report.
The GAO report also noted the first phase of the FAA's modernization effort includes more than 11,000 distinct projects with no integrated master plan.
"While that may work, it increases the risk of outages, especially when dealing with these older systems, which are prone to failure," Walsh said.
But the Trump administration defends its approach.
"Some of you will say I'm moving too fast. Some of you say, I'm moving too slow. Um, maybe I'm Goldilocks and I'm going just right here," said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy after meeting Republican Senators at the Capitol on Tuesday. "But I'll just tell you, the longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes."
There's another reason, experts say, the Trump administration might want to move quickly.
After decades of air traffic control modernization attempts that took longer and delivered less than promised, the FAA wants to show Congress that it's serious this time, said Eric Soskin, a former inspector general at the Department of Transportation.
"That's a powerful signal to say, hey, we're going to get it done. We are going to carry out this important effort," Soskin said.
The FAA still has a lot of modernization work left to do, with the potential for more disruptions ahead, other former agency leaders warned.
"I don't expect another major US shutdown. The FAA is going to avoid that at all costs," said Michael O'Donnell, a former senior executive at the agency.
"We'll get some disruptions, but I don't think it'll be anything like we saw on Friday night … I'd be really shocked and surprised, and a little worried, if that happened again."
summary: The FAA says the telecom outage that led to Friday's nationwide ground stop began with an upgrade to fiber-optic cables. Industry experts say the work is long overdue.
title: Why the U.S. air traffic control system still relies on an 'antique' network

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.
Anthropic’s shares jumped 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.
Anthropic’s floation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
summary: Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down Business live – latest updates Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies. Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%. Continue reading...
title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.
Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.
Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.
Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.
“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.
summary: State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang. Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions. Continue reading...
title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China

Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.
NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.
summary: Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said. NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia. Three sectoral deals to be signed, but won't enter into force until tuition fees issue resolved
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset deals will not materialise unless the UK reaches a settlement with the EU over tuition fee rates for European students.
EU sources said on Friday that the three deals – on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility – will not enter into force without equal treatment for European students at British universities.
In a statement seen by the Guardian from the EU council and European Commission spelt it out:
“The Council and Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students. The Council and Commission acknowledge that these four agreements form a package of the 2026 EU-UK summit.”
The EU wants to ensure its students pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees, rather than the far higher international rate. In a concession last night, the bloc agreed to defer agreement on tuition fees by six months, but that does not mean they have accepted the UK’s position that their students pay higher rates
As the Guardian has reported, it intends to use its leverage, by making the three deals contingent on an acceptable agreement on tuition fees.
An EU official said:
“I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed.”
Tuition fees hold up mostly political, - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
Just to highlight Jennifer’s point there (10:40): the “hold-up” over tuition fees is nowhere near as catastrophic or dramatic as some headlines elsewhere would have you think – and, in fact, was pretty anticipated.
The three sectoral deals are still getting signed today and it counts as a genuine step forward in the post-Brexit relationship; it’s just that their full implementation get suspended until the tuition fee issue is resolved.
The explicit link on their implementation does create a new high-pressure political deadline in six months’ time, adding urgency for the two sides to resolve the tuition fees issue and unblock the whole process.
Ah, classic EU-UK negotiations stuff.
Just like the good old days (gets Brexit flashbacks).
'Heavily choreographed' welcome ceremony with several ministers in attendance
Peter Walker
Senior political correspondent
in Brussels
The arrival of Burnham and his European hosts was heavily choreographed – there were no words to the assembled media, or any shouted questions – but one notable element was the sheer number of ministers the UK PM has brought with him, in a sign of how seriously the summit is being treated by London.
These included Lou Haigh, the first secretary of state; John Healey, the chancellor; Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary; Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary; Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.
Three sectoral deals to be signed, but won't enter into force until tuition fees issue resolved
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset deals will not materialise unless the UK reaches a settlement with the EU over tuition fee rates for European students.
EU sources said on Friday that the three deals – on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility – will not enter into force without equal treatment for European students at British universities.
In a statement seen by the Guardian from the EU council and European Commission spelt it out:
“The Council and Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students. The Council and Commission acknowledge that these four agreements form a package of the 2026 EU-UK summit.”
The EU wants to ensure its students pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees, rather than the far higher international rate. In a concession last night, the bloc agreed to defer agreement on tuition fees by six months, but that does not mean they have accepted the UK’s position that their students pay higher rates
As the Guardian has reported, it intends to use its leverage, by making the three deals contingent on an acceptable agreement on tuition fees.
An EU official said:
“I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed.”
The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and the European Council president António Costa are now in position and waiting for UK’s Andy Burnham.
Tuition fees deferral seeks to neutralise London's leverage in talks - snap analysis
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.
Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.
But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.
This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.
It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.
New EU-UK deals to provide 0.5% boost to UK's GDP, Burnham says
During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP.
He has previously said it could provide a 0.4% boost.
He said:
“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”
He told business leaders:
“Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single biggest growth intervention in this Parliament.”
Deals on food and drink, emissions trading, youth mobility agreed, but tricky question of tuition fees 'kicked down the road'
Peter Walker and Jennifer Rankin
With Andy Burnham arriving soon at the UK-EU summit the position is – well, much as it was last night, with a broad agreement but the most tricky issue kicked down the road for six months.
The official mood music from EU officials on Friday morning was positive, with talk of “concrete deliverables” for citizens on both sides in the three key areas: a deal on food and drink imports and exports; emissions trading; and the planned mutual “youth experience” exchange scheme.
One official said:
“We expect the leaders to confirm and unlock the conclusion of three important negotiations that have been ongoing.”
There is, however, one snag remaining: no agreement on whether EU students coming to the UK to study should pay lower tuition fees than currently, and ideally for Brussels, the domestic rate. This aspect is subject to six more months of negotiations, and none of the other deals will be completed until this is also done.
While EU officials are not explicit about this, the assumption is that they are seeking UK tuition fee levels. This would, for Burnham and his ministers, be a tricky sell, especially to the university sector, who currently get fees several times higher than the UK rate for EU students.
For now, there is something of an impasse.
“I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed,” one EU official said.
'It just makes sense to get closer,' Burnham tells business leaders
We are getting some lines from that meeting with business leaders in Brussels.
“It just makes sense to get closer,” PM Burnham told the meeting, hailing today’s summit as “a big day and, hopefully, a positive day.”
“My aim as prime minister has been to put the country on a better path, more hopeful about the future, more sense of possibility and positivity around the country,” as he wanted to break with “a decade of low, stagnang growth … [and] rising costs.”
He said that “the vast majority of the public” appeared to back a closer, more practical working relationship with the EU.
“So what we’re doing today is completely in step with where people are,” he stressed.
“We want that for the benefit of business and … consumers,” chancellor John Healey told the meeting, stressing that the changes will mean that “you as leading European-wide businesses can trade more easily.”
“Today’s deal reduces the red tape that gets in your way; it should produce savings,” he said, “and help boost growth.”
“In a world of greater threats, greater uncertainties, greater global economic shocks, this makes us more resilient,” Healey said.
Press Association says that executives from energy firms Iberdrola and Octopus and the National Grid were among the attendees, along with Burnham’s de facto deputy Louise Haigh.
UK and EU plan first talks on sending refused asylum seekers to third countries
Rajeev SyalandLisa O’Carroll
The UK and the EU plan to establish formal talks for the first time about sending rejected asylum seekers to third-country hubs, according to a leaked document.
A draft of a joint statement expected to be signed by Andy Burnham and Ursula von der Leyen at a summit on Friday morning states that both sides will establish “a structured dialogue” to discuss “returns to third countries”.
Until now, the Home Office has been seeking bilateral agreements with third countries allowing the removal of migrants, but with no obvious success.
Last week, five EU countries – Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands – announced an agreement in principle with Rwanda to establish a migrant “return hub” there in 2027.
Burnham hinted at possible cooperation with EU countries last week when he told reporters that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that [the five-country deal] with interest, learning from what went on in the past”. He said: “The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The UK has been fighting for deeper cooperation with the EU on migration, with the new deal on a “strategic dialogue” secured in the last two weeks by negotiators in Brussels.
It is a key part of the UK-EU reset pact, which also covers a youth mobility scheme, tariffs on Chinese imports, food and drink exports to the EU and a wider restatement of commitment on defence and security.
Informed sources confirmed this was the first time the UK and the EU had agreed to “open a dialogue on returns” after the launch of the bloc’s Channel action plan in June this year.
Whitehall sources said the UK was now open to the possibility of sending rejected claimants to Rwanda – a recent pivot from the position under Keir Starmer’s government, which rejected the move.
According to a draft of the joint agreement, negotiations over third-country hubs will be part of increased cooperation to tackle irregular migration.
Row over voting rights dispels myths that UK comes to negotiations from position of strength - snap analysis
Lisa O’Carroll
Senior correspondent
France’s insistence that the UK could not have voting rights at any stage during the shaping of legislation on food standards and public health risks relating to food and agri products is a line in the sand for Andy Burnham.
The last night tensions at the ambassadors meeting will be a sharp lesson for anyone in the UK who clings to the idea that negotiating with the EU comes from a position of strength: the UK is not a member of the EU and despite the warm feelings to the Labour government in European capitals, benefits of the club are not extended to non members.
It also underlines the feeling expressed by several large member states this week that the way forward after this summit is not more iterative reset summits or mini-deals.
Yes, there will be negotiations on allowing the UK into the energy single market as this is in the joint interests of both sides in the wake of the Ukraine war. But no talks on pharma or chemicals, according to some capitals.
As one diplomat said:
“It puts down a marker warning the UK that cherry picking bits of the single market mean you are a rule taker.”
“It makes the choice for Britain starker and more binary” and shows that “the alternatives are basically muddling along with a version of the status quo or rejoining,” they said.
UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be welcomed with a rendition of God Save the King and the Ode to Joy when he attends the opening ceremony around 10.30am local time.
Talks to seal today’s reset in relations between the UK and the EU went write down to the wire this morning.
In what is known as a “silence procedure”, the EU issued a late night compromise text to all member states after a meeting of crunch hours long meeting of ambassadors in Brussels last night.
Under the procedure if no member states breaks the silence the text is considered “adopted” and would then be made available for signing by the UK – bar any last minute hitches on its side.
This morning diplomats said “no one had broken the silence”.
The headline agreements are:
Food and drink deal, setting up sanitary and phyto sanitary common area
An electricity carbon emissions deal
Cap of 100,000 EU citizens under 31 years old to come to the UK under a new youth mobility scheme
The issue of tuition fees kicked down the road - a supplementary agreement has been reached to sort this out within the next six months
This allows the UK to hold up the youth deal if the EU does not give it what it needs in the Made in Europe legislation which is expected to reach its final negotiations stages by Easter too.
No voting rights for the UK when the EU comes to writing new laws about food standards; this was never a realistic option as the UK is not a member of the EU, but the French led the resistance as the UK pushed for it equally as hard, instead the UK will be consullted at key stages
Industry groups say that must mean UK regulators are in the room at the early stages. Food regulation is very technical, the say and this is where the real decisions are taken.
The two sides will also open talks on UK entering the energy single market.
Morning opening: Second post-Brexit EU-UK summit gets under way in Brussels
Jakub Krupa
The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.
It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.
As our Brussels correspondent, Jennifer Rankin, explained:
“The two sides hope to announce three deals, which were initiated under Starmer’s government.
First, a food and drink agreement that will remove a lot of Brexit red tape on animal and plant products, making it easier to trade meats, cheese, wine and flowers. To secure the deal, which is not expected to take effect until 2028, the UK will align with EU standards, meaning the government, for example, must abandon a planned ban on foie gras imports.
A second agreement will link the British emissions trading system with its bigger EU cousin, restoring a link severed by Brexit. It is a significant step for industry because EU and UK businesses will be exempt from each other’s charges on high-carbon imports such as steel, cement and electricity. This agreement also requires alignment with relevant EU rules.
The third deal has proved the most contentious: a youth mobility scheme that will give those aged 18-31 the right to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years. The scheme may not be up and running until 2030 – which is bad news for anyone in their late 20s.”
The leaders are expected to arrive 9.30am GMT (10.30am Brussels time), with “the leaders’ meeting” between Burnham, von der Leyen and Costa to follow.
A plenary session with UK ministers and EU commissioners is expected at 10.45am GMT (11.45am Brussels), and if all goes well we should then see the leaders tell us what they agreed around half past midday (1.30pm Brussels time).
I will bring you every single detail of the day here today. You won’t miss a thing.
It’s Friday, 20 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
