Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spends discussing Brexit and Europe, the Guardian has been told, moving the Conservatives away from an issue that defined the party for many years.
While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject.
Instead, Badenoch intends to focus on areas the party believes are more fertile electoral ground, in particular the economy, the cost of social security and defence.
One source said Badenoch had been advised to shift the narrative away from Brexit by Stephen Gilbert, a former Conservative official who is now a peer and who joined the Tory leader’s team as a senior political adviser a year ago.
Although another party source said Gilbert’s advice was “more nuanced” than this, Badenoch’s recent run of speeches and interventions appears to demonstrate the change.
In eight sets of prime minister’s questions since Burnham entered No 10 over the summer, Badenoch and her deputy, Alex Burghart, who took one session when Burnham was away, have focused on Europe just once, on 28 October, when she challenged the PM on whether or not he wanted a new Brexit referendum.
Every other outing has focused on various aspects of the welfare state, the cost of living, or defence, also including subjects such as the budget, debt and whether or not the UK should drill for more North Sea oil and gas.
“The way I see it, this is less of a conscious attempt to sideline Europe than it is a way to talk more about the subjects we think are our strong points, like the economy and defence,” one senior Conservative said.
One Tory shadow minister said the wider party was firmly behind the idea: “Europe does still come up from time to time, but as a former remainer even I think we should move on. I’m not sure what is likely to change by us talking about it all the time.”
Another shadow minister said: “We don’t want to be talking about Brexit for multiple reasons – including the simple one that it was so awfully divisive.”
Badenoch does still at times defend Brexit to selected audiences, for example in Thursday’s Daily Mail piece, where she disputed Burnham’s charge that it had hampered the UK’s economic growth, saying the prime minister “wants to reopen arguments from 2016 because he has no answers for the world as it is”.
At other times her language on links with the EU has been more nuanced than the period when the Conservatives liked to disparage the continent as economically moribund and less relevant than more distant economies.
Asked about Burnham’s attempt to renegotiate the post-Brexit trade agreement during a press conference on defence earlier this month, Badenoch said: “They say they want to end red tape on food checks – that’s a good thing”, while then predicting this would not actually happen.
Badenoch also said she accepted that the deal with the EU could and should be updated: “The free trade agreement that we have with the EU, like many others, is one that needs constant negotiating. So I want to see Labour negotiating and improving on deals with all countries. That’s what you do when you have your own trade policy.”
A Conservative spokesperson said: “As Kemi has said, the last thing the country needs is to be dragged back into a debate on Brexit. That absolutely does not mean Kemi and the Conservatives won’t discuss the EU, but we will be very clear that Andy Burnham is only trying to reopen old wounds on Brexit because he doesn’t have anything to say about the challenges facing the country.
“Bringing down the welfare bill, funding defence, cutting taxes to promote growth can all be done outside the EU. Burnham’s reset is one big distraction and we will never shy away from saying so.”

While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject. body:
The British Library has sparked outrage over plans to outsource its security workforce and hand over to a private company three of its public reading rooms, to be “repurposed” as business spaces for hire – despite having reportedly received millions of pounds from the public purse to refurbish those spaces.
Almost 70 guards have been told that their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor, STM, on 1 December. Their union, the PCS, has in turn been informed that STM has rejected union recognition for those staff.
The union is balloting for strike action over what it describes as management’s “appalling approach to industrial relations”.
Nick Marro, the PCS culture group secretary, said serious questions around public money had been sparked because the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport was understood to be investing up to £14m in renovating the British Library’s reading rooms,“which the British Library is then going to immediately privatise”.
Marro said: “That’s absolutely ridiculous. We believe this raises important questions about the future of publicly funded cultural institutions, the treatment of workers and the government’s own commitments on insourcing and trade union rights.”
The library is proposing to close three of its 11 reading rooms – the science and social science spaces – turning them into a privately operated “flexible business workspace”. Sources believe this will involve the loss of 340 reader desks.
As one of the world’s most important research libraries, the British Library holds more than 150m items, including a copy of Magna Carta. Security staff affected by the latest plans include guards, supervisors and managers. Some patrol the reading rooms; others monitor CCTV.
Fran Heathcote, the PCS general secretary, has written to Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, calling for her “swift intervention”, saying that outsourcing is “in defiance of government policy”.
The letter, seen by the Guardian, reads: “What on earth is a government department doing investing in a resource only to privatise it, and outsourcing workers and stripping them of union recognition?”
She pointed out that at the Labour party conference, Louise Haigh, the first secretary, had announced an insourcing unit that promised to deliver on the pre-election pledge of “the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation”.
The PCS is questioning why the library is proposing to privatise reading rooms that are a vital resource for students and academics, among others.
On its website, the library notes a “huge demand in London for high-quality workspace”, while arguing that it is “running a financial deficit”. It says: “This year we expect to spend around £7m more than our total income … At the same time, research behaviours have changed. As online demand increases, in-person visits to our reading rooms have dropped.”
It estimates that the plans will affect about 20% of the more than 1,400 reading room desks across the St Pancras site, and that “the income generated by the new flexible business workspaces will make a vital contribution towards ensuring that our core library services – including reading room access – remain free to users”.
Charles Darwin is among famous scientists who have used the British Library, whether in its previous home in Bloomsbury or its current site in St Pancras. Marro said that these scientists would be turning in their graves over the latest plans, while today’s scientists would also be appalled as it was “already difficult to get a desk at the reading rooms”.
Marro added: “Any time I’m in the building, it’s hard to find a place to work. The library has pointed to falling use in the past five or 10 years, but that’s slightly disingenuous as there was a catastrophic security attack where they lost complete access to their systems and of course there was a drop in use when nobody could access it.
“The library has not stated that any jobs are at immediate risk of redundancy. However they have refused to rule out redundancies or a restructure in the future. It’s impossible to envision a situation in which they’re going to be closing reading rooms and losing hundreds of reader desks, without redundancies.”
Although the British Library’s chief executive, Paul Bate, announced the DCMS’s multimillion-pound refurbishment funding to dozens of staff members who attended a meeting last week, the DCMS yesterday denied that it has been allocated.
But documents seen by the Guardian include an internal slide from a British Library presentation delivered to staff, which states: “The cost of fitting out the space is £8m to £13m.”
Insiders said that the DCMS denial could mean that the funding simply had not been formally allocated yet.
The British Library declined to confirm the figures, initially suggesting that it does not recognise them. It said that its “commitment to science remains steadfast”, adding: “The new space will enable businesses, researchers, entrepreneurs and innovators to work and collaborate at the heart of London’s Knowledge Quarter, while generating income that can be reinvested in the library.”
STM has been contacted for comment.
summary: Exclusive: Guards told their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor that has rejected union recognition The British Library has sparked outrage over plans to outsource its security workforce and hand over to a private company three of its public reading rooms, to be “repurposed” as business spaces for hire – despite having reportedly received millions of pounds from the public purse to refurbish those spaces. Almost 70 guards have been told that their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor, STM, on 1 December. Their union, the PCS, has in turn been informed that STM has rejected union recognition for those staff. Continue reading...
title: British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces

body:
Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.
The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September, which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.
“Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS.
Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month-on-month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April.
Textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January.
The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month-on-month in October.
Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges.
However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose.
“October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal.
“Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season.
“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”
summary: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies Business live – latest updates Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency. Continue reading...
title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring

A woman who was drugged and raped by her husband and strangers he had invited to their family home has been praised for her bravery in exposing the crimes.
The judge in the case and women’s rights advocates said Joanne Young’s courage had been a feature of the trial. Her decision to waive her anonymity and attend court has drawn comparisons to Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged and raped by her husband as well as dozens of strangers in France. Waiving her right to anonymity, Pelicot said shame “must change sides”.
In a statement outside court on Thursday, Young said the convictions meant “that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward, and more likely to have faith in the criminal justice system”.
Saying that she now lived “with a pain that’s hard to put into words”, Young added: “Consent has to come from the person themselves. No one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed. At no point did anyone ask me for my consent. I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.”
All survivors of sexual abuse are granted automatic lifelong anonymity and only they are able to waive that right. Women’s rights activists appeared outside Winchester crown court for the trial of the men accused of sexually assaulting Young, brandishing banners such as “Shame must change sides” and “A drugged woman never consents”.
On Thursday, four men were convicted by jury of various sexual offences against Joanne Young. Her ex-husband, Philip Young, pleaded guilty in January to more than 50 offences, including raping and drugging his then wife.
Her daughter Alex has also now called for a change in the law on consent to make it clear that third-party consent cannot be used as an argument in a court of law.
She wrote on LinkedIn: “I am calling for the Sexual Offences Act 2003 to be looked at and updated. We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone. We live in a world where someone’s partner can consent for them, and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law. This is simply unacceptable.”
Jess Phillips, a former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, has suggested online safety laws should be updated to prevent these cases from happening in future.
The Labour MP for Birmingham Yardley told LBC: “The ability of these men to find each other on websites that you and I could just log on to now – it just means that these cases are going to keep on coming.”
After the verdicts on Thursday, women’s rights groups and others heaped praise on Joanne Young for her bravery. Farah Nazeer, the chief executive of Women’s Aid, said: “We stand in solidarity with Joanne Young – a woman of extraordinary bravery who has chosen to waive her right to anonymity when giving evidence against her former husband, who drugged her and invited other men to sexually assault her.
“Chemical coercion is a horrific crime, one that leaves women questioning their own sense of reality and sanity, just as the men they trust abuse them, coerce them and lie to them. The bravery of women like Joanne, and Gisèle Pelicot in France, have been fundamental in exposing this crime and the men that commit it.”
Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, praised Young’s “profoundly courageous” decision to waive her anonymity but emphasised that there was “no right or wrong way to react after rape or sexual abuse, just as there’s no right or wrong decision when it comes to reporting it”.
She said: “Survivors of sexual violence and abuse impress us with their courage in millions of ways, whether or not they report what happened to the police … For those who pursue criminal justice, as Joanne has done, reporting to the police and giving evidence in court can call for particular kinds of courage: the tenacity to see a case through to trial, to see the defendant and their supporters in court, and to speak about deeply painful experiences in graphic detail in a room full of strangers. And the strength to carry on with everyday life while waiting for an outcome they can’t control.”
Janaya Walker, a co-executive director of End Violence Against Women, said: “We extend our solidarity to Joanne Young, who has shown incredible courage in this case, including the difficult decision she has made to waive her anonymity. Whilst society may wish to think that such horrors are a total deviation from the norm, they demonstrate the horrifying reality that the greatest danger to women is often inside their own home.”
The Labour peer Thangam Debbonaire told the BBC’s Newsnight the statement outside court was “extraordinary”, adding: “ I feel really moved by her … She is an extraordinary example, and the fact that she has done what she has done, for women, and she said that so clearly, is really moving.”
Young briefly gave evidence in person at the trial, glancing occasionally towards the defendants in the dock. At one point, Mr Justice Saini asked her to keep her voice up. Much of her evidence was given in police interviews that were filmed and shown to the jury.
James Foster, a specialist prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service’s Wessex complex casework unit, said: “Joanne Young’s decision to waive her anonymity and attend this trial speaks volumes about her courage and resolve … she sat in court [and] listened to the most intimate and distressing details of what was done to her while she was drugged and unaware.”
Foster said waiving anonymity was an entirely personal decision with no right or wrong choice. He said he wanted to reassure the public that victims of sexual offences retained full entitlement to complete anonymity when reporting crimes.
summary: Woman who waived anonymity says she hopes her case will mean other victims of abuse are more likely to come forward A woman who was drugged and raped by her husband and strangers he had invited to their family home has been praised for her bravery in exposing the crimes. The judge in the case and women’s rights advocates said Joanne Young’s courage had been a feature of the trial. Her decision to waive her anonymity and attend court has drawn comparisons to Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged and raped by her husband as well as dozens of strangers in France. Waiving her right to anonymity, Pelicot said shame “must change sides”. Continue reading...
title: Joanne Young praised for bravery in exposing rape by husband and strangers

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.
In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts.
Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly.
“However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.”
The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October - £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997.
Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs.
Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s.
Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran.
“This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added.
Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend.
In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war.
Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs.
After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year.
Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.
Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.
Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.
Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”
summary: UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn. Continue reading...
title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex, with a goal to end all incarceration at the current facility and relocate its remaining jail population by the end of 2032.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane. This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprive people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146m in the evidence-based supports that helps break the cycles of incarceration.”
Described by Mamdani’s administration as “the city’s first comprehensive plan to close Rikers Island”,it comes as the city faces a legally mandated deadline to close the facility by August 2027.
That deadline was established under legislation passed by the city council in 2019 and signed into law by then mayor Bill de Blasio. The legislation called for Rikers to be replaced by four borough-based smaller, modern jail facilities located in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Manhattan.
However, the city is not on track to meet the August 2027 deadline, with construction behind schedule, and an increase in the city’s jail population since 2020, which has raised concerns about the city’s ability to reduce its population enough to accommodate the capacity of the four new facilities. The four facilities are expected to have about 4,500 beds, while roughly 6,600 people remain held in jails on Rikers Island as of early November.
Mamdani’s plan states that the Brooklyn facility is on track to open in 2029, followed by the Bronx and Queens facilities in 2031, and the Manhattan facility in 2032. It also states that his administration hopes to bring the 6,600 number down to no more than 4,100 people by the end of 2032, with a population of no more than 5,500 at the time of the Brooklyn Facility’s opening in 2029.
In a news release on Friday, the mayor’s office said the plan also includes the creation of hundreds of therapeutic beds “for New Yorkers with serious mental health conditions and complex medical needs”; and an investment of $146m from the city next fiscal year toward “mental health care, substance use treatment, educational and vocational programming both inside jails and in communities as well as victim services”.
As part of the proposal, the city will also work to reduce pretrial detention and case delays, modernize the department of correction, “and plan for the future reuse of the island”, per the release.
In the plan document, it states that Mamdani’s administration will “work closely with City Council on legislation to bring this plan into law, as well as the Remediation manager, federal monitor and the Board of Correction”.
The Mamdani administration cannot unilaterally decree a new legal closure date, it will require the city council to pass a new law extending the deadline, per Politico,
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Working alongside the City Council, Courts and nonprofit partners, we will meet it – for the people in our custody, the staff who serve them, victims of crime, and every New Yorker.”
The Rikers Island complex has, for years, faced criticism over the conditions of the jails, the infrastructure, staffing challenges and reports of violence and deaths. The conditions have drawn sustained scrutiny from civil rights advocates, local lawmakers and more.
Last year, under former mayor Eric Adams, a federal judge moved Rikers Island out of the city’s direct control, and placed it under the authority of an outside official who was tasked with making the decisions affecting the jail facility. That official was appointed this January. In the plan on Friday, Mamdani’s administration said it would work with the federal monitor, as well as councillors and more, to “bring this plan into law”.
In a Friday statement, city council speaker Julie Menin said “delays under previous administrations have made it clear that more time is needed to fulfill the commitment the City Council made to New Yorkers in 2019 when we legislated closing Rikers Island”.
“With Rikers now under federal court-ordered oversight, we must bring this troubling chapter in our city’s history to an end once and for all” she said.
The proposal shared on Friday includes plans to restructure and modernize the department of correction, aimed at ensuring that “the operational challenges faced at Rikers Island are not transferred to the new facilities” per the report shared with press. It includes plans to “optimize jail staffing”, modernize data collection systems, improve processes for investigating, addressing and disciplining misconduct, and more.
The plan also proposes the administration invest $50m next fiscal year to “expand access to vocational training, educational programming, mental health counseling, substance use services and other supports”.
The news release states that the proposal includes plans for the city to restore its online bail payment portal in 2027, which it says has been unavailable since 2023. According to the news release, the city will also invest an additional $76m next fiscal year in “community-based services for New Yorkers” such as expanding access to “reentry services and community diversion programs, such as supportive housing”.
The plan also includes investment of $16m in support services for crime victims and survivors, to “expand access to mental health care and legal services”.
The lengthy proposal also discusses the planning “for the Future Reuse of Rikers Island” and said that the administration is “exploring near-term renewable energy and sustainability projects for Rikers Island”.
Since taking office, Mamdani has emphasized his administration’s commitment to closing the complex. He appointed a “Close Rikers Czar” and selected Stanley Richards to lead the city’s department of correction, making Richards the first formerly incarcerated person to head the department.
In June, Mamdani also announced the closure of North Infirmary Command, a facility at Rikers that first opened in 1932 and was described by the administration as a “vacant jail”. Officials said the facility was not housing people in custody, and it was transferred to the department of citywide administrative services, along with large portions of two other centers.
“This report is only the beginning,” the proposal unveiled on Friday states. “We are committed to demonstrating progress transparently and frequently, through quarterly updates.
“Together, these steps will result in the closure of Rikers Island, once and for all.”
summary: Mayor plans to close jail by 2032 and relocate its remaining population to smaller facilities across four boroughs Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex, with a goal to end all incarceration at the current facility and relocate its remaining jail population by the end of 2032. “It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane. This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprive people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146m in the evidence-based supports that helps break the cycles of incarceration.” Continue reading...
title: Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close Rikers Island jail complex
